items.text: Plan capacity on the basis that one video brief yields about three videos; in one weekend an {editor} turned five briefs into 15 new videos.
items.why: It shows what an editor can deliver.
items.when: planning video ad output per editor

items.title: Give outside reviewers an artifact
items.text: Send outside reviewers such as {creator}s a simple page with pictures and approve or notes buttons, translated into their language if needed, so they never have to use the tools. In one case English-to-Thai translation worked well.
items.why: They do not have to use the tools. English to Thai works well.
items.when: getting approvals from creators or partners outside the team

items.title: Ask creators for video clips, not photos
items.text: Ask {creator}s for video clips of themselves from different angles rather than photos. Video gives the angles and motion an AI system needs.
items.why: Video has the angles and motion the system needs.
items.when: collecting creator references for AI generation

items.title: Edit without Premiere
items.text: Instead of paid editing software, have an AI assistant line up clips with the voiceover and cut on the beats on your own computer while you direct the changes. It is faster, needs no paid software and can be directed from a phone.
items.why: It is faster, needs no paid software, and can be directed even from a phone.

items.title: Batch many briefs or videos in one run
items.text: Ask the AI to do a batch, such as six briefs, in one go and let it run unwatched. A batch can finish in hours with no babysitting.
items.why: A batch can finish in hours with no babysitting.

items.title: Skip briefs that carry too much slop
items.text: If a brief comes out with heavy flaws and would take a long time to fix, skip it and move to the next one. Time is better spent on briefs that finish cleanly.
items.why: Time is better spent on briefs that finish cleanly.

items.title: Mark every brief section clearly
items.text: Label every part of a brief with its section and the exact words used, so the AI can swap one part at a time. Clear sections let headlines or hooks change without rewriting the brief.
items.why: Clear sections let headlines or hooks change without rewriting the brief.

items.title: Make variations from a winner by awareness level
items.text: Take the brief of a performing ad and generate new variations across awareness levels, with new headlines and scroll stoppers. Variations of a proven ad are likelier to win than starting fresh, and the system does it without hand edits.
items.why: Variations of a proven ad are likelier to win than starting fresh, and it no longer needs hand edits.

items.title: Program the edit style into reusable rules
items.text: Write the edit style (transitions, timing, motion, camera moves) down once as reusable rules so an edit can be triggered rather than rebuilt. The same look becomes repeatable and nothing gets remade.
items.why: The same look is repeatable and nothing gets remade.

items.title: Share fixes back through the shared repo
items.text: When you find a fix, push it to the shared repository and tell the {founder} and team to pull it, so everyone gets it. Both sides can push updates back and forth without rebuilding.
items.why: Both sides can push updates back and forth without rebuilding.
items.when: teams sharing AI tools and prompts

items.title: Use plan mode only for big jobs
items.text: Use the AI's planning mode only for big jobs that need mapping out, and auto mode for normal work. Auto just does things; plan maps them first.
items.why: Auto just does things; plan maps them first.

items.title: Match the model to the job
items.text: Match the AI model to the job: a light model to fetch, a mid model for daily tasks, and the top model only when it needs to think. Smarter models cost more usage.
items.why: The smarter models cost more usage.
items.when: running AI workflows on a usage budget

items.title: The repo is the memory
items.text: The AI has no memory, so keep everything in a shared repository; when a session fills up, start a new one. The repository carries the information between sessions.
items.why: The repo carries the information between sessions.

items.title: Say you are not technical
items.text: Tell the AI you are not technical and ask it to explain simply and do the work itself. It can handle the technical steps.
items.why: It handles the technical steps.

items.title: Ask for an action-item artifact
items.text: Ask the AI for a visual page showing who you are speaking with, what they want, and the action items. It turns a pile of messages into one view.
items.why: It turns a pile of messages into one view.

items.title: Pull, then start a new session to use new skills
items.text: After pulling the latest shared tools, open a new AI session before using a newly added skill. A running session does not see skills added after it started.
items.why: A running session does not see skills added after it started.
items.when: teams sharing AI skills through a repository

items.title: Run mini compare after changing a component
items.text: After editing a component, compare it against the copy on the always-on worker machine to see whether that copy is outdated. The worker copy is a snapshot from the last migration.
items.why: The mini copy is a snapshot from when it was last migrated.
items.when: teams running tools on a shared background worker machine

items.title: Use the feed to find swipes by keyword
items.text: Give the team a feed where anyone can type a keyword and pull matching content for swipes. Anyone can feed ideas in without knowing the tools.
items.why: Anyone can feed ideas in without knowing the tools.

items.title: Rewrite machine scripts to sound natural
items.text: Read each machine-written script aloud and rewrite lines that sound stiff; the chain's structure is right but the wording can be off. AI is not perfect at conversational copy.
items.why: The tool is not perfect at conversational copy.

items.title: Pull real B-roll through the asset index; render separately
items.text: Use an index of owned footage to add real B-roll or fix choppy cuts in the timeline, and remember a timeline is not a finished video until it is rendered. Real footage helps credibility, and rendering is a separate step.
items.why: Real footage helps credibility and the render step is separate.
items.when: video editing with owned footage libraries

items.title: Judge ads on clean funnel orders only
items.text: Judge ads on funnel orders from cold new customers only, not storefront sales, to see which ad drives purchases. Mixing storefront sales muddies attribution.
items.why: Mixing storefront sales muddies attribution.
items.when: ad performance review with a dedicated ad funnel

items.title: Compare CPA to a break-even set by the offer
items.text: Compare each ad's CPA to the break-even CPA the {offer} allows, over a window such as 14 days. An ad can only be judged against what the offer can afford.
items.why: An ad can only be judged against what the offer can afford.

items.title: Line up ad elements on one approval board
items.text: Put the content, headlines, primary text, description and landing page for each ad on one approval board and approve there before pushing to the ad platform. You see the whole ad at once.
items.why: You see the whole ad at once.
items.when: approving paid social ads before upload

items.title: Plan the email calendar two weeks ahead
items.text: Generate the email calendar two weeks ahead, mark each email sent or scheduled, and add creative one-offs such as a holiday email. Proactive planning leaves room for new data and fun ideas.
items.why: Proactive planning leaves room for new data and fun ideas.

items.title: Keep creator delivery on one platform
items.text: For one {brand}'s {creator}s, all video delivery runs through a single creator platform only. One path is simpler to manage.
items.why: One path is simpler to manage.

items.title: Let organic content and SEO compound
items.text: Treat organic social as repurposed content and keep publishing blogs so brand searches find them. Content published now keeps working and compounds over time.
items.why: Content published now keeps working over time.

items.title: Send big teardown batches to the mini
items.text: Do not run large teardown batches (20 or more videos) on your working computer; send them to a background machine in batches of about five. Local batches slow down your working session.
items.why: Local batches slow down your working session.
items.when: large AI teardown or processing jobs

items.title: Rank a competitor's ads by how many times they are duplicated
items.text: Index a competitor's top creatives and sort them by how many times each ad is duplicated, then pick which to tear down. The ads a brand duplicates most are likely its winners.
items.why: Ads a brand duplicates most are likely winners.
items.when: competitor ad research on paid social

items.title: Run the video chain in order, reviewing between stages
items.text: Run the video process in order with a review between stages: teardowns, then writing, review, then production, then edit. Each stage needs the previous stage's approved output.
items.why: Each stage needs the previous stage's approved output.

items.title: Run live instead of a dry run
items.text: Skip the dry run and do the live run when it checks the same thing; a real run also doubles as the test and gives a real result.
items.why: A real run also doubles as the test.

items.title: Do not build a dashboard before you use the process
items.text: Do not build a dashboard before you actually use the process; focus on what is used this week, and sometimes a quick visual page beats a dashboard. A dashboard for many people takes weeks, and unused ones waste effort.
items.why: A dashboard for many people takes weeks, and unused ones waste effort.

items.title: The mini cannot see your Drive folder
items.text: A tool that looks for a locally mounted shared drive will fail on a background server; make it fall back to the storage provider's API. The local mount exists only on one person's machine.
items.why: Your Drive folder exists only on your machine.
items.when: moving tools onto shared or remote machines

items.title: Approve images before the timeline is built
items.text: Check and approve generated images before the video timeline is built; nothing downstream should run on an unapproved kit. Unapproved clips block later steps and create backlogs.
items.why: Unapproved clips block later steps and create backlogs.

items.title: Put required photos where the mini can reach them
items.text: Keep required assets, such as the {hero product} pack shot, in a clear shared location the automated runner can reach. A run fails if a needed photo is missing.
items.why: A run fails if a needed photo is missing.

items.title: Make hidden steps explicit so others can run the chain
items.text: Write down the steps your own AI assistant assumes, such as approvals and brief IDs, so teammates and background machines can run the chain. Your assistant knows how the chain links; nobody else does.
items.why: Your Claude knows how the chain links; the mini and teammates do not.
items.when: handing an AI workflow to others

items.title: Run everything you will use and learn from failures
items.text: Run each component you expect to use on the shared machine now and read why it breaks. Failures tell you what to fix before you depend on it.
items.why: Failures tell you what to fix before you depend on it.

items.title: Production quality decides how easy editing is
items.text: Spend effort on scene production quality; once the scenes are laid out, editing is straightforward. Editing cannot fix weak scenes.
items.why: Editing cannot fix weak scenes.

items.title: Connect ad data to the P&L for media buying
items.text: Join ad results with P&L figures when reviewing performance and planning media buying. Ad results alone do not show whether you actually make money.
items.why: Ad results alone do not show if you actually make money.

items.title: Watch the Drive item limit
items.text: Remember that each shared cloud-drive folder has an item limit (500,000 items in the example) and trashed files count toward it. Hitting the limit slows scans and blocks uploads.
items.why: Hitting the limit slows scans and blocks uploads.
items.when: storing large asset libraries in shared cloud drives

items.title: Fix only what blocks this week output
items.text: Ask what must ship this week, such as video ads, and fix only what blocks that. Fixing everything delays real output.
items.why: Fixing everything delays real output.

items.title: Confirm files really come from the shared Drive
items.text: Check that every script reads from the shared drive, not a local copy on one computer. A script that finds a local copy works for one person but fails for everyone else and for background machines.
items.why: A script that finds a local copy works for you but fails for everyone else and for the mini machine.

items.title: Expect Claude to take the easy path
items.text: When a tool works only for you, check where it reads files from, because the AI may have taken a local shortcut. The shortcut hides missing assets until someone else runs it.
items.why: The shortcut hides missing assets until someone else runs it.
items.when: AI-built tools used by a team

items.title: Make approvals visible to the team
items.text: Put approvals in a shared place others can see, not on one personal computer. If approvals live on one machine nobody else can help.
items.why: If approvals live on one machine nobody else can help.

items.title: Trace the file flow first, then debug
items.text: Before debugging, write out exactly which folder each step reads and writes and what the next step expects. Most breaks are a missing folder or key file.
items.why: Most breaks are a missing folder or key file.

items.title: Plan for the review time AI output creates
items.text: Decide who approves AI output so the review load does not all land on one person. More AI output means more review time and mental load.
items.why: More AI output means more review time and mental load.

items.title: Debug the earlier steps first
items.text: Debug the earlier steps of a chain first, then production, then editing. A broken early step spoils every later step.
items.why: A broken early step spoils every later step.

items.title: Try new layout with finished creative assets
items.text: If an email layout looks too basic, reuse the finished creative assets in a new layout rather than recreating them. The email looks better without new asset work.
items.why: The email looks better without recreating the assets.

items.title: Strip Claude's default context for machine runs
items.text: For automated chain runs, strip out the AI tool's default instructions at every step. In one email run this cut token use by about half or more, and default context can also change results.
items.why: Every step reloads the default context, which costs a lot and can change results.

items.title: Do not batch overnight runs while debugging
items.text: While a chain is still being debugged, run it during the day when someone can watch, rather than queueing a night of runs. One random failure can mean nothing gets done.
items.why: One random failure can mean nothing gets done.

items.title: Keep creative feedback loops in the ad account manual
items.text: Keep the creative feedback loop manual: review ads in the account yourself, give feedback on the creatives and refine. AI cannot do that judgment yet, and the judgment is what makes an ad good.
items.why: The judgment is what makes an ad good.

items.title: Compare two runs for 'obviously worse', not 'different'
items.text: When comparing two runs of the same chain, ask only whether one is obviously worse, not whether it is different. AI output varies between runs even with the same prompt.
items.why: AI output varies between runs even with the same prompt.

items.title: Keep chain results independent of anyone's personal settings
items.text: Make chain runs independent of any person's own AI settings so anyone gets the same result. Different personal settings can change the output.
items.why: Different personal settings can change the output.
items.when: shared AI chains run by multiple people

items.title: Read a creator agreement for what you agree to
items.text: Before using a {creator} agreement, read it (or have the AI summarize it) in plain terms for what you are actually agreeing to. Once signed, it is a real agreement about what you expect from them.
items.why: If you sign it, it is a real agreement about what you expect from them.

items.title: Change the layout of a view, not the data
items.text: Let each person customize how a shared page looks, but never change the data or hide data with a function. The page keeps doing its job for everyone.
items.why: The page keeps doing its job for everyone.

items.title: New teammates only use Claude Code to edit artifacts
items.text: For new non-technical teammates such as designers, set up the AI tool only to adjust their own pages and give feedback, and skip repositories and component-building. They are not blocked by tools they do not need.
items.why: They are not blocked by tools they do not need.
items.when: onboarding non-technical teammates to AI tools

items.title: Do not write to two output folders
items.text: Make each tool write to only one output folder, and remove the old folder after checking no one uses it. In one case a tool wrote to two folders for a long time and created hundreds of thousands of duplicates.
items.why: Teardown wrote to both for a long time and created hundreds of thousands of duplicates.

items.title: Change one funnel element at a time and log each conversion rate
items.text: After launching a page, ship small revisions one at a time (headline, FAQ, layout) and log the offer-page-to-checkout rate for each. In one case the rate went 7% to 11% to 10% over two weeks; small stacked tweaks show which change moved the number, big rebuilds do not.
items.why: Small stacked tweaks tell you which change moved the number; big rebuilds don't.

items.title: Know your break-even CPA from product cost before buying traffic
items.text: Work out break-even CPA from product cost and what each order contributes, and give that number to whoever buys traffic. If a stock-out removes the upsell that props up AOV, break-even drops and the affordable CPA falls.
items.why: If the upsell that lifts AOV disappears, the CPA you can afford drops.
items.when: before and during paid traffic buying

items.title: Build a no-brainer offer: bonus item plus free portal
items.text: Stack a no-brainer {offer}: real before-and-afters, a free bonus item, and a free customer portal where buyers unlock store credit by sharing results. Cold traffic needs a reason to say yes now, and the extras make the {hero product} feel like a bargain.
items.why: Cold traffic needs a reason to say yes now; the extras make the main product feel like a bargain.

items.title: Post-purchase upsells lift AOV; watch which one carries it
items.text: Track what share of buyers take each post-purchase upsell (in one funnel about 18-19% took the main add-on and about 10% the secondary one), and add more upsells to hold AOV if the main one goes out of stock. One upsell often carries average order value, and losing it changes the economics.
items.why: One upsell often carries the average order value; losing it changes the economics.

items.title: Don't load cold-traffic checkout pages with trust info
items.text: Keep checkout simple for cold traffic: guarantee, payment options, done. In one test adding an FAQ and a business-story section to checkout dropped checkout conversion from 15% to 5%, because cold traffic is not warm traffic and extra reading adds friction.
items.why: Cold traffic is not warm traffic at checkout; extra reading adds friction.
items.when: checkout pages receiving cold paid traffic

items.title: Judge an order bump by AOV gain versus conversion loss
items.text: Judge an order bump by AOV gain against conversion loss, comparing checkout versions side by side. In one test a bump for an accessory took AOV from $65 to $73 with only a small conversion dip, so it was kept; higher AOV can more than pay for a small dip and sells through more of the add-on.
items.why: Higher AOV can more than pay for a small conversion dip, and it also sells through more of the add-on product.

items.title: Offer a bigger supply as a bump and roll it into every upsell
items.text: Offer a bigger supply (for example 75-day or 150-day) as a bump, and when it wins, copy the same structure onto every other upsell. In one funnel it raised both conversion and AOV, and the secondary upsell converted at 34%; supply length also sets usage expectations.
items.why: A win in one place is a pattern to reuse; supply length also sets product usage expectations.
items.when: consumable products with bumps and upsells

items.title: Talk to real customers; the line that clicks beats the problem language
items.text: Talk to real customers and find the simple comparison that makes the mechanism click; that line beats problem language. In one case buyers ignored problem talk, but describing the {hero product} as 'a toothbrush for your face' made it click and the person bought.
items.why: The simplest comparison that makes the mechanism click is the angle.

items.title: Test top-of-funnel headline: problem-aware vs mechanism
items.text: Test the top-of-funnel headline with the same {offer}: one page with a problem-aware headline against one that leads with the mechanism or a vivid comparison. Different traffic temperatures respond to different entry points.
items.why: Different traffic temperatures respond to different entry points.

items.title: Log every test in a keep-or-kill database
items.text: Log every funnel test and its result in a simple database with one criterion: keep it or kill it. Learnings are not lost and the team can refer back.
items.why: So learnings aren't lost and the team can refer back.

items.title: Auto opt-in at checkout feeds the email list
items.text: Collect first name, last name and email at checkout with auto opt-in so every visitor who starts checkout lands on the email list, then work that list hard. Cold traffic is expensive, and the lead list lets you recover it.
items.why: Cold traffic is expensive; the lead list lets you recover it.
items.when: DTC funnels with paid cold traffic

items.title: Click through your own funnel as the customer and fix language that doesn't fit
items.text: Click through your own funnel as the {avatar} and fix any add-on copy that does not fit why they would actually want it. In one case travel-focused language for an accessory did not match the buyer, so it was reframed around hygiene.
items.why: Add-on copy must match why the buyer would actually want it.
items.when: funnel copy review, especially bumps and upsells

items.title: AI-generated headlines still need a stop-the-scroll test
items.text: Give AI the customer's own words before it writes headlines, and check every headline for whether it actually stops the scroll. AI with no context writes generic lines that are statements, not headlines.
items.why: AI with no context writes generic lines.
items.when: AI-written headlines for ads and pages

items.title: Build funnel pages out of the customer's exact words and results
items.text: Build funnel headlines from customers' exact words, beliefs and results, and show a wall of before-and-afters across ages and skin tones so every viewer sees someone like them. Proof that looks like the viewer is what persuades.
items.why: Proof that looks like the viewer is what persuades.

items.title: Turn photo and video reviews into customer profiles and hooks
items.text: Index every review with photos or video, match it to what the person bought and their feedback answers, then build customer profiles (age, skin tone, awareness stage, story) and hooks in their voice. Real customers' words are the best raw material for ads and emails.
items.why: Real customers' words are the best raw material for ads and emails.

items.title: Estimate awareness stage from how deeply a reviewer describes the problem
items.text: Tag each customer's awareness stage from how they describe their problem and how experienced they already are in the category. Awareness stage decides what kind of ad speaks to them.
items.why: Awareness stage decides what kind of ad speaks to them.

items.title: Allocate creative effort by customer mix, and ask if the current avatar is maxed out
items.text: Break customers down by demographics (such as age and skin tone) and put creative production in proportion to who actually buys. Before testing a new {avatar}, ask whether the current one is truly maxed out; usually it is not.
items.why: Don't spread across avatars when the main one still has room.

items.title: Get customers on calls and run interviews to find new audiences
items.text: To open a new audience, find a few existing customers from that group, interview them on recorded calls, and make content from exactly what they say. Amplified word of mouth beats guessing.
items.why: Amplified word of mouth beats guessing.
items.when: expanding into a new customer segment

items.title: Lean into the simple ad that is working instead of overthinking
items.text: When a simple ad is working (in one case just the {hero product} compared to a dirty rag), stop second-guessing it and make variations of it. Variations of something simple that works are the safest next ads.
items.why: If something simple works, variations of it are the safest next ads.

items.title: Take yourself out of the ads so they can scale
items.text: Take the {founder} out of the ads if their presence is a liability or a bottleneck, and switch to statics and other {creator}s. In one case the best returns came from ads with nobody from the team in them, and creative that depends on one person cannot be made at volume.
items.why: Creative that depends on one person can't be produced at volume.
items.when: founder-led brands trying to scale creative

items.title: Wait a few days, then cut the bad ads and iterate on the rest
items.text: On a new test, let ads run a few days, then cut the clear losers and move the survivors through iteration cycles; never call a winner off one sale. Early data is thin, so cutting or scaling too soon both waste money.
items.why: Early data is thin; cutting too soon or scaling too soon both waste money.
items.when: new ad tests on paid social

items.title: Supplement angles: speak to the belief the buyer already holds
items.text: For a supplement, line up the buyer's existing habits and beliefs (in one case: already taking supplements, believing the problem is internal, fearing a prescription drug's side effects) and present the alternative rather than educating. The buyer has already done the education.
items.why: The buyer has done the education; you just present the alternative.

items.title: Read CPC and CTR first, then conversion
items.text: Read CPC and CTR first, then conversion: low CPC and high CTR (86-cent CPC in one test) mean the market wants the product and the remaining problem is after the click, which is fixable. Ads at normal AOV and over 2x ROAS are promising but not yet proven for scale.
items.why: Low CPC and high CTR mean attention is working; the fix lives after the click.
items.when: reading early results on a new product

items.title: Turn winning statics into video briefs by bridging organic hooks
items.text: Turn a winning static into video briefs by searching short-form video for content on the same problem with reach but few likes, and bridging those hooks and formats to your {hero product}. A proven message plus a proven organic format makes a safe brief.
items.why: A proven message plus a proven organic format is a safe brief.
items.when: expanding a winning static into video

items.title: Make ads, not organic; focus on product, problem, value props, angles
items.text: Stop trying to make polished organic content; make every piece an ad built on product, problem, value prop and angle. Ads can be measured and scaled; polished organic cannot.
items.why: Ads can be measured and scaled; polished organic can't.
items.when: small teams choosing what content to produce

items.title: Use a humor scroll-stopper that plays on the main objection
items.text: Make a humorous scroll stopper that plays on the {avatar}'s biggest objection, built from a winning straight ad with a shocking opener. In one case the person's face was rendered oily and dripping with the caption 'this made my skin too smooth', mocking the fear of greasy skin.
items.why: Guys relate to humor and the shocking opener stops the scroll.

items.title: Make hook variations from a winning creator ad
items.text: Make hook variations from a winning {creator} ad by screenshotting the creator, removing the text, and animating them with an AI video model or stitching them onto other clips. The body of the proven ad stays; only the opener changes.
items.why: The body of a proven ad stays; only the opener changes.

items.title: Read the new-product test: CTR double, CPC half means more room
items.text: Compare new products on CTR and CPC: in one 7-day test one product had more than double the CTR and half the CPC of another, showing more market appetite. High cost per add-to-cart (a $43 cost per purchase on a $47 AOV in that case) means optimize the page, not the ad.
items.why: 85-cent CPC means attention is there; conversion is the gap.
items.when: testing new products on paid social

items.title: Define sprints with detail and velocity: pick winners, script video versions
items.text: Define sprints in detail: find the ads that drove sales, write video scripts for those winners and use AI to produce them until real {creator}s are in place. Break sprints by product, then by creative type around each product.
items.why: Winners in one format become the brief for the next format.

items.title: Keep ideas to a fixed list and target four videos a day
items.text: Keep ideas to a fixed weekly list and pick one narrow repeatable format (such as AI voice plus B-roll) to raise output, in one case from two to four videos a day, stacking learnings week to week. Volume comes from a narrow, repeatable format.
items.why: Volume comes from a narrow, repeatable format.

items.title: Execution beats research: pick two to three concepts a week
items.text: Execution beats research: choose about three concepts a week (around twelve a month), roughly three variations each, each with matching statics, instead of saving and making every swipe. The ad account fills with tested ideas rather than a backlog.
items.why: The ad account fills with tested ideas, not a backlog of ideas.

items.title: A brief crystallizes a vision; it's not a rigid rule
items.text: A brief shares the vision; it is not a rigid rule. A video is not bad just because the {editor} did not follow the brief word for word, and rigid briefs kill the creativity that makes video engaging.
items.why: Rigid briefs kill the creativity that makes a video engaging.

items.title: Bucket your footage so you can check if you already have the assets
items.text: Sort footage into buckets (B-roll, before-and-afters, behind the scenes, routines, who is in it, best versus worst), and after a video breakdown check scene by scene whether you already have each asset. You can only build fast if you know what you have.
items.why: You can only build fast if you know what you have.

items.title: Make a matching static for each video concept
items.text: For each video concept, have AI extract scenes from the video's breakdown into matching statics, so videos and images carry the same message. It fills the ad library without diluting the message and shows which angle wins.
items.why: Same message in two formats keeps testing clean.

items.title: When an ad wins, test what the comparison is against
items.text: When an ad that compares the {hero product} against something wins, test what it is compared against (in one case a dirty towel, then bar soap, a loofah and a razor). The comparison object changes who the ad speaks to.
items.why: Which thing you compare against changes who the ad speaks to.

items.title: Make the variation weird enough to be a scroll stopper
items.text: Make a variation weird enough to be a scroll stopper rather than a generic one. In one case a presenter's face was made glossy, animated dripping oil, with the original audio on top; a strange variation earns attention, a generic one does not.
items.why: A generic variation doesn't earn attention; a strange one does.

items.title: Spot the core hook in competitor ads and then differentiate
items.text: Find the core hook the market shares in competitor ads and reviews (for example 'everything else I tried didn't work until I used this'), use it, then differentiate with what the {brand} owns (origin, specific ingredients, what it leaves out, gentleness, scent). The hook belongs to the market; the difference is yours.
items.why: The hook is shared by the market; the difference is what you own.

items.title: Treat swiped ads as free market research
items.text: Treat swiped ads as free market research: extract the high-level concepts from top-performing content and turn them into short or mid-form clips that can be bolted onto long form. Someone else already paid to test it.
items.why: Someone else already paid to test it.

items.title: Offer ads are the easiest bottom-funnel ads: headline, product, 2-3 value props
items.text: For a holiday or sale, make an offer static with the {offer} as headline, the {hero product} image, two or three value props and a close, plus a lifestyle flat-lay with a banner as a second version. Offer ads are fast and give you a bottom-funnel baseline while research continues.
items.why: They're fast to make and give you a baseline running while research continues.
items.when: sales and holiday promotions on paid social

items.title: Research on TikTok by typing the problem and reading what people say
items.text: Research on short-form video platforms by typing in the problem or product and studying the comments, likes, scroll stoppers, hooks and flow; learn from them but do not copy directly or you look like everyone else.
items.why: You learn the language, the hook structure and what the market responds to.

items.title: Find the shared lead ingredient in the swipes and lean in
items.text: Across many swipes, find the lead ingredient the market keeps mentioning (turmeric in one case) and lead with that ingredient plus the body part, keeping the rest about how it works. The market already believes in it, so do not re-educate.
items.why: The market already believes in it; don't re-educate.

items.title: Write one angle across awareness levels: solution, product, ingredient
items.text: Write one angle across awareness levels: for solution-aware, address their fears (such as bleaching); for product-aware, show what other similar products exist and what makes the {hero product} different; for ingredient-aware, speak directly to the ingredient. The same offer needs a different message at each stage.
items.why: Same offer needs a different message at each awareness stage.

items.title: Piggyback on a trend: Thai skincare as the natural alternative to Korean
items.text: Piggyback on an existing trend by positioning the {brand} as its alternative; in one case a product from a less-known origin was framed as the natural alternative to a hugely popular origin seen as chemical. It borrows awareness that already exists.
items.why: It borrows awareness that already exists.
items.when: positioning in a category with a dominant trend

items.title: Have the team do the reps themselves before hiring editors
items.text: Have team members who are close to the market make the ads themselves in a simple editor, with briefs and refinement from the {founder}, before hiring {editor}s. Doing the reps first teaches what the briefs need.
items.why: Doing the reps first teaches what the briefs need.

items.title: A campaign is just a business objective: what, who, how
items.text: A campaign is one business objective: what you sell, who you sell to, and how. Put different formats of the same message in the same campaign; the ad platform rewards simplification, and splitting budget across campaigns for the same objective wastes spend.
items.why: Meta rewards simplification; splitting budget across campaigns for the same objective wastes spend.

items.title: Read frequency to tell top-of-funnel from bottom-of-funnel ads
items.text: Read frequency to tell top-of-funnel from bottom-of-funnel ads: 1.05 means about 5% saw the ad twice (top of funnel), while 1.6 means about 60% did (bottom funnel). Then check CPM for reach cost and CPA for acquisition cost, since an ad's position tells you what job it does.
items.why: Where an ad sits tells you what job it is doing and how to judge it.

items.title: One campaign shows which ad, angle and format gets the spend
items.text: Keep ads for one objective in one campaign so the platform sends budget to the winner and you can see which angle and format drove conversions. Split campaigns hide that and draw spend inefficiently.
items.why: You learn from where the algorithm puts the money.

items.title: Only turn ads off when clearly out of KPI over time; new ads must beat the old
items.text: Only turn ads off when they are clearly out of KPI over time, consolidate, and let data build a library of angles and formats. Every new creative's goal is to beat the previous best, which tells you what to make next.
items.why: That is how you prioritize what to make next.

items.title: Set the performance goal to maximize conversions, not conversion value
items.text: Set the Meta performance goal to maximize number of conversions, not value of conversions, and raise value through LTV on the back end. In one case a duplicated ad set silently carried 'maximize value', which made the platform hunt high spenders and raised CPA, so check settings after duplicating.
items.why: Check settings after duplicating; a hidden setting caused the bad CPA.
items.when: Meta ad set setup and duplication

items.title: CPA is a function of conversion rate and traffic quality
items.text: CPA is a function of conversion rate and traffic quality: when CPA is bad, check the landing page and mixed tests before blaming the ad. Consolidate, keep one message, tighten the landing page, and use better hooks to raise CTR and lower CPC and CPA.
items.why: Don't blame the ad if the page or offer isn't converting.

items.title: Use a flexible ad with 3-6 creatives, 2 texts, 2 headlines
items.text: Use a flexible ad format with 3 to 6 creatives, 2 primary texts, 2 headlines, 1-2 descriptions and one URL instead of one ad per variation. It keeps every variant of a concept in a single ad.
items.why: It keeps all variants of one concept in a single ad.

items.title: Name ads so the problem, format and creator are readable
items.text: Name each ad by problem, archetype or format, and creator or message, and keep a creative tracking sheet that makes each ad's thesis clear. Learnings can then be reviewed later.
items.why: So learnings can be reviewed later.

items.title: Find an angle from a trend video: 'if you're dark, it's probably not your serum'
items.text: Search seasonal topics on short-form video to find angles beside the {brand}'s main claim; in one case a summer glow routine video revealed an angle positioning the product as a natural glow for a specific skin type. Seasonal behaviors can open a distinct position.
items.why: Seasonal behaviors can open a distinct position beside the brand's main claim.

items.title: Feed AI the video, its transcript and top comments to write copy
items.text: To write ad copy, give AI the swipe video and its transcript for a breakdown, then feed that breakdown plus the video's top comments into a writing model and ask for natural-language body copy. Comments and transcripts give real language to borrow.
items.why: Comments and transcript give real language to borrow.

items.title: Treat AI copy as 80% done, then edit for human voice
items.text: Treat AI copy as 80% done: remove dashes, shorten it to feel like a real caption, ask for three detailed variations, read them aloud, and cut anything generic or common knowledge by asking 'would a human actually say that?' AI writes the base; you remove what sounds like AI.
items.why: AI writes the base; you remove what sounds like AI.

items.title: Make copy specific to the viewer's real experience
items.text: Make copy specific to experiences the {avatar} actually has, so the {hero product} sits in their life; drop lines that are not relevant to them. Use the core ingredient list, and keep the hard selling on the page, not in the ad.
items.why: Specific scenes make copy believable.

items.title: Open with a curiosity hook then shift to what the product did to the routine
items.text: Open with a curiosity hook (for example 'I need to talk about this because I've been keeping it to myself'), then the product, how it works and what it changed in the routine, then the call to action. Curiosity opens; product benefit comes second.
items.why: Curiosity opens; product benefit comes second.

items.title: Copy the format, not the product: scroll stoppers, CTAs, storylines
items.text: Copy the format, not the product: competitors in adjacent categories have proven formats, scroll-stopper styles, calls to action and storylines. Ask why each works and rebuild it for your {avatar}.
items.why: Proven structure plus your own product is safe and original.

items.title: Pick swipe brands that share your customer base
items.text: Pick swipe brands that share your customer base, even in a different category, and check whether their angles fit your positioning. Same customer means the angles transfer.
items.why: Same customer means the angles transfer.

items.title: Use top-creator data to recruit creators and borrow their formats
items.text: Use social-commerce analytics to see which {creator}s drive a brand's sales over 30 days (one made about $100k in one case), then watch their videos to copy formats as ads or recruit and brief those creators. Their audience and style match your target and the format is validated.
items.why: Their audience age and style match your target and the format is validated.
items.when: creator recruitment and TikTok Shop-style research

items.title: Keep researching because formats change; blend with customer language
items.text: Keep researching because short-form formats go through cycles; blend proven formats with what customers are saying and doing to get breakthrough creative. Do not get stuck on one format.
items.why: TikTok formats go through cycles.

items.title: Shared vocabulary: angle, concept, scroll stopper, hook
items.text: Give the team one shared vocabulary: an angle (how you approach the conversation) becomes concepts, concepts become videos, videos get scroll-stopper variations, then hook variations. A result like 'scroll stopper one, hook three won' only compounds if everyone means the same thing.
items.why: Shared words let the team compound learnings instead of guessing.

items.title: Same angle, new concept: compound learnings
items.text: After a batch, keep the winning angle but change the concept so you learn which layer drives the result, and track everything. Changing one layer at a time shows what worked.
items.why: Changing one layer at a time shows what worked.
items.when: creative iteration after a test batch

items.title: Angles come from watching real life, then confirm on TikTok
items.text: Find angles by watching how the {avatar} lives in real life, then confirm on short-form video that people already make content about it. Observation gives the idea; the platform proves people care, so nothing is invented.
items.why: Observation gives the idea; TikTok proves people care.

items.title: Pattern-match the hooks in a batch of swipes
items.text: Watch a batch of swipes in one category and pattern-match the hook they share (in one case nearly all used a before-and-after 'now you see it, now you don't'), then find a twist that makes yours feel unique. The common format is the safe base; the twist gives uniqueness.
items.why: The common format is the safe base; uniqueness comes from the twist.
items.when: creative research on a format category

items.title: Write the scripts first, in a clean doc, before any editing
items.text: Write one script per video under each concept in a clean document before any editing, checking the wording against how people actually speak on the platform and hitting direct-response points. Then plan B-roll, the scroll stopper and scene-by-scene alignment; separating script from edit keeps the message tight.
items.why: Separating script and edit keeps the message tight.

items.title: Use before and after plus dramatization as the scroll stopper
items.text: Use before-and-after application and a dramatization as the scroll stopper (in one case throwing water on a leg to show the product holds), and check that every scene lines up with the words. Demonstration proves the claim faster than telling.
items.why: Demonstration proves the claim faster than telling.

items.title: Tag every ad with who, what, where, archetype
items.text: Tag every ad with who made it ({creator}), what it is (archetype or content type), where it runs and where it sends traffic, and track it. Without defined types you cannot tell why something worked.
items.why: Without defined types you can't tell why something worked.

items.title: Merge a loser's good element into a winner and rewrite
items.text: When a losing ad had one solid element, merge that element into what is working, or rewrite it if it was not specific or its hook did not open strongly enough. A loser may still have one good part.
items.why: A loser may still have one good part.
items.when: creative iteration after a test round

items.title: Recruit creators from Kalodata instead of Fiverr UGC
items.text: Recruit {creator}s found through social-commerce sales data rather than generic UGC marketplaces; in one case three or four such creators cost less per video, already knew how to sell, and expected commission or product. They need no training and deliver more volume.
items.why: They need no training and deliver more volume.

items.title: Skincare needs before and afters up top
items.text: On a transformation product's page (skincare in the example), move before-and-afters to the top and show more faces, and earn more of them through better customers and gamified review requests. A transformation sale needs visible transformations to scale.
items.why: Skincare is a transformation sale.

items.title: Raise AOV and LTV with bundles, free-gift top offer, and optional subscription
items.text: Raise AOV and LTV with bundles, a friendly top-of-funnel {offer} with free gifts, and subscription as a preselected but deselectable option. Higher AOV and LTV let ads break even upfront.
items.why: Higher AOV and LTV let ads break even upfront.

items.title: Do ads first, storefront next, Amazon last
items.text: Get the ad engine working first, then maximize storefront value (email, LTV), and only then go to marketplaces like Amazon, which dilute the {brand} and take fees. Only test new landing pages after an angle is validated in ads.
items.why: Foundations upstream drive everything downstream.
items.when: channel sequencing for a growing DTC brand

items.title: Benchmark repeat rate: 20% second order, 10% third
items.text: Benchmark repeat rate (in one consumable business, about 20% should place a second order and about 10% a third). Missing the benchmark signals weak messaging or no back end.
items.why: Having benchmarks tells you when retention is broken.

items.title: Read early results in one consolidated campaign and ask why the winner works
items.text: Read early results in one consolidated campaign, where the winner is obvious (in one case after two days one {creator}'s video had three sales at $26 CPA while another's had spend and none), turn off the non-converter, then ask which elements of the winner are working.
items.why: A single place makes the winner obvious; the next step is learning why.
items.when: early reads on a new creative test

items.title: Watch for the ad set serving to the old audience
items.text: In an account with history, watch for ads serving mostly to the existing customer audience; consider splitting old versus new customers or testing a fresh pixel. You want to pay to reach new customers, not people who already bought.
items.why: So you pay to reach new customers rather than people who already bought.
items.when: Meta accounts with prior customer history

items.title: Audit a brand by comparing its ads to the category leader
items.text: Audit a {brand} by comparing its ads to the category leader's: in one case a product's ads were technical and feature-led while the leader's showed the outcome (cooking simple meals). Get the product to creators who show the outcome, repurpose their content as cheap ads, and consider pricing toward an impulse buy.
items.why: The category's winning playbook is about the outcome (food), not the engineering.

items.title: Drill into ad sets to find the one ad driving the good CPA
items.text: Drill from campaign to ad set to ad to find what drives a good CPA rather than judging the average. In one case campaign CPAs were $145-260, but one ad set was at $41 and one {creator}'s ad inside it drove that.
items.why: Averages hide the single winner.

items.title: Test in a shared environment instead of $100 a day per ad
items.text: Test ads together in one shared environment so the platform funnels spend to the best, instead of giving each ad its own budget (such as $100 a day each). Treat it like the scientific method: variables in one environment, and the winner is found far cheaper.
items.why: It finds the winner cheaper.

items.title: The angle was 'dull old skin', not acne
items.text: Let the winning ad tell you which problem to speak to. In one case results showed the angle was not the problem the team assumed but a related, honest one (removing dull, old skin), which connected with an older {avatar} without making them feel bad.
items.why: The winning ad told him which problem to speak to.
items.when: after a test reveals an unexpected winning angle

items.title: For this market keep creative simple: people using the product on camera
items.text: For some markets, keep creative simple: real people using the {hero product} on camera, natural and problem-focused, with consistent B-roll, without over-editing or over-writing. In one market experienced agency owners confirmed you cannot AI your way out of this.
items.why: Realistic usage is believable to this audience.
items.when: markets where realistic product usage drives trust

items.title: Automated kill rule: spend over $60 with zero purchases turns off
items.text: Set an automated kill rule: any ad that spends past a threshold with zero purchases turns off. In one case the line was $60, from a $40 baseline CPA plus room for a couple of purchases to bring it back to $40.
items.why: Baseline CPA from the winner sets the line.
items.when: Meta ad accounts with a known baseline CPA

items.title: Repurpose old founder footage and old reactions by re-editing
items.text: Repurpose old raw {founder} footage, reactions and before-and-afters by re-editing them: for example, green-screen the founder to match a {creator}'s words, or add timeline overlays ('five years later') for transformation content. A competent {editor} can re-cut real footage into fresh ads without new shoots.
items.why: Real footage is the source for fresh ads without new shoots.
items.when: brands with an archive of raw footage

items.title: Use real before-and-afters as the AI baseline
items.text: Use real before-and-afters as the baseline in AI image and video tools, building timelines and storylines from them rather than generating proof from scratch. Real proof as the base keeps the output believable.
items.why: Real proof as the base keeps the output believable.

items.title: Upload customer segments as named batches so you can see which works
items.text: When uploading contact segments to a partner (for example recent clickers and buyers), name each batch by file and segment and fill required fields such as phone, so you can compare which segment works. You can only optimize what you can tell apart.
items.why: You can only optimize what you can tell apart.

items.title: Use an ad-library tool to track competitor brands and download their ads
items.text: Use an ad-library tool to follow a few competitor brands, see how many ads they launch, their formats and landing pages, and download their images and videos. It lets you study many competitor ads quickly.
items.why: It lets you study many competitor ads quickly.

items.title: Break a swiped static down with Gemini, then rebuild it with your customer research
items.text: Break a swiped static down with one AI model (what the person in it is doing, the headline, how to format it for future ads), then take that breakdown plus your customer research to a second AI that holds {brand} context and ask for new headlines and images. One sees ad structure; the other holds your brand and customer insight.
items.why: Gemini sees ad structure; Claude holds your brand and customer insight.
items.when: rebuilding swiped static ads with AI

items.title: Gemini for ad analysis because of YouTube video data
items.text: Choose AI tools by the data they were trained on; one operator prefers a model from the company that owns the largest video platform for video and image breakdowns because its video intelligence reflects what people watch.
items.why: Tool choice by data it was trained on.
items.when: choosing AI models for ad analysis

items.title: Dictate prompts with a voice tool
items.text: Dictate prompts with a voice-to-text tool instead of typing, so you describe an ad the way you talk. It is faster and the language is more natural.
items.why: Faster, and the language is more natural.

items.title: Think in multiples: same format, different person or background
items.text: Think in multiples: with a good static format, test the same headline across different people, backgrounds, products and comparison layouts, and reuse the images on product carousels and funnels. One format becomes many tests and assets.
items.why: One format becomes many tests and assets.

items.title: Fix trust on a brand site: add social proof and think objections
items.text: If a {brand} site feels dry, add social proof (before-and-afters, product in {creator}s' hands) first, and list the hesitations that stop people clicking or buying, then answer them. Most people never click or buy, so the page must remove doubts.
items.why: Most people never click or buy, so the page must remove doubts.

items.title: Turn a product difference into a visual proof: gentle water-shell exfoliant
items.text: Turn a product difference into visual proof: when skeptics fear a feature (such as a harsh scrub grain), show it close-up and explain why it is natural and gentle. Teaching why it is different beats fake testimonials.
items.why: Make the product point visible, not just claimed.
items.when: products with a feature buyers are skeptical of

items.title: Search the way the customer would to avoid objection terms
items.text: Search the topic the way the customer would, both positive and negative phrasings, to see which terms bring up objections and which bring up the process. Use that real search language to decide what to mention and what to avoid.
items.why: Your copy should match real search language.
items.when: copy and messaging around a sensitive product feature

items.title: Turn one real experience into many ads from the same footage
items.text: Turn one real experience into many ads from the same footage: image ads (remove people, zoom in, add an offer headline), a storytelling ad from the B-roll, and a UGC reaction ad. One real moment becomes a family of formats.
items.why: One real moment becomes a family of formats.

items.title: Study video content daily or your formats won't connect
items.text: Study ads and short-form video daily; formats are learned by watching, and without that your formats will not connect.
items.why: Formats are learned by watching.

items.title: Build format banks and turn each into a skill
items.text: As you study ads, record formats (such as review plus before-and-after plus product) in a bank and turn each into a reusable AI skill, so one experience can be matched to many formats. Reusable formats scale ideation.
items.why: Reusable formats scale ideation.

items.title: Match the product timing to the story: a scrub isn't a 'get ready with me' item
items.text: Match the format to when the {hero product} is truthfully used; in one case a product used before and after an event did not fit a 'get ready with me' format, so the ad was reframed around returning home and aftercare. A format only works if the product's real use fits it.
items.why: A format only works if the product use truthfully fits it.
items.when: choosing a format for a product story

items.title: Ad script frame: hook, lead, body (problem, failed solution, mechanism, demo, proof), offer
items.text: Write ads with one frame: hook, lead, body (problem, failed solutions, new mechanism or ingredient, demonstration, social proof), then offer and comparison. Long-form video only elaborates each point, so long and short form share the same skeleton and blanks are easy to fill.
items.why: A frame makes it easy to fill in blanks and edit.
items.when: ad scripting, short and long form

items.title: Write the idea yourself first, then let AI flesh it out
items.text: Do not start with AI for the idea: say your real baseline experience out loud, transcribe it, and ask AI to flesh it into a one-minute script, then edit by hand. AI does not know the real experience.
items.why: AI doesn't know the real experience.

items.title: Find customer words by looking where they actually say things
items.text: When unsure what words buyers use, look where they actually say things (comments and posts on short-form platforms), and build a customer-language bank to load into AI. Copy should say it how they say it; a comment-reply video is also a usable format.
items.why: Copy should say it how they say it.

items.title: Match the script to the B-roll you have, and make or generate what's missing
items.text: Line up each spoken line with real footage, and where a shot is missing, use another {creator}'s clip, a UGC clip, or a generated image animated into motion. It does not have to be the same day, year or person; the story is what matters.
items.why: Assets are interchangeable; the story is what matters.

items.title: Launch scrappy in two days instead of perfecting for two weeks
items.text: Launch scrappy in two days rather than perfecting for two weeks: a rough ad from existing clips and AI voice, then see. If it gets zero ROAS, do not spend more on that approach.
items.why: Speed to a test beats perfect execution.

items.title: Scale a message in order: statics, AI voiceover video, then creators
items.text: Scale a message in order of cost: turn research into statics to test the message, turn winning messages into AI-voiceover videos, and finally hand the proven script to {creator}s. The cheapest test comes first and expensive production goes only to proven messages.
items.why: Cheapest test first, expensive production only for proven messages.

items.title: Mine competitor comments for customer phrases and new angles
items.text: Read comments on competitors' videos and highlight phrases people literally use; in one case this surfaced terms like 'mature skin' and an unexpected benefit angle nobody on the team had considered. Comments hold the customer's own words and unexpected benefits.
items.why: Comments hold the customer's own words and unexpected benefits.

items.title: Picture the avatar by searching their keywords on TikTok, Pinterest, YouTube
items.text: Picture the {avatar} by typing review keywords into short-form video, image and video search platforms and seeing who talks about them; in one case this showed the speakers were about 27 to early 40s. It makes the avatar real from evidence when review sites hide ages.
items.why: This makes an avatar real from evidence.

items.title: One keyword search reveals different awareness levels
items.text: One keyword search shows different awareness levels side by side (a professional, an influencer, a casual user). Bank those links into baseline categories, then map formats against the funnel.
items.why: Awareness levels show up in the same market.

items.title: Choose the benefit that overlaps across avatars (demand-based thinking)
items.text: Treat demographics as one data point and prioritize benefits that overlap across several audiences, then test the same angle across several {avatar}s. Very different groups can want the same offer, so you reach a broader market with one message.
items.why: You find a broader market with the same message.
items.when: choosing which benefits and problems to lead with

items.title: The avatar picks the on-camera person, not the other way around
items.text: Use {avatar} research to decide who appears in ads, not to box in who the product is for; the on-camera person does not have to be the avatar, and aspirational casting can pull more than a mirror.
items.why: Showing someone the viewer aspires to be can pull more than a mirror.

items.title: Test four avatars and problems to find the winner, then drill into it
items.text: Test several {avatar}s and problems broadly (four creators on four problems in one case), find the one that gets sales, then break down why it won and build deeper experiences and angles inside it. Go broad first, then deep on the winner.
items.why: Broad first, then deep on the winner.
items.when: early creative testing for a product

items.title: Read age breakdown: 45+ had lower CPA than younger audience
items.text: Read the age breakdown in ad results and let spend data say who buys; in one case 45+ had a lower CPA than younger groups, showing the audience skewed older, so the next step was a fresh pixel and more ads.
items.why: Let spend data, not guesses, say who buys.

items.title: Don't make the static a literal copy of the video; change the format
items.text: Do not make a static a literal copy of a video's text; format is how the creative is laid out (before-and-after with product and testimonial, offer static, and so on), and the same message can be shown in a different layout. Ask what the person is thinking after seeing the ad, since static winners usually look different from video winners.
items.why: Static winners usually look different from video winners.

items.title: Swap the headline to something customers say, keep the same image
items.text: Replace headlines nobody would actually say with customer language (in one case a generic line became a customer's own description of how the product felt on their skin), keeping the same image. Specific, real phrasing stops the scroll; generic headlines blend in.
items.why: Specific, real phrasing stops the scroll and generic headlines blend in.

items.title: A new angle is a different angle, not a rewording of the winner
items.text: A new angle is a different angle (for example feel versus problem versus cutting clutter), not a rewording of the winner's lines. Iterate by building another set off a related thought; being too literal kills creativity.
items.why: Literal copying kills creativity.
items.when: developing new angles from a winner

items.title: Ask 'what awareness stage is this ad?' on every swipe
items.text: Ask 'what awareness stage is this ad?' on every swipe; for example a static that only makes sense if you know the product is product-aware. Static ads often assume the traffic already came from somewhere, and the stage decides who the ad can work for.
items.why: The stage decides who the ad can work for.

items.title: Don't over-promise: a modest before and after builds trust
items.text: Do not over-promise: a mechanism that claims total results erodes trust, while a modest, realistic before-and-after for the {avatar}'s age builds it. Skeptical buyers trust honest results.
items.why: Skeptical buyers trust honest results.
items.when: claims and proof for skeptical audiences

items.title: Make polished AI statics look native, like an iPhone photo
items.text: Make AI statics look native, like a phone photo, rather than polished studio images; in one case a reference image was adapted into a family member snapping a casual beach photo with everyday props. Native-looking images perform better because they do not look like ads.
items.why: In-feed ads that don't look like ads get less scroll resistance.

items.title: Use a good generated image as a reference for variations
items.text: Once a generated image is good, use it as the reference for variations (changing the situation, model or quality) rather than rewriting the prompt. It keeps the look consistent while changing one thing.
items.why: Keeps the look consistent while changing one thing.

items.title: Why statics still matter when video spends more
items.text: Keep statics even when video spends more: video carries more message and can spend longer, but statics are faster and suit promotions (for example '20% off') and different stages. An ad library is a portfolio of messages in different formats doing different jobs.
items.why: Different formats do different jobs in the decision process.
items.when: balancing creative formats on paid social

items.title: Fix the leak: email and back end before more cold video spend
items.text: Before scaling cold video spend, check that email and a back end exist; in one case storefront sales came from people searching the brand name after the ads, so email had to catch them. More spend into a leaky funnel just loses more.
items.why: More spend into a leaky bucket just loses more.

items.title: When a message wins, update the whole customer journey
items.text: When an angle wins in ads, update the whole customer journey to match: hero image, product page, emails and social. The message should be consistent from ad to page to email.
items.why: The message should be consistent from ad to page to email.

items.title: Expect a 5% hit rate and don't chase perfection
items.text: Expect roughly a 5% hit rate on ads, so get many shots up rather than perfect ones, and keep pushing only real outliers (for example an ad where CPA drops 30% and it takes off). More shots beat polish.
items.why: More shots beat polish.

items.title: Copy proven public formats instead of reinventing them
items.text: Instead of asking AI to invent ad templates, feed it proven static formats (five in the example) from competitor ad libraries. Formats that already spend are validated.
items.why: Formats that already spend are validated.

items.title: Remember 96% never see your page: bridge from ad to page
items.text: Even at 4% CTR, 96% of people never see your page, so ask what the {avatar} thinks after the ad and before the page, and support the portfolio with middle-of-funnel content. The ad's job is the next step, not the whole sale.
items.why: The ad's job is the next step, not the whole sale.

items.title: Ads are the same thing everywhere: why it matters, why relevant, then proof
items.text: Every ad does the same job: tell people what is going on, why it matters and why it is relevant to them, then show as much proof as possible. The key is knowing why each asset works or does not, which only tests reveal, so beginners can start with this frame.
items.why: Beginners can start without product knowledge by using this frame.

items.title: The sauce is the customer's language; nothing is made up
items.text: Build everything from research so nothing is invented: the words customers use and the visuals they respond to. Keep it simple; the customer's language is what makes copy land.
items.why: Real language is what makes copy land.

items.title: Make an ad look like the native format: an Instagram story
items.text: Make ads look like the native format they sit in, such as a social story: a phone photo with a small casual caption about the experience (for example someone unboxing a new product). Take what people already see in feeds and apply ad language to it.
items.why: Native formats don't feel like ads.
items.when: story and feed placements on social

items.title: The headline stops the scroll; the first clip or image supports it
items.text: The headline is the most important element because it gets people to stop; the scroll stopper (the first three seconds of video or the image) then holds them. Without the stop, nothing after matters.
items.why: Without the stop, nothing after matters.

items.title: Ask yourself what content you stop for, because your market does the same
items.text: Ask yourself and the team what content you personally stop for and why, because your market does the same; the ad should be content people want to consume, not an interruption.
items.why: The goal is content people want, not interruption.

items.title: Study what your market watches, not what competitors script
items.text: Study what your market watches and listens to and the conversations in their heads, not competitors' scripts, then turn that into videos, photos and headlines. Competitors may be wrong; the audience tells the truth.
items.why: Competitors may be wrong; the audience tells the truth.

items.title: Old-school scripted direct response only works on older viewers
items.text: Match content style to the audience's generation: aggressive, low-quality scripted direct response works mainly on much older viewers, while younger people consume POV content. A style mismatch signals 'ad' and gets skipped.
items.why: Style mismatch signals 'ad' and gets skipped.
items.when: choosing ad style by audience age

items.title: A scroll stopper is just the first three seconds, and anything can be one
items.text: A scroll stopper is just the first three seconds, and anything surprising or curious can be one; in one case a video that made about $200k opened with the creator pointing at an old photo of herself under a cheeky transformation headline. Surprise in three seconds beats polish.
items.why: Surprise or curiosity in 3 seconds beats polish.

items.title: Use real lived experience as content (boat trip) instead of staging
items.text: Use the team's real lived moments (in one case, a team boat trip) as content instead of staging shoots; tell stories from real experiences and tie them to using {hero product}.
items.why: Real moments feel like the experience customers want.
items.when: organic and paid content planning, whenever the team or {founder} has real-life footage

items.title: Map every ad on a funnel-stage spectrum
items.text: Place every ad on a top-to-bottom funnel spectrum; format and medium change by stage. A video can carry someone through several awareness levels, while a single image sits in just one.
items.why: This decides what each ad needs to say.
items.when: planning or briefing any ad, before deciding what it must say

items.title: Define awareness stages with real examples
items.text: Train the team to label any asset's awareness stage with concrete examples: a holiday ad with an offer is product-aware, comparing to another solution is solution-aware, talking about the unique mechanism is problem-aware. Quiz them until they can categorize assets on sight.
items.why: You learn to categorize any asset in your head, which is how you know how the machine works.

items.title: Unique mechanism is how the product delivers its transformation
items.text: The unique mechanism is how {hero product} delivers its transformation: the science of how it works (e.g. caffeine in a drink, active ingredients in a serum). Ads and brands stand out when there is a new thing that makes the result happen.
items.why: It differentiates the product at the product layer.

items.title: Mechanism vs angle vs brand values
items.text: Keep mechanism, angle and brand values separate: mechanism lives at the product layer, the angle is how you open the conversation, and the brand is who you are (e.g. sustainable packaging is a brand value, not a mechanism).
items.why: Keeping them separate prevents muddy briefs.

items.title: An angle is the way you start a conversation; mechanism explains it
items.text: An angle is how you start the conversation and the mechanism explains it: nobody reacts to a mechanism name cold, so open with a felt angle (e.g. a seasonal glow) and let the mechanism explain why the problem exists. Pure mechanism talk is for the most aware audience, such as the email list.
items.why: Start the conversation where they are.
items.when: ad hooks and leads for colder audiences; mechanism-heavy copy for email/owned audiences

items.title: Awareness depends on the person, so define the customer first
items.text: Awareness stage depends on the person, so define {avatar} first: demographic is the high-level frame (age, gender), the avatar is the story (a specific person with a specific problem). Without an avatar, awareness labels stay arguable.
items.why: Without an avatar, awareness labels are arguable.
items.when: before labelling awareness or writing briefs

items.title: Go to the second layer of research: stories, clinical journals, history, root cause
items.text: Go past baseline demographics into the second layer of research: people's stories, clinical journals, the history of products in advertising, the root cause and the psyche. That is where differentiated angles come from.
items.why: That's where differentiated angles come from.

items.title: Model price vs ROAS vs COGS vs cash before dropping price
items.text: Before dropping price, model price against front-end ROAS, COGS as a share of sale, contribution and cash position in a spreadsheet. In one case, at one price the ads hit 0.7 ROAS and the months went red, while a lower price had produced 1.23.
items.why: Don't change price on instinct; see contribution and cash.

items.title: Restarting old ads sends them to the hottest audience then fades
items.text: Restarting old ads sends them to the hottest audiences first, so the first few days look good and then fade (in one case to 0.94 ROAS on $3k spend). Don't read a relaunch's first days as the true result; fresh creative is what's needed.
items.why: Don't read the first days of a relaunch as the true result.
items.when: Meta paid social, when turning paused ads back on

items.title: Change one variable at a time: price on funnel vs website
items.text: Change one variable at a time: test a new price on the funnel only first and read one-touch conversion, then roll it to the whole site only if needed. Two prices at once hide which caused the result.
items.why: Two prices at once means you can't tell which caused the result.
items.when: price or offer tests across funnel and site

items.title: Anchor effect: a discounted price can't easily go back up
items.text: Once {hero product} runs at a discounted price it is seen as a discounted product and can't easily go back up; new versions (new colors, new refills) are how you reset perception.
items.why: Lowering price has a cost to perception.
items.when: before cutting price on a core product

items.title: High CPM means the ad account is still serving to older women
items.text: Account history steers where new ads go: very high CPMs can mean the ad account is still serving to the audience it was optimized around (in one case mostly 55-65+ women). Use the peak season for what works and test a new pixel with fresh creative in the off period.
items.why: Account history steers where new ads go.
items.when: Meta paid social, when trying to reach a new audience from an established account

items.title: Product page vs offer page made little difference
items.text: In one test, product page vs offer page made little difference to CPA (results varied more by creator than by page), so page type was not the lever; the constant need is fresh ads. Move on from tests that don't change the result.
items.why: Move on from tests that don't change the result.
items.when: landing page tests on paid traffic

items.title: Raw creative breakdown: download, Gemini for transcript and scenes
items.text: Break down raw creative by downloading the video and using an AI model to pull the full transcript and each scene. For pure direct response, study the script, because the copy drives it and visuals only explain.
items.why: Copy carried the old DR winners.

items.title: Read the script line by line: comparisons make it tangible
items.text: Read a winning script line by line and note how its comparisons paint exactly what is happening in the viewer's head; tangible comparisons keep attention.
items.why: Tangible comparisons keep attention.

items.title: Place the creative first: problem-aware or solution-aware?
items.text: Before iterating on a creative, place it: problem-aware or solution-aware? If the market already buys solutions in the category, most of it is solution-aware; don't sell the category to people who have never bought it.
items.why: Don't sell skincare to people who don't use skincare.
items.when: before writing variations of an existing ad

items.title: Brief the AI with mechanism, awareness and sophistication level
items.text: Brief the AI with the transcript and scenes plus constraints: which mechanism to keep, which awareness stage to speak to, the sophistication level (e.g. four to five), and what to change (hooks and leads) versus keep (a strong pitch).
items.why: Constraints keep variations on-strategy.
items.when: using AI to write ad variations

items.title: Use CPC and CPM to say what to fix: engaging hooks to cut cost per click
items.text: Use CPC and CPM to decide what to fix: in one case a $5.82 cost per unique outbound click and $300 CPM showed the hook needed work, so write more engaging headlines and hooks to lift watch time, then a body with more life experience rather than only the problem.
items.why: Metrics point to which part of the ad to rewrite.
items.when: paid social, diagnosing an underperforming video ad

items.title: For sophisticated, solution-aware markets, use identification
items.text: For sophisticated, solution-aware markets, use identification: speak to their life stage and experience, not just the problem. Dig the identification out of customer research and turn it into hook, headline and lead.
items.why: They've heard every problem pitch; recognition gets attention.
items.when: markets that have heard every problem pitch

items.title: Study a strong full-funnel static account; position against the incumbent
items.text: Study a competitor running strong full-funnel statics, and position {brand} against a known incumbent (in one case a natural alternative to a well-known treatment). An unknown brand needs bold creative for awareness.
items.why: Positioning against a known thing explains you fast.
items.when: positioning a lesser-known brand; static ad planning

items.title: Let ads run and optimize; the winning product gets the next creative
