items.text: Let ads run and optimize for a few days before judging (CPAs came down by waiting), then give the next creative to whichever product is winning. It comes down to making more ads and testing them weekly.
items.why: Patience plus focus beats flipping.
items.when: paid social, early in a campaign

items.title: Seed creators so content feeds ads, email and organic
items.text: Seed products to {creator}s so their content can be repurposed across paid, email and organic, and so how they present {brand} inspires more angles.
items.why: One shoot feeds every channel.

items.title: Offer a pause or schedule change before cancelling a subscription
items.text: Before cancelling a subscription, offer a pause or schedule change first; cancellation is the last option because saving a customer is cheaper than winning a new one. (In one setup subscriptions lived in the commerce platform, not the order system.)
items.why: Saving the customer is cheaper than winning a new one.
items.when: subscription customer service and cancellation flows

items.title: Brief a creator scout: define the avatar by age cues and values
items.text: Brief a creator scout with an exact {avatar} definition: age range (and who to exclude), people who state their age, their lifestyle and values. Matching avatars who trust each other matters more than how old someone looks.
items.why: A clear definition lets someone else find creators without guessing.

items.title: Find creators by searching the avatar's own words on Instagram
items.text: Find {creator}s by searching {avatar}'s own words on Instagram, then look at who they follow and who is in the comments. Small accounts (e.g. 13k followers) can have strong engagement; community strength beats follower count.
items.why: Community strength matters more than follower count.

items.title: Partner with creators instead of stealing their videos
items.text: Partner with {creator}s directly instead of stealing their videos as other brands do: approach them as a real brand with proof (customer count, a {founder}) and ask them to put their own life and personality in. You get better content you can legally reuse.
items.why: Partnership gives better quality content that you can legally reuse.

items.title: Read each creator's bio for angle ideas
items.text: Read each {creator}'s bio for angle ideas: their niche (e.g. helping a group recognize themselves in photos again) hints at the self-image problems and desires {avatar} has, and how {hero product} fits.
items.why: Creator niches reveal angles.

items.title: Use TikTok Shop trending data to find proven formats and aging-focused creators
items.text: Use TikTok Shop trending data (e.g. Kalodata top sellers) to find proven sales formats and creators who already know them; apply those newer formats with {avatar} to get ahead of the market.
items.why: Newer formats with an older avatar get ahead of the market.
items.when: format and creator research, TikTok Shop

items.title: Split creator search time: 80% Instagram and TikTok, 20% YouTube
items.text: Split creator search time about 80% on Instagram and TikTok (short-form content works for organic and ads at once) and 20% on YouTube; start with lifestyle creators who match {avatar}, not experts.
items.why: Short-form content is directly reusable.

items.title: Diagnose a stale brand site as needing real content and branding
items.text: When a brand site feels stale, the fix is real content: product seeding, more before-and-afters and real faces on the page and in the ads. Believability rises when people see the same faces everywhere (one ad becomes five in the feed).
items.why: Believability goes up when people see the same faces everywhere.
items.when: brand site and landing page refresh

items.title: Get from an idea to a markdown brief, then let the AI tool generate the images
items.text: Go from an idea to a written markdown brief (researched with an AI model), then feed it to an AI image/video tool with the look specified (e.g. 'very native looking') and the model chosen. A written brief makes generation fast and repeatable.
items.why: A written brief makes generation fast and repeatable.

items.title: Rebuild a trending TikTok format with your own character: swipe, break down, rewrite, generate
items.text: Rebuild a trending TikTok format with your own characters: swipe the example, break it into scenes, rewrite the script for {brand} and {hero product}, make the character images (e.g. {founder} and an AI persona), then generate scene by scene. The same format works across brands with each brand's script and character.
items.why: Formats are scraped, then reused with each brand's script and character.
items.when: AI video production from organic formats

items.title: Pick the model per job: logic models for reasoning, generative models for pictures
items.text: Pick the model per job: a logic model (e.g. Claude) for understanding the brief, and generative image/video models for pictures and clips. If the tool picks the wrong one, re-prompt; the wrong model wastes generations.
items.why: Wrong model equals wasted generations.

items.title: Tie clipper payouts to views and revenue
items.text: Tie clipper payouts and views back to revenue to know whether the channel pays (e.g. $100 paid on 67,000 views looks great, but needs attribution). On TikTok Shop, clippers need about 1,000 followers to apply as affiliates.
items.why: Without attribution you can't tell if the channel pays.

items.title: Don't scale a format that uses other people's content without a deal
items.text: Don't scale a format built on other people's content without a deal; it may slide at small volume but risk grows with scale. Double down on compliant formats such as AI remakes or your own {creator} with the real problem.
items.why: Risk grows with volume.
items.when: organic and clipping formats using third-party footage

items.title: Make sure content ties back to what the product does
items.text: Views alone are not the goal; keep producing volume of clips relevant to what {hero product} does, even if they get fewer views, because irrelevant views don't create buyers.
items.why: Irrelevant views don't create buyers.

items.title: Deep research is reverse-engineering what the market watches and putting your message inside
items.text: Deep research means reverse-engineering what the market watches and consumes, then putting your message inside it. For some audiences (in one case mature creators) the experience of using the product matters more than the mechanism.
items.why: The market's habits set the format.
items.when: any brand's research and format selection

items.title: Bank every good format: download, save, rewatch, extract
items.text: Bank every good format every time you find one: download it, save it, rewatch it, extract from it, and use the platform's similar-creator suggestions to find more.
items.why: A bank is built by doing this every time.

items.title: Look for comments exceeding likes: a sign of a gem
items.text: A post with more comments than likes is a rare sign of real community resonance; treat that creator and format as worth pursuing, and cross-check it against what big brands are doing.
items.why: Strong community engagement signals real resonance.

items.title: Pay for the research tool and mine creators from winning products
items.text: Pay for the research tool (in one case upgrading from $40 to $100 a month) and mine creators from winning products in your space: find a top seller, pull its creator list and adjacent creators, and reach out with intent.
items.why: The data pays for itself in better outreach.
items.when: creator sourcing via TikTok Shop data tools

items.title: Spot an outlier: same spend, CPA half of anything else, multiple purchases in a day
items.text: Spot an outlier: at the same spend, an ad with CPA half of anything else and several purchases in one day (in one case four purchases at $27 CPA) is worth a feedback loop. Note ads may only pick up real spend days after launch.
items.why: Several purchases in a day at the same spend is a positive sign worth following.
items.when: Meta paid social, reading new ad results

items.title: Name the creative type and angle for the winner
items.text: Name the winner's creative type, format and angle (in one case an 'AI authority' format with a naturalist origin-story angle) and record its scene breakdown, so you can find it again and vary it.
items.why: Naming the format and angle lets you find it again and vary it.

items.title: Swipe organic formats rather than other people's ads
items.text: Swipe organic formats rather than other brands' ads: ads are commercial versions of organic content and things get lost. Break down why the organic format works and reverse-engineer it into an ad, keeping the rawness.
items.why: Organic shows what people actually choose to watch.

items.title: Go deeper into the sub-avatar in the next variation
items.text: When an ad wins on a specific callout (in one case a problem on one body area), the next variation goes deeper into that sub-avatar: pull Reddit and forum language about it, write hook variations in their words, and keep the curiosity line.
items.why: The winning detail is the specific callout.

items.title: Pair a problem callout with curiosity in the hook
items.text: Pair a callout of the specific problem and area with curiosity in the hook (e.g. 'it works too well'); the callout finds the right person and the curiosity keeps them. Weave how each ingredient works on that area into the body and keep the rest unchanged.
items.why: Callout gets the right person, curiosity keeps them.

items.title: Update the language bank after every deep dive
items.text: After every deep dive, have the AI update the customer language bank with exactly how {avatar} describes the experience, then generate hook and script variations from it; the bank compounds with every test.
items.why: The bank compounds with every test.
items.when: after research or a winning test

items.title: Claude is poor at analyzing video; use another tool for the breakdown
items.text: Claude is poor at analyzing video directly; use a video-capable model for the breakdown, then paste its result into Claude for strategy.
items.why: Pick the tool that reads video well.

items.title: Look for the second angle behind a price angle
items.text: Look for a second angle behind a price angle: in one case, a cheaper health device added 'don't let a subscription gatekeep your data, own it with a one-time purchase'. Price alone limits creative diversity.
items.why: Price alone limits creative diversity.
items.when: brands whose only angle is being cheaper

items.title: Move up the awareness ladder: show symptoms, then solutions, then your price
items.text: When every ad is bottom-funnel price comparison, move up the awareness ladder: add creatives that show the problem or symptom, personify other solutions, then wrap back to the core message. More attention at the top feeds the bottom.
items.why: More attention at the top feeds the bottom.
items.when: ad accounts stuck on bottom-funnel creative

items.title: Find formats by scrolling the niche, not the product
items.text: Find formats by scrolling what people in the niche watch on Instagram, TikTok and YouTube (not the product itself), then rework those formats; the same content runs everywhere and platform differences are small.
items.why: Same video content everywhere; platform differences are small.

items.title: Make culturally native versions of a format for each audience
items.text: Make culturally native versions of a format for each audience, shaped by platform rules: in one case a cartoon in a sports-video-game style (cartoons can show what live footage can't on Facebook), with commentary language researched from the audience's forums and inspired by a commentator style, not the person.
items.why: Platform rules and audience culture decide the style.
items.when: Meta ads with restricted visuals; audience-specific creative

items.title: Put direct response in the back half, attention first
items.text: Don't make direct response the core of the ad: capture attention first with the native format, then sell in the back half.
items.why: Attention is the scarce resource.

items.title: Marketing is reminders: be present everywhere your customer is
items.text: Marketing is reminders: be present everywhere {avatar} is, don't force the purchase, speak like friends and invite them into a club of people chasing the same outcome. Familiarity builds trust, then sales.
items.why: Familiarity builds trust, then sales.

items.title: Create a group chat for creators and customers
items.text: Create a group chat (e.g. WhatsApp) for {creator}s who work with {brand} to share inspiration and guidelines and welcome new members; a customer group chat is also good market research.
items.why: Community creates content and insight.

items.title: Let the market speak: you can't control what they say
items.text: When the strategy is letting the market speak for {brand}, you can't control everything they say; work with what they say, because conversation creation builds trust and brand voice follows customer voice.
items.why: Brand voice follows customer voice.

items.title: Write once, then adapt hooks, headlines and body to each channel
items.text: Write once from customer language, then adapt hooks, headlines, scroll stoppers, body copy, objections, benefits and desires to each channel (email/SMS, social, paid, site, marketplace). One language bank feeds every asset.
items.why: One bank of language feeds every asset.

items.title: A split test changes one variable and picks a metric that fits
items.text: A split test changes one variable and uses the metric that fits it: subject lines measure open rate, design measures clicks, links measure sales. Pick the variable you believe is highest-leverage; email and landing pages are where direct split tests happen.
items.why: Isolating one variable shows the cause.

items.title: Set weekly baselines before changing formats
items.text: Set weekly baselines (CPM, open rates, revenue per email, week over week) before changing formats, so new formats can be judged against them.
items.why: You can't call a change good without a baseline.
items.when: before testing new ad or email formats

items.title: Capture every creator tag or story automatically
items.text: Use a tool that automatically archives every story or post that tags {brand}; stories expire, and a missed one is lost proof.
items.why: Stories expire; a missed one is lost proof.

items.title: Seeding math: 163 DMs, 30 products out, 17% accept
items.text: Track seeding acceptance rate to know if the offer works: in one round, 163 creators were DM'd a free-product offer and 30 accepted (about 17%). Most declines are because the product doesn't fit their interests.
items.why: Track the acceptance rate to know if the offer works.

items.title: Run up first creator videos quickly; don't wait for perfect
items.text: Run first creator videos as ads quickly instead of waiting for perfect: a rough video is still native to that creator's audience. Add headline captions, test comment-reply-style formats, and improve quality with volume.
items.why: Quality can improve with volume; the audience finds it native.

items.title: Borrow the creator's audience: research their followers before briefing
items.text: You are borrowing the {creator}'s audience: research who comments on her page, refine your avatar sheet from it, and write a unique brief that fits her brand and resonates with her market.
items.why: The brief should resonate with her market.

items.title: Have the creator talk through her experience before writing the brief
items.text: Before writing a brief for a bigger {creator}, have the outreach person talk with her about how she is experiencing {hero product}, so the content fits her feed and reflects real experience.
items.why: Real experience gives truer content.

items.title: Use existing creator posts to recruit more creators
items.text: Each time you land a {creator} who fits {avatar}, use her results (who you work with, the views their videos got) as proof when pitching the next ones.
items.why: Social proof helps the next pitch.

items.title: Define the niche broadly (pro-aging) and sub-avatars within
items.text: Define the niche broadly (in one case 'pro-aging women 50+') with sub-avatars inside it (e.g. wellness, fashion, beauty; natural vs treatment users), and develop real profiles as creators say yes, rather than locking into a tiny box.
items.why: A broad message with sub-avatar profiles keeps reach.

items.title: Build partnerships: 10-15 videos per creator monthly
items.text: Build partnerships: ask each {creator} for batches of 10-15 videos a month (some from your briefs, some their own) and keep working with the best few rather than seeding 100 new people every time.
items.why: Long-term relationships improve ad performance.

items.title: Put usage rights in the agreement and be clear about AI repurposing
items.text: Put marketing usage rights in the creator agreement, say plainly if you will repurpose content with AI, and keep any repurposing to things the {creator} would say and not find demeaning.
items.why: Builds trust and avoids disputes.

items.title: Top videos are real people, not AI; use AI for iterations
items.text: Top brands' top videos are real people with real product experience, not AI; use AI to iterate and test new scripts, not to replace {creator}s.
items.why: Real stories win attention.

items.title: Reuse one creator story as an ad, an email and a landing-page proof
items.text: Reuse one {creator} story several ways: save it with a downloader, run it as an ad first, turn it into a social-proof email ('she shouted us out'), and place it on a landing page.
items.why: One piece of proof does four jobs.
items.when: whenever a creator posts about the brand

items.title: Where AI fits depends on the product, category and audience
items.text: Where AI fits depends on product, category and audience: in one account an AI video built from formats the audience already accepted gave maybe the lowest CPA ever, while the same demographic on TikTok only responded to UGC. Scale AI where it matches what the audience accepts.
items.why: AI isn't universal; it must match the format the audience accepts.
items.when: deciding where AI creative goes per product and channel

items.title: Build the landing page to continue the ad's story
items.text: Build the landing page to continue the winning ad's story from the same perspective (in one case a grandmother's recipe: a step-by-step story of each ingredient, then proof and offer), so it feels like the same conversation.
items.why: A page that continues the ad feels like the same conversation.
items.when: landing pages for a winning ad

items.title: Keep offer boxes simple; before and afters and social proof are everything
items.text: Keep offer boxes simple: a carousel of square product pictures, real benefit callouts, then before-and-afters and social proof. Don't over-design; the sale happens on proof and clarity.
items.why: The sale happens on proof and clarity.
items.when: landing and product page offer sections

items.title: Replace AI images with real ones where it matters
items.text: Replace AI mock-up images with real ones where credibility matters: real photos of {founder} at the source, natural-looking lifestyle shots, and realistic before-and-afters. The page must look legit.
items.why: The page must look legit.

items.title: Match ad types to funnel stages and destinations
items.text: Match ad types to funnel stages and destinations: top of funnel breaks out of the feed for attention, middle hits with proof and UGC, bottom uses offer images sent to the offer page. Build pages from reusable sections.
items.why: Each stage needs its own message and destination.

items.title: Anytime you have a question, spend 5-10 minutes researching it
items.text: Whenever a question comes up (e.g. a {creator} says something specific), spend 5-10 minutes researching it with AI; written versions of social stories often exist on Reddit. Curiosity finds the angles.
items.why: Curiosity finds the angles.

items.title: Turn a shared life experience into hooks ('I regret following 1960s sun advice')
items.text: Turn a shared generational experience into a hook (in one case 'I regret following the 1960s sun advice'): calling it out shows you understand {avatar}, then you bring in your narrative.
items.why: A lived experience continues the conversation in their head.
items.when: hook writing for a defined age group

items.title: Research from raw sources (Reddit, TikTok, YouTube), not by asking the AI blindly
items.text: Research from raw sources where people disclose details (Reddit, TikTok, YouTube), then use AI to organize; don't just ask an AI to 'do research', because its summaries lose the real details.
items.why: AI summaries lose the real details.

items.title: Rebuild the brand from the market, forgetting what you did before
items.text: When a new format starts working, rebuild {brand} from the market: set aside everything you did before and look at what the market cares about, talks about, wants and consumes, keeping only real proof like before-and-afters.
items.why: The past brand constrained the market fit.

items.title: Study the top TikTok Shop brand in your category and extract its structure
items.text: Study the top TikTok Shop brand that sells to a similar customer, even in another category, and extract how it structures creators, affiliates, content and funnel.
items.why: Similar target customer means their structure transfers.
items.when: building a TikTok Shop or creator ecosystem

items.title: Views are only the top of funnel: plan education and ascension
items.text: Views are only the top of funnel: plan the education that converts viewers and the ascension that raises lifetime value by selling buyers more of the range.
items.why: Views don't pay unless the rest exists.

items.title: Attach content to revenue so clippers and creators earn a percentage
items.text: Once direction is clear, attach content to revenue so clippers, {creator}s and affiliates earn a commission or percentage built into {brand} from the start.
items.why: Incentives keep volume going.
items.when: scaling creator, clipper or affiliate programs

items.title: Rename product sets as 'methods' using the audience's vocabulary
items.text: Name offers in the audience's vocabulary: in one case product sets were renamed '<ingredient> Method' after research showed the community talked in 'methods' and liked that ingredient. Offer names that match how the audience talks sell better.
items.why: Offer names that match the audience vocabulary sell better.

items.title: The closer your team gets to the source of inspiration, the faster you refine
items.text: Get the content team to share exactly where they find inspiration; the closer the team is to the source, the faster you understand the market and refine a crystal-clear buying experience.
items.why: Refinement means making a buying experience crystal clear.

items.title: Let the tool extract top slideshow formats and recreate them for your brand
items.text: Have an AI tool extract the top slideshows in the niche, define each as a named format, then recreate them for {brand} (e.g. swapping in {hero product}). Defining each format lets you remake it.
items.why: Defining each format lets you remake it.

items.title: Slideshows are top of funnel: broad headlines to cast a wide net, then narrow
items.text: Slideshows with broad headlines are top-of-funnel awareness that cast a wide net and drive views; to convert, move to problem-specific content and real UGC. You need a mix of formats for each stage.
items.why: You need a mix of formats for each stage.

items.title: AI UGC doesn't hit for this brand; real people do
items.text: In one brand, AI UGC tested extensively since 2022 never hit, and top brands' ads use real people; use real {creator}s for problem- and solution-aware marketing, because buyers don't buy from fake people talking.
items.why: Buyers don't buy from fake people talking.

items.title: A $69 gadget is commoditized; sell the lower-price version
items.text: When {hero product} is commoditized (in one case a $69 gadget against $20-30 lookalikes), the market sets the price anchor: sell a simpler, lower-priced version and refine offers.
items.why: The market sets the price anchor.
items.when: gadget or device categories with cheap competitors

items.title: Pay affiliates a visible percentage; more people means a bigger brand
items.text: Pay affiliates a visible percentage; even 10% works with good volume. The more people in the ecosystem, the more sales, the more commissions and the bigger {brand} gets.
items.why: Aligned pay attracts more creators.

items.title: Break down placements before making anything new
items.text: Break down placements before making anything new: in one account Instagram Stories was the top placement for the target age group, with stories and reels at lower CPA than feeds, so research went to tall, story-style formats.
items.why: Data on where it works tells the format to research.
items.when: Meta paid social, before new creative research

items.title: Research what formats your avatar consumes natively, ignoring ad libraries
items.text: Research the static formats {avatar} actually consumes natively, ignoring other brands' ads and ad libraries, then plan statics with intent and inject {brand} using a context tool.
items.why: Native formats beat copied ads.

items.title: Double down on the narrative that is spending
items.text: Double down on the narrative that is spending: in one case a variation with a different narrator telling the same story got spend within a day. Distill the winning style into formats and keep driving it; the story is the asset, the format the vehicle.
items.why: The story is the asset; the format is the vehicle.

items.title: Pick formats from your own gut, then validate with research
items.text: Pick formats from your own lived experience first (in one case a recipe-card carousel inspired by family recipe cards), then validate with research; intuition gives ideas, data keeps them honest.
items.why: Personal intuition gives ideas, data keeps them honest.
items.when: choosing new static or carousel formats

items.title: Don't deviate from the proven message: Thai grandma five-ingredient recipe
items.text: While a message is winning, don't deviate from it: keep every new static on the core message (the origin story, the steps, the avatar's own word for the problem) and change only the format, e.g. 3 versions each of two new static formats.
items.why: Change format, keep message while the message is winning.
items.when: making new formats from a winning message

items.title: Review AI briefs: voice must come from the grandma
items.text: Review AI-written briefs for voice: if the concept is that a character is speaking (in one case a grandmother addressing {avatar}), every line must read as hers, the {founder} stays in the narrative in their true role, and each carousel card must stand on its own. Voice errors break the concept.
items.why: Voice errors break the concept.
items.when: reviewing AI drafts of character-led creative

items.title: Dramatize the scroll stopper while keeping the message clear
items.text: Dramatize the scroll stopper while keeping the message clear and relatable: if a literal visual is off-putting, exaggerate a cleaner version (e.g. an oversized ingredient scrubbing the problem away).
items.why: Exaggeration grabs attention but must stay relatable.
items.when: visual hooks for image and video ads

items.title: Test a more native version of the same static (typed note vs cursive)
items.text: Test a more native or more legible version of the same static (e.g. typed phone note vs handwritten cursive); legibility is a variable to test.
items.why: Legibility is a variable to test.
items.when: static image ads with text-heavy designs

items.title: Product to message to story to native format, then scale the format
items.text: Run a repeatable factory: distill a message and a story from {hero product}, put the story through native formats, find which format works, then scale that format until it stops working.
items.why: A repeatable factory.

items.title: Run creator posts as partnership ads
items.text: Run {creator} posts as Meta partnership ads: choose partnership ad, enter the post link or ad code, and the creator approves by DM. The ad appears as her post, gets more reach, and gives access to run future ads through her handle.
items.why: Looks native and gives access to the creator's handle.
items.when: Meta paid social with creator content

items.title: Do it by hand first, export, then use the export as the automation template
items.text: Do the work by hand first, export it, then use the export as the automation template; in one case a script to upload ads to Meta failed until a campaign was set up manually once. Automating what you haven't done yourself bakes in errors.
items.why: Automating something you haven't done yourself bakes in errors.
items.when: automating any ad-platform or ops workflow

items.title: Check Meta settings after any import: conversion event, Advantage+, gender, age
items.text: After any import into Meta, check the settings: purchase conversion event, attribution, Advantage+ on, both genders on, age not capped (e.g. 18+ not 35), and the right objective and destination. Imports can quietly set wrong defaults.
items.why: Imports can quietly set the wrong defaults.
items.when: Meta Ads Manager, after bulk imports or automated uploads

items.title: Stay in the tool: Meta changes constantly
items.text: Meta changes constantly, so work inside the tool rather than only watching tutorials, and stay aware: too much automation can kill what is working.
items.why: You must see what actually happens.

items.title: Naming: the campaign carries avatar ID and angle; ad sets carry deck and card
items.text: Name things so results are readable: the campaign name carries the avatar ID and angle, ad sets carry deck and card number so carousel cards sort in order, with one headline and copy shared across cards.
items.why: Names make results readable.
items.when: Meta campaign and ad naming, carousels

items.title: Ask your content people how they research so a tool can do it for them
items.text: Ask content people exactly how they research so a tool can do it for them: scrape proactively, organize formats by views, and do breakdown plus offer injection from a single link. Automate what doesn't need human judgment.
items.why: Automate what needs no human judgment.

items.title: A repeated headline across winners shows what to double down on: 'It works too well'
items.text: When the same element repeats across winners (in one case one curiosity headline, 'it works too well', on every new static that sold), it is validated; double down and build videos around it.
items.why: A repeated element across winners is the signal.
items.when: reading results across several new creatives

items.title: Turn the hook's question into the next hook
items.text: Turn the question a hook raises into the next hook: ask what the consumer would ask (works too well compared to what?), use their skepticism ('too good to be true, but here's why'), and back the claim with {founder} on camera or AI variations.
items.why: Playing with their existing doubt earns trust.

items.title: Break the winning video into statics, hooks and creator briefs
items.text: Break the winning video into statics, hooks and creator briefs: test more angles from it, dial in the headline, and give UGC {creator}s the same hook briefs. Variations of variations of proven assets compound.
items.why: Compounding feedback loop.

items.title: Watch for CPA creep and turn down budget on a fading winner
items.text: Watch for CPA creep on a winner (in one case after more than a month) and turn its budget down; winners fade, so variations must be ready to refill the pipeline.
items.why: Winners fade; the pipeline must refill.
items.when: Meta paid social, managing mature winners

items.title: Rank a creator's videos, filter for usable ones, then brief from what they actually do
items.text: Rank a {creator}'s own top videos, drop creators with nothing worth reverse-engineering, run a deeper breakdown on the usable ones, and output briefs based on what the creator already does, which are easier for them to execute.
items.why: Briefs based on what the creator already does are easier to execute.

items.title: A new test that doesn't win spend isn't a failure; the winner is just better
items.text: A new test that doesn't win spend isn't a failure; the current winner is simply better. Keep testing new angles, formats, avatars and scroll stoppers until one beats it; it's not a sign media buying is broken.
items.why: The number one stays number one until someone beats it.
items.when: Meta paid social, reading new tests against a winner

items.title: Proof: same videos in their own campaign got one purchase
items.text: In one test, videos that got no spend in the main campaign were moved to their own campaign with equal spend and produced only one purchase between them. Keep one campaign per offer with all angles and tests inside; the structure isn't the lever, the creative is.
items.why: The structure isn't the lever; the creative is.

items.title: Judge by blended CPA, not by each angle
items.text: Judge by blended CPA (blended cost per purchase) and whether the business makes money, not by each angle; different angles bring different AOV buyers, so focus on core offers and unit economics.
items.why: You can't control why people buy, only whether the economics work.

items.title: A format change beat a legacy winner and the account scaled
items.text: Format can matter more than angle: in one account a new ad with a similar angle and message but a different format beat a legacy winner with hundreds of thousands in spend, CPA dropped sharply and the account scaled.
items.why: Format can matter more than angle.
items.when: accounts stuck on an aging winner

items.title: One hero ad at the top; everything else works underneath
items.text: Expect one hero ad at the top of funnel with everything else working underneath for middle and bottom; most new ads won't get big spend, and that's fine as long as they come in below target CPA.
items.why: Most marketing funnels work this way.
items.when: Meta paid social, evaluating an ad portfolio

items.title: Swipe-file loop: find, break down, reverse engineer, inject brand, draft
items.text: Run the swipe-file loop: take an example you like, break it down, reverse-engineer it for {brand} and {avatar}, and recreate it. It can run in the background in batches and deliver drafts ready for a designer.
items.why: Ad creation is reconstructing a vision for your own taste.

items.title: Choose brands to track in a spy tool, rank by variants and sort by awareness
items.text: Research which brands are scaling, pull their ads into a spy tool, sort by most variants or duplications and by angle, categorize by awareness level, then tear each down and show how to inject {brand}. Heavy duplication suggests what a brand keeps spending on.
items.why: Variants and duplication suggest what a brand keeps spending on.

items.title: Feed a run with brand, product and avatar folders full of first-party language
items.text: Trigger every creative run from brand, product and avatar folders full of first-party material: language banks, product details, offers, mechanisms, customer journey and large volumes of real customer phrases from reviews and forms. Real customer data keeps drafts on-target.
items.why: Real customer data keeps drafts on-target.

items.title: Build the avatar picture from indexed reviews, not imagination
items.text: Build the {avatar} picture (what they look like, what the problem looks like) from indexed customer reviews and brand context, not from imagination; proof-based avatars avoid wrong assumptions.
items.why: Proof-based avatars avoid wrong assumptions.
items.when: avatar visuals and AI character creation

items.title: Pick an organic ad with real engagement and swipe it
items.text: Swipe an organic post with real engagement that tells a story (in one case about a thousand likes and 130 comments) and reverse-engineer it to sell {hero product}; engagement signals the story resonates.
items.why: Engagement on an organic post signals the story resonates.

items.title: Give each AI project one job and one set of files
items.text: Give each AI project one job (market research, scripts, briefs) and load it only with the files that job needs, like a specialist employee who knows one thing well.
items.why: A narrow specialist with the right files gives better answers than one AI that is told everything.
items.when: setting up AI workspaces for marketing work

items.title: Keep every piece of research in one searchable wiki
items.text: Keep every research finding in one searchable knowledge base (e.g. Notion) connected to the AI, so you can ask for a research page by topic; always ask for the link and a one-paragraph summary to confirm it found the right page.
items.why: Research that only lives in one chat is lost; research the AI can find again makes every later brief faster and better informed.

items.title: Check the AI actually opened the right document
items.text: When the AI says it found a document, make it give the link and open it yourself; if it pulled from the wrong place, redirect it with exact directions.
items.why: AI still needs direction and can quietly grab the wrong thing.
items.when: any AI work over company documents

items.title: Feed the AI all your customer context before writing a team brief
items.text: Before writing a thesis or brief for the creative team, have the AI read your customer and market research so the brief carries real background, and hand that document to the team so they understand the why.
items.why: Teams execute better when they get the customer and market context, not just instructions.

items.title: Build the foundation pack a new strategist reads first
items.text: Give anyone joining a foundation pack: {founder} story, raw customer feedback, comment research, review research and a short partnership doc; start with the partnership doc, then go deeper. Raw customer words are the truth every decision is checked against.
items.why: The raw customer words are the bedrock every decision is checked against, so everyone must start from the same truth.
items.when: onboarding strategists, agencies or new hires

items.title: Dump raw customer feedback into AI and ask one specific question
items.text: Paste raw customer feedback-form answers straight into an AI with one very specific question, then arrange messaging around what comes back; it is the customer's own voice.
items.why: It is the customer's own voice, so anything built on it connects with the market.

items.title: Scrape comments from your top videos and sort by funnel stage
items.text: Have someone scrape comments from your all-time top videos, note the video type, label each comment top, middle or bottom of funnel, and link the video beside the comments. It shows exact customer words and which awareness stage each video attracts.
items.why: Comments show exactly what people say in their own words and what stage of awareness each video attracts.

items.title: Download competitor videos and break them down in Gemini
items.text: Download a batch of niche videos and run them through a video-capable AI (e.g. Gemini) to break down the market's language, what it watches and how competitors position; also break down competitor funnels and the other solutions people use.
items.why: You learn the market's language and positioning without guessing.

items.title: Keep a swipe bank of your own top ads and note why they won
items.text: Keep a swipe bank of your own all-time top ads and a monthly running creative-learnings doc of top videos and why you think they work; reviewing winners on a schedule turns results into rules.
items.why: Reviewing winners on a schedule turns results into rules.

items.title: Founder-led and story beats generic when targeting men
items.text: Write proven findings into the agency or partner brief so they don't retest them: in one brand, stories beat generic look-good messaging and a man speaking to men mattered.
items.why: Writing proven findings down saves the agency from repeating failed tests.

items.title: Find deeper angles beneath the obvious wash-your-face message
items.text: Give creative feedback by checking which concepts top evergreen spend, then push for a deeper, more surprising hidden cause beneath the obvious message (in one case a little-known root cause of the problem led spend). Surprising causes stop the scroll better than generic advice.
items.why: Deeper, more surprising causes stop the scroll better than the same generic skincare message.

items.title: Test whether AOV drives CPA with your own data
items.text: Test whether AOV drives CPA with your own data: in one case 33 months of orders and ad spend in an AI showed about 85% correlation, with CPA rising as AOV rose. Raising order value to fight CPA may push CPA up, so check instead of assuming.
items.why: Raising order value to fight CPA may actually push CPA up, so check the data instead of assuming.
items.when: offer and pricing decisions on paid acquisition

items.title: Show Meta a lower conversion value than you really earn
items.text: Because Meta bids against the purchase value it sees, one plan was to report a lower purchase value to Meta (about $60) while the real funnel still captured the full order (about $125); a lower visible AOV tends to bring cheaper CPAs and the extra order value is bonus margin.
items.why: If Meta sees a lower AOV, it tends to find cheaper CPAs, and the extra order value is bonus margin.
items.when: Meta pixel/conversion value setup with high-AOV funnels

items.title: Read the account history to explain why CPA moved
items.text: Read the account history month by month and match each CPA move to a change: new offer, new landing page, subscriptions, new audience, a holiday. Margin opens when something creative changes and closes as it saturates.
items.why: Knowing what caused a jump or dip tells you which lever to pull again.

items.title: Inject founder content back to bring back creative diversity
items.text: Inject {founder}-led content back into the funnel to restore creative diversity and fresh energy; in one account the founder-content period had the best margin.
items.why: Founder content was the period of best margin and keeps the market engaged.

items.title: Iterate on the winners by combining two proven elements
items.text: Iterate on winners by combining two proven elements: find top-spending creatives, read their soft metrics (CPC, CPM, watch time), then put one video's validated hook on another video's proven body.
items.why: Both parts are already validated, so the combination starts with a head start.
items.when: making variations from winning video ads

items.title: Read CPC, CPM and watch time to see what to scale
items.text: Ads with very low CPC, very low CPM or high watch time even on small spend show the market is interested and there is room to spend and convert more.
items.why: Cheap clicks and long watch times show the market is interested before purchases pile up.
items.when: paid social, choosing what to scale

items.title: Raw skits beat polished production
items.text: A raw skit with no real production value can outperform polished work; ask whether the video is just funny and real, because that feels like content, not an ad.
items.why: Real and entertaining feels like content, not an ad.

items.title: Do not fight Meta's spend allocation in one campaign
items.text: In a single-campaign structure, don't fight Meta's spend allocation with minimum spends on weaker ads; if an ad isn't spending, it isn't better than the one that is. Read spend as Meta's verdict.
items.why: Meta is already telling you which ad is best.

items.title: Use a winner to make a feedback loop of new variations
items.text: When a concept rips, keep its core message and make new versions: a new format, a new {creator}, a new angle or avatar. Spending more of the winning message in new packaging is how you keep scaling.
items.why: Spend more of the winning message in new packaging.

items.title: Start an angle from customer insights, then go deeper
items.text: Start every new angle from existing customer insights (feedback forms, ad comments, competitor video analysis loaded into an AI project), then run a second deeper round of research on top. The angle drives everything and can then be applied to any format or {creator}.
items.why: The angle is what drives everything else, so it deserves the most thinking.

items.title: You are the operator, not the AI's assistant
items.text: You are the operator of the AI, not its assistant: feed it specialized information, question how it reached every answer, and never publish fully AI-written copy, because it misses nuance in language, visuals and instinct.
items.why: AI cannot match a human's read of language, visuals and instinct.

items.title: Mine ad comments for top-of-funnel beliefs
items.text: Have an AI go through thousands of comments on a top ad and pull out the ones showing top-of-funnel beliefs (in one case that the problem is purely internal); comments from a cold audience show the ad is reaching new people whose beliefs you can speak to.
items.why: Comments that show a cold audience mean the ad is reaching new people whose beliefs you can speak to.

items.title: Do a second round of deep research before running an angle
items.text: Don't stop at the first analysis: take the top belief and run a second round asking the AI why people believe it, who teaches it to them, what is really happening, and where {hero product} fits. Round one gives a mediocre angle; round two finds the one that smashes.
items.why: Stopping at round one gives a mediocre angle; round two finds the one that smashes.

items.title: Start from what the market already believes, then find the gap
items.text: Open the ad by agreeing with a belief {avatar} already holds, show where it falls short, and place your new information in that gap; they aren't wrong, there's a missing piece. Entering through their belief makes the new idea believable rather than confrontational.
items.why: Entering through their existing belief makes the new idea believable instead of confrontational.

items.title: Know why the product works before asking AI
items.text: Before asking AI to link {hero product} to the problem, write down yourself what the product actually does and the sequence of the problem; then ask AI to check whether the claim is factual and sayable. You can't let AI decide what your product does.
items.why: You cannot let AI decide what your product does; you have to know it first.

items.title: Order angles by how broad the entry belief is
items.text: Order angles by how broad their entry belief is: use the most widely held belief (e.g. one everyone relates to) for top of funnel and narrower beliefs for niche audiences.
items.why: Broad entry points reach more people at the top of funnel.

items.title: Cross-check AI's avatar against real customers
items.text: When AI names an {avatar}, cross-check it against what real customers told you (feedback forms, behaviours like reading reviews before buying); AI can sound right and still be wrong about your buyers.
items.why: AI can sound right and still be wrong about your actual buyers.

items.title: Make the AI verify its sources before writing the brief
items.text: Before the final angle brief, tell the AI to check and re-check every element, showing sources and exact market language, with nothing invented; fix wrong facts in the ongoing document, because one wrong number spreads to every future brief.
items.why: Briefs built on invented language fail with the market; one wrong number (0.3-0.4 mm depth) spreads to every future brief.

items.title: Save the angle and creative elements into the research page
items.text: File the angle brief and its creative-elements library (what makes the ad work and the thesis behind it) in the market research doc, so future briefs and teammates reuse it without redoing research.
items.why: Future briefs and teammates can reuse the angle without redoing the research.

items.title: Pick formats your avatar actually watches, by hand
items.text: Pick formats {avatar} actually watches, by hand, instead of reusing formats from other categories (e.g. an audience that watches sports and fitness doesn't watch get-ready-with-me videos), then run your research through those formats.
items.why: A format that worked for women's skincare will not fit men who never watch it.

items.title: Prove an angle then spread it to creators
items.text: Once an angle becomes a script that works, send it to more {creator}s and adjust how it is said to fit each creator's style while keeping the angle; validated message plus new voices scales it.
items.why: Validated message plus new voices scales it.

items.title: Do not make ads before you know who you are speaking to
items.text: Don't make ads before you know who you're speaking to: swiping, UGC, podcasts and statics all fail without understanding {avatar}, and most wasted time goes to things the market was never going to respond to.
items.why: Everything depends on understanding the market first.

items.title: Know which platform serves which viewer
items.text: Know which platform serves which viewer: Meta has the full age spectrum, YouTube serves long-form podcast and trusted-influencer audiences, and TikTok shows new trends and new ways of explaining things that later reach Meta and YouTube.
items.why: Where your avatar hangs out decides the format you make.

items.title: Train a fresh account to be your avatar's feed
items.text: If you aren't {avatar}, create a fresh TikTok or Instagram account and like and search what they would, so the feed shows the organic content they see; that feed is where you find the formats your ads should look like.
items.why: The feed is where you find the formats your ad should look like.

items.title: Find formats from organic content, not competitor ads
items.text: Find new formats from viral organic content people actually scroll, not competitor ads, then ask how your research fits the format; adjacent categories are good sources. Organic gives a higher hit rate than copying competitors.
items.why: Organic shows what the market watches, giving a higher hit rate than copying competitors.

items.title: Split testing 80/20: market content vs swipes
items.text: Spend about 80% of testing on what the market is consuming now and about 20% on swiped competitor ideas, to keep ideas fresh.
items.why: Market-first keeps ideas fresh.

items.title: Write in their language, tone and humor
items.text: After angle and format, use deep customer research to learn how {avatar} speaks, what makes them laugh and what shocks them; that tone is what makes the ad work.
items.why: Raw inputs only work when delivered in the audience's own voice.

items.title: Baseline research: purchase survey with a coupon
items.text: Baseline research: email customers a short survey (in one case 12 questions with a $20 coupon) asking why they bought today, what problem they had, what they disliked and how they heard about you; ask leads why they didn't buy.
items.why: Customers and non-buyers tell you the reasons and objections in their own words.

items.title: Research the 98 percent who never answer
items.text: Feedback only comes from a small slice of customers, so mine Reddit (anonymous, detailed), YouTube (stories and professionals; watch for sponsored) and TikTok for the unaware and problem-aware majority who never talk to you.
items.why: The people who do not talk to you are most of the market.
items.when: customer research beyond your own buyers

items.title: Product-versus-competitor ads are the lazy bottom-funnel
items.text: Features-and-benefits and us-versus-them ads only work when the category is already well known; otherwise lead with awareness and stories and put features and comparisons at the end, because cold people don't care about features yet.
items.why: Most cold people do not care about features yet.

items.title: Refresh the research every month
items.text: Every month, drop the last month of feedback forms, leads, comments and Reddit/YouTube stories into an AI and ask specific questions; problems stay the same but the language evolves.
items.why: Problems stay the same but the language evolves.

items.title: Go deep on the customer's daily story
items.text: Go deep on {avatar}'s daily story: what they feel waking up and looking in the mirror, what they fear others will see, what situations they dread. Keep asking why until you reach what they don't consciously comprehend, and answer those unasked questions.
items.why: Answering the questions they are not asking themselves is what makes the marketing land.

items.title: Learn the clinical language and root cause
items.text: Learn the clinical language and root cause: look up clinical journals and medical sites, find the true root cause and what keeps the problem persistent, and tie it back to what the customer tried. Speaking both the customer's and the doctor's language creates authority.
items.why: Speaking both languages creates authority and a believable story.

items.title: Watch where the market's belief about the cause is heading
items.text: Track where the market's belief about the cause is heading and get there early: in one case comments pointed to an internal cause, so a related supplement was tested as an order bump and gained about 300 subscribers in weeks. New brands emerge on the cusp of new beliefs.
items.why: Be on the cusp of where the market is heading or someone else takes the spot.

items.title: Keep digging the root cause to find a fresh mechanism
items.text: Keep asking the next why about the root cause to find a fresh unique mechanism (in one case tracing a habit to a little-known underlying cause and building {hero product}'s mechanism around it); a deeper mechanism makes the product clearly different.
items.why: A deeper unique mechanism makes the product clearly different.

items.title: Different sub-avatars have different root causes
items.text: Different sub-avatars have different root causes for the same problem (e.g. one lifestyle causes it through friction, another through stress), so write different angles for each; identity plus cause makes the message feel personal.
items.why: Specific identity plus cause makes the message feel personal.

items.title: Tie every angle to a primal desire
items.text: Tie every angle to a primal desire {avatar} has (in one case being attractive, and being successful or a leader), so the angle stays connected to the outcome they want.
items.why: It keeps the angle tied to the outcome men want.

items.title: Deep research lifts hit rate and lowers CPC
items.text: The extra level of research shows in the numbers: in one account hit rates rose and CPCs fell, and it produced contrarian creatives.
items.why: The research shows up in the numbers.

items.title: Use cheap organic-looking statics to fill top of funnel
items.text: Put a share of budget into ultra top-of-funnel meme-style, organic-looking statics (in one case 1-30 cent clicks and about $3 CPMs) and the rest into middle-funnel creator and promotional ads; cheap top-of-funnel traffic lowers the cost of the promotional campaigns, so CAC falls as the account scales.
items.why: Cheap top-of-funnel traffic lowers the cost for the promotional campaigns that follow, so CAC comes down as the account scales.

items.title: Split budget by funnel stage
items.text: Give a set percentage of budget to ultra top of funnel and the rest to middle-funnel creator work, so the full funnel is covered and each stage does its job.
items.why: Each stage does a different job in lowering cost and scaling.

items.title: Click every link in a launched email before it sends
items.text: QA every email by clicking every link before it sends: in one case a missing slash sent a free-gift email to the wrong offer page and wasted a seasonal offer worth about $120 per customer.
items.why: Small errors waste a whole send. Launch with finesse and double check.

items.title: Compare Meta numbers to your store before trusting them
items.text: Compare Meta's reported numbers to your store before trusting them: in one case Meta reported about 1,000 purchases on $52K spend while the store showed 391 orders and $35K sales, so the setup went back to a simpler pixel configuration.
items.why: If Meta is over-reporting, you are making decisions on fake data. Simplify and compare to real orders.

items.title: Show the subscription price clearly on the offer page
items.text: Show subscription pricing clearly on the offer page: today's price, then the refill price per unit, written as 'refills monthly at <price>, skip or cancel anytime', with the most popular option pre-selected.
items.why: People should know it is a subscription and what they pick, with less friction.

items.title: Trim headline copy and remove unneeded proof on the page
items.text: Clean the top of the page: put the sub-headline right under the headline, break it onto two lines, and cut proof elements (e.g. a star-rating badge) that already appear elsewhere.
items.why: A clean top section reads faster and repeats nothing.

items.title: Test the whole path: checkout, home button, messaging
items.text: Click through the whole funnel: check it goes to the new checkout not the old one, that the home button returns to the right page, and that messaging matches throughout; mismatches make people ask where they landed.
items.why: Mismatched messages make people ask where they landed.

items.title: Use spend to tell which creative works
items.text: Use spend to see what Meta thinks is the best creative, study the top 10%, and put a fresh perspective on the fundamentals of what works.
items.why: If a creative earns more spend, it earns more results for the business.

items.title: Engagement is not sales
items.text: Engagement is not sales: views can come from the person on screen rather than the message (in one case an attractive presenter got engagement but the topic lost people). Acknowledge why it got views, but let sales data decide.
items.why: Views and engagement can come from the person, not the message.

items.title: Post one to three net-new pieces a day per platform
items.text: Post one to three net-new pieces per platform per day; reuse means a new hook on the same body, not reposting the same video.
items.why: The content system makes more than enough, and fresh content avoids looking like a repeat.

items.title: Cut one long video into three hook versions
items.text: Cut one long video (e.g. a podcast) into topic clips and make three versions of each by changing only the hook or scroll stopper; track which version has posted. Same body, new hook gives fresh content and shows which opening works.
items.why: Same body, different hook, gives you fresh content and tells you which opening works.

items.title: Match content type to funnel level
items.text: Match content type to funnel level: podcast cuts, Q&A and review reactions are middle funnel (educate without being pushy), high-production update videos are upper-funnel brand aura, and direct response or branded entertainment is separate.
items.why: Each kind of post has a different job, so schedule it accordingly.

items.title: Branded ads that entertain can go on organic social
items.text: Branded ads that genuinely entertain (e.g. a music video about the problem, a {founder} story) can also go on organic social; skip anything that looks like it is pushing people to buy, because social audiences reject posts that feel like ads.
items.why: Social audiences reject posts that feel like ads.
items.when: deciding what goes on organic channels

items.title: Bad ad examples to avoid
items.text: Keep examples of failed ads to train taste: in one brand a manipulative relationship-betrayal story and a 'what this problem costs you' calculation expected to win both failed. Not everything you think will win does.
items.why: Learning what failed teaches taste. Not everything you think will win does.

items.title: Work in threes: post version one, then version two, then learn
items.text: Work in threes: post every topic as version one, then version two, then three, and at every third cycle do a full learning on that creative to see which wording works.
items.why: Cycling variations shows which message and wording work.

items.title: When a post pops, speed up its feedback loop
items.text: When a post takes off faster, run its feedback loops faster and prioritize that creative; fast signals tell you what to make more of.
items.why: Fast signals tell you what to make more of.

items.title: Post from the phone and write captions yourself
items.text: Post from the phone, watch the video three times and write the caption yourself in the vibe of the comments, without AI; collab-post with the {creator} when the video features them to share social proof.
items.why: Captions should sound like the community; collabs share social proof.

items.title: Do not only make broad "get ready with me" videos
items.text: Broad get-ready-with-me style influencer videos get views but speak to everyone; use them only for very top of funnel and still bring the story back to the specific problem {hero product} solves.
items.why: Broad views do not sell; people with acne looking for a solution need to be addressed.

items.title: Do not be too salesy or too technical
items.text: Don't be too salesy (a hard discount pitch reaches nobody) or too technical (over-explaining happens when you haven't read the landing pages for consumable language); say the science casually, the way {avatar} would.
items.why: Natural and simple language gets people to listen.

items.title: Set up the story before the offer
items.text: Set up the story before the offer: build from hook to story to benefits to offer (e.g. a day in the life of someone with the problem, their routine, then the deal). Get people invested before features and price.
items.why: You cannot jump straight to features and price; get people invested first.

items.title: Test everything, including ugly and lo-fi
items.text: Test everything, including ugly and lo-fi: in one brand a high-production ad expected to win lost to a lo-fi version, and a scripted-sounding streamer wasn't believable. Taste is a guess; testing finds what works.
items.why: Taste is a guess; testing finds what works.

items.title: Give creators broken-down briefs, then tell them not to copy
items.text: Give {creator}s briefs built from proven videos (original script, example video, instructions, hooks, body), and tell them to use it as inspiration in their own words and format, not word for word.
items.why: A script read verbatim will not sound like them or fit their format.

items.title: Turn a concept into a different format by changing the visual hook
items.text: Turn one concept into another format by changing the visual hook: the same idea can be a selfie talk or an action clip from {avatar}'s world, with the action as the visual hook followed by the spoken line. The idea stays; format and hook fit the creator.
items.why: The idea stays; the format and visual hook fit the creator.

items.title: Creator pre-submit checklist
items.text: Give {creator}s a pre-submit checklist: would I stop scrolling, does it feel made for the viewer, is the product a natural injection, am I solving a problem or just showing products, do I sound like a helpful peer not an influencer, are lighting and quality clean, did I hit the brief's key points.
items.why: Simple self-checks catch weak videos before they cost review time.

items.title: Film extra takes and organize the raw files
items.text: Have {creator}s film a few takes of each variation without self-judging, put raw files in one folder, and name them by video and concept before sending; {editor}s only work fast on clearly labelled footage.
items.why: Editors can only work fast on clearly labelled footage.

items.title: How the team judges a posted ad: is it getting spent?
items.text: Judge a new ad simply: is it getting spend, how much, and is it within targets? If not, turn it off; if yes, keep pressing spend. A simple rule means fast, unemotional decisions.
items.why: Simple rule means fast, unemotional decisions.

items.title: Run ads through the creator's handle with partnership access
items.text: Link the {creator}'s account so ads run through their handle: they gain followers, engagement and commissions (link in bio or TikTok Shop), and weak ads can be cut without muddying their organic feed.
items.why: Creator content gets paid distribution while the creator does not risk their organic page.

items.title: A weak first video is normal; coach with multiple briefs
items.text: A weak first creator video is normal; coach with several briefs. In one case a {creator}'s first video failed, and four more briefs (more direct response, then a new angle) produced one of the top-spending ads.
items.why: The first attempt rarely hits; the coaching loop makes creators better.

items.title: Open with a reaction hook that does not look like an ad
items.text: Open with a reaction hook that doesn't look like an ad: in one top-spending ad a person reacts to a clip as if replying to a comment, never mentioning the problem at first, which opens a curiosity loop that keeps people watching before the pitch.
items.why: People keep watching to find the payoff, so you open the audience before you pitch.

items.title: Open a loop, show the product, then reveal the problem
items.text: Order a winner this way: curiosity hook, show {hero product}, the transformation, describe the situation vividly, only then name the problem, then the story and mechanism. You earn the right to talk about the problem after they're hooked.
items.why: You earn the right to talk about the problem after they are hooked.

items.title: Name a celebrity everyone knows in the hook
items.text: Name or compare to a celebrity everyone knows in the hook (ideally tied to a moment that is viral right now); familiar names make a hook relevant and funny with no explanation. Big creators work too.
items.why: Familiar names make a hook relevant with no explanation.

items.title: Watch the winners and viral videos repeatedly and ask why
items.text: Watch winning ads and viral videos over and over asking why they work, then reread the landing pages and say the language out loud until connections form. Frameworks let you manufacture creativity; being blocked means not seeing enough new things.
items.why: Frameworks help you manufacture creativity; blocked people are not inspired enough.

items.title: Test a new hook on the same video
items.text: Test a new hook on the same video before remaking it: in one case the funniest line from the middle of an ad was moved to the opening with everything else identical, and that version beat the original.
items.why: The opening hook decides the winner, so swap hooks before remaking the video.

items.title: Use a skeptical host and a live unboxing of the knockoff
items.text: Use a skeptical host doing a live side-by-side unboxing of a knockoff next to {hero product}, reacting honestly to the differences, then close with the proof claim (e.g. a patent). Real reactions prove quality better than claims and it doesn't feel like an ad.
items.why: Real reactions prove quality difference better than claims.

items.title: A winning ad is hook, lead, body, call to action in that order
items.text: A winning ad runs hook or scroll stopper, lead, narrative body, then call to action, in that order; get the hooks and leads right first, because nobody sees the rest otherwise.
items.why: Anything after the opening matters only if they stay.

items.title: Do not take plain bathroom scrubbing videos
items.text: Plain product-use footage in a neutral setting (in one brand, someone scrubbing their face in a bathroom) was tested many times and didn't move the needle; ask {creator}s for situational lifestyle content in context instead.
items.why: Lifestyle content in context draws engagement; bathroom scrubs do not.

items.title: Use your own humor as the hook
items.text: Use your own humor as the hook: what you find funny and what your audience already finds funny about you becomes the hook and caption, then bridge into the belief and the body.
items.why: A hook that sounds like you stops the scroll.

items.title: Study the foundation, then add your own sauce
items.text: Study the foundation of what already works and build your own twist on top of it, rather than tossing the base; fundamentals are the roots and your style makes them better.
items.why: Fundamentals are the roots; your style makes them better.

items.title: Better videos earn more spend and more reach
items.text: Better videos earn more reach and more spend, which brings more sales and more creator commissions; quality of the video is the lever.
items.why: Spend follows quality, so quality is the lever.

items.title: Podcast, interview and street-interview formats have the widest reach
items.text: Podcast, street-interview and streamer-style formats work like news (people want to know what's happening) and carry the widest reach; treat them as ultra top of funnel.
items.why: They carry the largest reach as a content style.

items.title: Reaction videos: react, then debunk what you believed
items.text: Reaction videos work: watch a clip, say your piece, then debunk what you used to believe. Simple, repeatable, and natural reactions don't read as ads.
items.why: Natural reactions do not read as ads.

items.title: Skits only work if done incredibly well
items.text: Skits sell through poorly because people expect entertainment, not a pitch; they either go off or don't. They only work done incredibly well: a genuinely funny performer, a studied audience (including who actually buys), and a current format trend.
items.why: Skits are high risk and need real specificity.

items.title: Barber haircut-and-explain videos go viral
items.text: Transformation content from a relevant professional (in one case a barber doing the cut, showing and explaining the product, then the after) is clean, repeatable and tends to go viral; it only works if the person really is that professional.
items.why: People love transformations.
items.when: categories with a natural professional service setting

items.title: Insider "what the CEO just said" format
items.text: Use an insider format: reenact an employee or ambassador sharing 'what the CEO just said', the research behind it, then their own problem, what they learned and their result. A story from inside {brand} feels like news.
items.why: A story from inside the brand feels like news.

items.title: Problem-focus and product-only videos do not scale
items.text: Videos that just read the page ('three reasons you have this problem') or only say 'buy it at 30% off' don't go the distance; open with a failed solution (the well-known product that wasn't working) instead.
items.why: The page already does that work, and plain product videos make little money.

items.title: Testimonials only work if engaging, serial reviews are better
items.text: Plain testimonials lack structure, so keep them for the site and organic; a serial review (day 1-7, 7-14, 14-30) is more interesting, because a review can only be said so many ways.
items.why: You can only say a review in so many ways.

items.title: Save viral reels and break down the format weekly
items.text: Each week, save viral reels from your feed, break down the format by watching it repeatedly, then work out how to inject {hero product}; feed-proven formats are cheaper to test than invented ones.
items.why: Formats proven in the feed are cheaper to test than invented ones.

items.title: Swap your brand into a proven viral concept
items.text: Swap {brand} into a proven viral concept (e.g. a meme video with a text caption): keep the mechanics and change only the wardrobe, background and caption to brand context, writing the joke around it.
items.why: You keep the proven mechanics and change only the brand and caption.

items.title: Order of work: format, then angle, then storyboard
items.text: Order the work: pick the format, pick the angle from the landing pages, then write the storyboard or shot list and film.
items.why: Having the format and the research settled lets you move into creation.

items.title: Rank formats by what has worked for you
items.text: Rank formats by what has worked for you (in one brand: reactions, skits, experiences with the problem, lifestyle integration); natural and funny beats polished, and it must look native to the feed.
items.why: Native feed content avoids looking like an ad.

items.title: Viral and selling are different; teach creators to add the sale
items.text: Teach {creator}s the difference between videos that just go viral and videos that go viral and sell; get them to add a gentle sales pitch to what they already do well, so the viewer appreciates the product, not only the laugh.
items.why: The viewer should come away appreciating the video, not only laughing.

items.title: Explain the product with a real mechanism, not just claims
items.text: Explain {hero product} with a real mechanism in plain comparisons (e.g. likening it to an everyday tool people trust), plus concrete specs, materials and a money-back guarantee; analogies and proof make it believable to cold viewers.
items.why: Plain analogies and proof make a product believable to cold viewers.

items.title: One video becomes five; one or two hit
items.text: Plan on each {creator} video becoming about five variations, expect one or two to hit, and have other briefs ready when they don't; volume plus variations finds the winner.
items.why: Volume plus variations is how you find the winner.

items.title: Creators fail from ego; know the customer deeper
items.text: Creators often fail from ego, assuming a video will work because it's creative; the real edge is knowing {avatar} at a deeper level (motivations, beliefs, language), because messages crystallize what people want for themselves.
items.why: Messages crystallize what people want for themselves.

items.title: Split the audience into age groups with different needs
items.text: Split the audience into age or life-stage groups with different problems and motivations, and give each group its own language.
items.why: Different life stages have different problems and motivations.

items.title: Know where customers live and how they dress and talk
items.text: Know where customers live (in one brand mostly large cities) and how people there dress and talk, and reflect that local language and style so videos feel native.
items.why: Local language and style make the video feel native.

items.title: Content should feel like a friend, not an ad
items.text: Content should feel like a friend explaining, not an ad: younger audiences skip ads but take a friend's advice as truth. Social is like FaceTime on a timeline.
items.why: People take friends' advice as truth.

items.title: Keep the video looking raw even when the strategy is deep
items.text: Keep the video looking raw even when the strategy is deep (in one case the top ad was a raw reaction video with over a million likes); the strategy goes underneath and the surface stays natural.
items.why: Knowing the audience lets you predict the reaction without making it look produced.

items.title: Turn a winning video script into a static brief in the same chat
items.text: Turn a winning video script into a static brief in the same AI chat: ask it to pull objections, write rebuttals and lead with product and offer; in one case it produced six static concepts with headlines, body and trust elements.
items.why: One refined script becomes many assets without redoing research.
items.when: extending a video concept into statics

items.title: Match the ad to the audience awareness level
items.text: Match the ad to awareness: for retargeting (most aware) lead with product and offer and hit one core objection (e.g. knockoffs can't do this, no subscription). Warm people need the offer and a reason to say yes, not education.
items.why: Warm people need the offer and a reason to say yes, not education.

items.title: Do direct response, then statics, then UGC
items.text: Develop the script as direct response first, then statics, then a simpler UGC creator version (phone, talking to camera, less ad-like); each format comes from the same research.
items.why: Each format is simpler; they all come from the same research.

items.title: Lo-fi product images beat polished ones
items.text: Polished statics work, but statics that look like a phone photo of the product worked even better in testing; raw feels real.
items.why: Raw feels real.

items.title: Check the offer facts in the AI prompt
items.text: Check offer facts in every AI prompt: in one case the AI wrote the wrong discounted price and missed a free gift. AI invents details, and a wrong price ruins an ad.
items.why: AI invents details, and wrong prices ruin an ad.

items.title: Give the image model your real product photos and fix wrong details
items.text: Give the image model real product photos and correct wrong details in the prompts (in one case the product color came out wrong); compare models at the target aspect ratio (e.g. 9:16) and pick what looks real.
items.why: Image models guess product details unless you give references.

items.title: Use AI freely for product pictures but be careful with people
items.text: AI is fine for product-based statics because viewers are less skeptical of product images; for people, use real UGC from the archive, because fake-looking people hurt trust.
items.why: Fake-looking people hurt trust; products are hard to tell apart.

items.title: Test every good static, do not pre-pick the winner
items.text: Test every good static instead of pre-picking the winner; you can't know which will perform until it spends.
items.why: You cannot know which will perform until it spends.

items.title: Avoid AI tells in copy such as hyphens and dashes
items.text: Cut long dashes and hyphen patterns that signal AI-written copy before using lines in an ad; viewers spot AI writing.
items.why: Viewers and readers spot AI writing.

items.title: Build creative learnings, culture and variations into the brief before production
items.text: Before production, run this sequence: creative learnings from the account, break down the winner, rewrite it with culture, turn it into a video brief with variations, then extract statics. The {editor} can start while statics test in parallel.
items.why: The editor can start while statics are tested in parallel.

items.title: Build a culture document and a sales-language document first
items.text: For a sale or discount ad, have an AI scan all comments, reviews, feedback and lead forms, pull only those about price or sales, and extract how those people talk (culture) and how they describe a sale; save both as markdown files and write from them.
items.why: Writing in how customers actually talk about price makes the ad believable.
