items.title: Ask the AI for one narrow task at a time
items.text: Ask the AI for one narrow task at a time and spell out the stages in the prompt (go through all documents, then find only people talking about X, then extract the culture); vague requests get shallow answers.
items.why: Detailed, staged asks produce exactly what you need.

items.title: Hear the budget behind "too expensive"
items.text: Hear the budget behind 'too expensive': in one case the comments said waiting for payday, out of budget, times are hard. Use that real meaning as the hook ('times are tough') and speak to the root cause.
items.why: Real meaning behind an objection becomes a stronger hook.

items.title: Ask AI to find gaps between your script and the research
items.text: Give the AI your finished script plus the customer-language research and ask it to list gaps (skepticism, past-failure validation, emotional intensity, 'finally' framing, vague claims), then choose which to add. Stay open to what the data shows.
items.why: Your own script can miss what customers say; an outside check finds it.

items.title: Use their words: expensive as hell, not pricey
items.text: Replace polished marketing words with customers' exact phrases (e.g. 'expensive as hell' rather than 'pricey'), and do one more rewrite for raw conversational language while keeping clear English.
items.why: Raw language feels like a person; marketing language feels like an ad.

items.title: Retargeting script: acknowledge the objection, then drop the price and the value
items.text: Write retargeting scripts like a salesperson greeting someone returning to the store: acknowledge skepticism, state the price drop and any free gift, no subscription, then mechanism, results timeline, guarantee and a low refund-rate line. They're ready to buy and want the deal plus reasons to trust it.
items.why: They are ready to buy and want the deal plus reasons to trust it.
items.when: retargeting / most-aware audiences during a promotion

items.title: Remove an angle that excludes people when the goal is reach
items.text: When the goal is reach, cut lines that narrow the audience (in one case a founder-identity mention) and keep the script on the ad's single message; that point can become its own angle for a specific audience.
items.why: Keep the script on the single message of the ad.

items.title: Hand the editor a shot list and style guide from the script
items.text: Give the AI the final script and your previous editor-guide format, have it produce a shot list and style guide, link the editing SOP, and add creator A-roll and any special B-roll, so the {editor} can execute with finesse.
items.why: The editor needs clear instructions to execute with finesse.

items.title: Make three hooks and three scroll stoppers for each script
items.text: After the baseline script, make three hook variations and three scroll-stopper variations on the same body, keeping only ones that relate to the ad's core message; hooks are the cheapest thing to vary and have the biggest effect.
items.why: Hooks are the cheapest thing to vary and have the biggest effect.

items.title: Heavy research is what separates your creative
items.text: A few hours of heavy, granular research with AI can replace the work of two or three people, and that depth plus speed is what separates and scales your creative.
items.why: Depth and speed together are the advantage.

items.title: Make a validated message into many formats
items.text: Once a message is validated, turn it into many formats: direct-response video, skit, statics, podcast, {founder} versions, and {creator} UGC. That is how proven messaging scales.
items.why: One proven message earns many different ads.

items.title: Check translated or non-native copy for natural U.S. phrasing
items.text: Check translated or non-native copy for natural phrasing in the target market (read it aloud and fix awkward lines), because awkward phrasing signals an ad.
items.why: Awkward phrasing signals an ad.
items.when: copy written by non-native writers or translated

items.title: Tie every script back to the current core angle
items.text: Tie every script back to the current core angle and the landing page it sends to, in the line that explains what {hero product} does; the ad and page must carry the same story.
items.why: The ad and the page must carry the same story.

items.title: Broaden a line so it does not exclude part of the audience
items.text: Broaden lines that would exclude part of the audience (e.g. a softer verb so people who don't do the specific behavior aren't alienated), to reach the less-aware edge of the aware audience. Narrow wording shrinks the market.
items.why: Narrow wording shrinks the market you can reach.

items.title: Make a version for each problem the same offer fits
items.text: Make a version of the script for each problem the same offer fits, when those angles are also proven; same offer, more audiences.
items.why: Same offer, more audiences.

items.title: Use the audience's apps for specific culture jokes
items.text: Use the apps and habits of {avatar}'s life for specific culture jokes (e.g. dating-app photo filters for younger buyers, a different line for married buyers); specific, believable details make people feel seen.
items.why: Specific, believable details make people feel seen.

items.title: Copy before edit: update the edit list when the copy changes
items.text: Lock copy before editing, then refine the edit list; editing needs copy, and rewrites after editing waste time.
items.why: Rewrites after editing waste time.

items.title: Make a sales ad feel like a favor, not a sale
items.text: Make even a sales ad sound like a friend doing a favor ('you asked for this deal, I got you'), and add one more pass of language matching and culture refinement after the first rewrite.
items.why: Less salesy delivery hits differently.

items.title: Revitalize a winning ad: update language only, keep the structure
items.text: To revitalize a winning ad, give the AI the original script, the scene-by-scene and the creative learnings, and update only the language for the new campaign, not the format or copy structure; then write a detailed scene-by-scene for {editor}s.
items.why: The ad worked for known reasons; change the words, not the winning structure.

items.title: Fill the brief tracker fields every time
items.text: Fill every brief-tracker field each time: campaign, awareness, type, {creator}, {editor}, designer, folder, format, identity, length, problem, performance, status. A complete tracker lets editor, {media buyer} and strategist see what's next without asking.
items.why: A complete tracker lets editor, media buyer and strategist see what is next without asking.

items.title: Match editors to what they are best at
items.text: Assign {editor}s by strength (e.g. one for direct-response ads, one for short-form organic, a separate graphic designer); specialization speeds work.
items.why: People specialize; right fit speeds work.

items.title: Let an ad run a week, then grade it S, A, B or not performing
items.text: Let an ad run about a week before judging, do creative learnings weekly, and grade each ad S, A, B, didn't perform, or still testing. The algorithm needs time to learn, and a standard grade avoids opinion fights.
items.why: The algorithm needs time to learn, and a standard grade avoids opinion fights.

items.title: Embed the original winning video in the brief
items.text: Embed the original winning video in the brief with the analysis link above it, so the {editor} sees what to match without hunting.
items.why: Unclear links cause confusion.

items.title: Analyze the ads that failed too
items.text: Run creative learnings on ads that failed too, to avoid repeating them and keep any good parts.
items.why: Understanding why something did not work prevents the same mistake.

items.title: AI does the repetitive work, your eye does the taste
items.text: AI does the repetitive work (transcription, injection); your eye does the taste. Still read every AI script or scene list scene by scene and decide what to keep, because it's strong but not bulletproof.
items.why: AI output is strong but not bulletproof.

items.title: Archive every top ad with its breakdown in the banknotes
items.text: Archive every top ad with its ad link (so you can read comments), transcript, scene-by-scene breakdown, analysis notes and iteration recommendations; when ads fatigue, go back to why things worked and merge old fundamentals with new trends.
items.why: When ads fatigue you can go back to why things worked and merge old fundamentals with new trends.

items.title: Understand why it worked before making variations
items.text: Understand why an ad worked before making variations; then make fewer, more intentional variations instead of endless copies.
items.why: Intent beats volume without understanding.

items.title: Scale by multiplying formats and creators for a few core messages
items.text: Scaling isn't writing more scripts; it's taking a few high-frequency core messages and having many {creator}s and formats explain the same message.
items.why: A few proven messages repeated by many voices resonate.

items.title: Ego does not matter until you see the data
items.text: Bring marketing fundamentals but expect most of what you think will win to fail; ego doesn't matter until you see the data, and you only learn from what really spent.
items.why: You only learn from what really spent.

items.title: Run learnings on the ads that take over half the budget
items.text: Run creative learnings on the ads taking over half the budget: look at one campaign over 14 days, sort by spend, and study the top five or six (in one case $25K of $35K).
items.why: The top spenders are the ones that really work.

items.title: Break each winner down in Gemini with a standard prompt
items.text: Break down each winner in a video-capable AI (e.g. Gemini) with one saved prompt asking for transcript, scene-by-scene, visual elements, audio, hook and structure, style, emotional triggers, market awareness and sophistication level, plus a style name, so every winner is comparable.
items.why: A standard breakdown makes every winner comparable.

items.title: Do the analysis with your own eyes before AI polishes it
items.text: Watch a winning ad over and over and break it down line by line and scene by scene yourself before handing the extracted elements to an AI model. Doing the analysis first trains your own judgment about why ads work.
items.why: Better marketers sell more product.
items.when: ad teardown and swipe analysis, before using AI to summarize

items.title: A discount ad dies when the offer changes
items.text: A discount ad built around one specific {offer} (e.g. buy two get one free) becomes useless the moment that offer ends, and it pulls in people who want the deal rather than the value. Keep the ad message and the page offer matched.
items.why: The message on the ad and the page must match.
items.when: promo and holiday ads tied to a time-limited offer

items.title: Hook words came straight from customer comments
items.text: Take hook wording straight from customer comments (in one example, 'too pricey' and 'insane deal' came from comments about the {hero product}). Real customer words make an ad feel native.
items.why: Ads built from real language feel native.
items.when: writing hooks for social ads, especially price-objection ads

items.title: Forced subscriptions broke trust
items.text: Forcing a default subscription on buyers can erode trust over time; loyal customers who feel tricked warn others. In one case, after nearly a year of default subscriptions, {brand} went back to a simple {offer} (a percentage off plus a free add-on, no subscription).
items.why: Trust matters more than a short-term lift.
items.when: offer design and checkout defaults for repeat-purchase products

items.title: Add the word parasite for urgency and explain the mechanism clearly
items.text: Name the root cause in vivid terms that create urgency (in one test, calling it a 'parasite' did this) and clearly explain the mechanism: the part of the {hero product} that makes the change happen. A believable 'how' is what makes cold buyers believe.
items.why: Cold buyers need a believable how.
items.when: problem-aware ads and pages for cold traffic

items.title: Paint the timeline and avoid early feature talk
items.text: Spend most of the ad painting the result timeline (e.g. week one smoother, week three fewer breakouts, week six not checking your face) before features, and keep any feature mention short and simple. Features come late, after belief.
items.why: Features come late, after belief.
items.when: ad scripts and VSLs for a transformation product

items.title: Give away the sticky repeat product to win the second order
items.text: Give away your stickiest repeat-purchase item free with the first order, so buyers try it, like it and come back to buy several at a time. A free first item sets up the second order.
items.why: A free first item sets up a repeat purchase.
items.when: first-order offer design for brands with a consumable add-on

items.title: Use risk reversal in the close
items.text: Close with stacked risk reversal: a long guarantee, a warranty, a loyalty credit for sending results, and the return-rate stat (in one example, '96% never return it, so the 4% get all their money back'). Say it the way customers say it.
items.why: It lowers the fear of trying.
items.when: the close of ads, VSLs and offer pages

items.title: Record yourself reviewing, then give the transcript to Claude
items.text: Record yourself talking through what you learned from an ad review, give the transcript and the original script to an AI model, and have it rewrite the script with those learnings and offer changes; then fine-tune by hand. Talking is fast and the AI does the rewrite.
items.why: Talking through is fast; AI does the rewrite.
items.when: iterating on ad scripts after a review

items.title: Writing comes first; visuals adapt with the platform
items.text: Writing comes first because it sets the scene; visuals layer on top and change with the platform (formats like comment-reply videos did not exist a few years ago). Copy is the base that lasts.
items.why: Copy is the base; visuals adapt.

items.title: Check small visual details: Android vs iPhone, casting signals
items.text: Check small visual cues: match the phone and emoji style most of your {avatar} uses (in one case iPhone, not Android), and know that who you cast in the opening can signal the platform to find similar people, so cast broadly when you want broad reach.
items.why: Small cues change who the ad is shown to and who trusts it.
items.when: Meta and short-form video ads, during creative review

items.title: Remove outdated product shots from the scenes
items.text: Never show products or bundles you no longer sell; update scenes to the current {offer} (e.g. use the {hero product}, then hold up the free add-on). Old items confuse buyers.
items.why: Showing old items confuses buyers.

items.title: Stop stealing stock clips; make your own B-roll
items.text: Stop using borrowed or stolen stock clips and make your own B-roll in house; borrowed content is a risk and does not scale. Humor in B-roll still helps an ad stand out.
items.why: Borrowed clips are a risk and cannot be reused.

items.title: AI misses the small details; check with your eyes
items.text: AI scene analysis misses small details (who exactly is on screen, what an on-screen comment says, emoji style), so review scenes with your own eyes. Those details decide trust.
items.why: Details like these decide trust.
items.when: using AI to break down or QA video ads

items.title: Prioritize by spend that still runs the business
items.text: Prioritize ads by how much you can spend on them while still running the business, and by their results, never by feeling. Check the last 14 days for trends and today for new pages.
items.why: Spend plus results is the only basis that matters.
items.when: paid media decisions and creative prioritization

items.title: Three kinds of weak ads: brain dead and over-polished
items.text: The weakest ads are 'brain dead' ones (pure AI voice, weak language, no emotion) and over-polished studio ads; lo-fi selfie/phone-style and reaction videos beat them. Life and rawness beat finish.
items.why: Life and rawness beat finish.
items.when: short-form video ads on social platforms

items.title: Hook the comment: show the objection on screen
items.text: Open a sales ad with a comment reply that shows the objection on screen (e.g. 'will you do a sale soon, it's too expensive'), then show the {hero product}. Answering a question people actually asked grabs attention.
items.why: Answering a question people actually asked gets attention.
items.when: offer and price-objection ads on social

items.title: Repeatedly study the ads to absorb copy, language and clips
items.text: Study winning ads repeatedly; over time you absorb the copy, language, clips and what makes an ad last. That pattern recognition is what lets you create the next winner.
items.why: Pattern recognition makes you able to create the next one.

items.title: Mutate the framework of an old offer ad to the new offer
items.text: When an {offer} ends, turn the old offer ad off and rewrite the same script, clips and framework for the new offer and the current season. The structure is what sold; only the offer changes.
items.why: The structure sold; only the offer changes.
items.when: offer changes and seasonal refreshes of proven ads

items.title: Replace stock footage with real creator UGC when remaking
items.text: When remaking an old high-production ad, swap stock footage for real high-quality {creator} UGC while keeping the big, powerful opening text. Real creators feel more real than stock.
items.why: Real creators now exist and feel more real than stock.
items.when: remaking past winning ads once creator content exists

items.title: Match the ad to a landing page for the same angle
items.text: Match each ad to a landing page built for the same angle; in one case the same video at the same CPM and spend saw CPC fall nearly 50% on an angle-matched page. Build standardized pages per angle where only the hero, bullets and problem language change.
items.why: When ad and page line up, clicks and conversions improve.
items.when: paid traffic to landing pages, multiple angles running

items.title: Re-test old ads on the new matching page
items.text: Before killing old creative, re-test it on a page that fits its angle; in one case videos that did nothing months earlier worked once sent to a matching page. The page may have been the missing piece.
items.why: The page was the missing match.
items.when: after launching a new angle-specific landing page

items.title: Spend 70 to 80 percent on iterating winners, 20 to 30 on new tests
items.text: Spend about 70-80% of creative effort iterating on winners and 20-30% max on new tests. If a test fails, compare it to the baseline and rerun with a higher baseline if it was far off.
items.why: Compounding winners beats random new ideas.

items.title: Scout creators who just made a trending video
items.text: When a funny video in a current trend appears, visit the {creator}'s page, watch their content, and DM from the {brand} account offering a collab with a specific product angle tied to the trend; if no reply, use the email on their page.
items.why: Trending creator plus relevant product angle is a fast match.

items.title: Do not templatize outreach DMs
items.text: Do not templatize creator outreach DMs: watch some of their videos and write a relevant, human message. Run outreach daily at high volume, but each message should feel personal.
items.why: Generic DMs get ignored.

items.title: Find creators who have not blown up yet
items.text: The real value is finding rising {creator}s before they blow up; big creators have managers, answer slowly and cost more.
items.why: Smaller creators answer and cost less.

items.title: Run creators through a group chat and ask for an angle first
items.text: Run qualified {creator}s in one group chat where they see others posting, and before inviting each, agree what product angle you could do together. The goal is experiences and funny videos with the {hero product} built in, not ads.
items.why: Group chat builds energy; angle clarity keeps content on-brand.

items.title: Culture-fit creators to the market
items.text: Pick {creator}s who fit the culture of your {avatar}; content must be funny, have on-point music, or show world-class skill, and humor scales best. Culture fit decides whether it lands.
items.why: Culture fit decides whether it lands.
items.when: creator selection for a culturally specific market

items.title: Read creator ads by 7-day spend and CPM
items.text: Read {creator}-led ads by last-7-day spend and CPM (in one example about $2,500 spend at an $11 CPM meant reaching people at a good cost), ask why the top spenders are spending, and make variations of them. More spend means the platform rates the video higher.
items.why: More spend on a video means Meta thinks it is better, like more views organically.
items.when: Meta paid social, reviewing creator ads

items.title: Feedback: problem-aware bathroom video, make the hook readable
items.text: Make the hook text readable: black on white (or the reverse) and moved off the face. Exaggerate the 'before' state in a funny way, not a fake one. A hook people cannot read does not stop the scroll.
items.why: A hook people cannot read does not stop the scroll.

items.title: Add a "why" line between the problem and the product
items.text: After showing the {hero product}, add one or two lines explaining what is happening in the problem (the cause) before the features, then a clear {offer} line. A little education makes it feel like a conversation, not a pitch.
items.why: A little education makes it feel like a conversation, not a pitch.

items.title: Fun music videos can add engagement even if they do not sell
items.text: Keep a mix of problem-aware content and just-for-fun content (e.g. a mini song about the problem); fun pieces can drive engagement and some spend even if they are not expected to sell. Entertainment feeds the top of the funnel.
items.why: Entertainment feeds the top of funnel.
items.when: content mix for paid and organic social

items.title: Barber transformation video: integrated demo, not an ad
items.text: An expert-practitioner demo works as integrated content: a funny scroll stopper, the {hero product} used in the process, the before and after, and client feedback. Replace 'my discount code' with a named gift ('my link to get the product plus the free add-on') so the {offer} is tangible.
items.why: A named gift is clearer than an unspecified discount.

items.title: Pull a funny moment out as its own hook
items.text: Pull a funny moment out of a longer video and use it as its own looping hook before the rest of the video. A funny moment is already a tested scroll stopper.
items.why: A funny moment is already a tested scroll stopper.

items.title: Bring your own ethos and context to the content
items.text: Have each {creator} bring their own ethos and context to the content (in one case a barber who is also an image consultant: 'your image is your income'). Authentic context stands out more than a generic script.
items.why: Authentic context beats generic scripts.

items.title: The stole-my-boyfriend's-skincare angle lets women sell to men
items.text: A woman can sell a men's product authentically with an angle like 'I stole my boyfriend's skincare because it works better'; the hook should make the angle clear, then explain the problem before the {hero product}.
items.why: Women can be authentic voices for the product too.
items.when: brands selling to one gender, looking for new voices

items.title: Give comedic creators situations with a slight product intro
items.text: Give comedic {creator}s a situation with only a light product intro, no hard sell; in one case a skit like this got heavy engagement. Use characters tied to the problem and just make the product appear.
items.why: Entertainment earns attention; the product just needs to appear.

items.title: Skeptic-to-believer testimonial arc
items.text: A skeptic-to-believer arc works: a real {creator} unboxes skeptically, gives week-by-week updates, admits it worked, and ends on the full {offer} (free add-on, no subscription, free shipping, guarantee and warranty). Skepticism turning into belief overcomes objections.
items.why: Skepticism that turns into belief overcomes objections.

items.title: Educational ads can carry the budget
items.text: Longer education-first ads (what is causing the problem, why other products fail) can carry most of the budget; they move through hook, root cause, why nothing worked, solution, and bring the {hero product} in only at the end. Narrative and education make a video worth watching, so it can absorb more spend.
items.why: Education lets you spend more because it feels like a video worth watching.

items.title: Do both: creator content and bigger educational ads
items.text: Run both layers at once: organic-style {creator} UGC and bigger educational ads that teach the market, using the creator voice in the education.
items.why: Different layers do different jobs.

items.title: Map the creative into five layers: educate, entertain, persuade, prove, buy
items.text: Map creative into five layers: educate the market, entertain it, persuade by showing the product in situation, prove (testimonials, experts), then just-buy-it promos. Focus most on the upper funnel; promotions matter least.
items.why: Promotions matter least; upper funnel builds demand.

items.title: Authority figures are a layer above testimonials
items.text: Authority figures are a layer above testimonials: practitioners show how to use it, and scientific or trusted health voices add authority. Use someone with real authority to speak on the science; the messenger changes how believable the claim is.
items.why: The messenger changes how believable the claim is.

items.title: Contrarian creative: make people question what they believe
items.text: Make contrarian ads that push viewers to question a belief they hold (e.g. that their current method cannot solve the problem, only the {hero product} can). Once they question it, you can shift it and replace their old product.
items.why: Changing belief is what changes buying behavior.

items.title: The flow: research, brief, in-house formats, creators to scale, editing, deploy
items.text: Run creative as one flow: research (customer calls, street interviews) -> briefs -> in-house production (podcasts, street interviews, authority figures) -> {creator}s scaling proven briefs -> editing -> deploy. Research comes first; without it you cannot write a brief.
items.why: Without knowing what people watch and how they word problems, you cannot write a brief.
items.when: setting up a creative production system

items.title: Diversify both format and medium for each brief
items.text: Make each brief in several formats (podcast, street interview, authority figure) and also as a static. Diversifying both format and medium gives the most shots on goal.
items.why: More angles on the same idea raise the chance one hits.

items.title: Founder content: react to objections and creator content
items.text: Have the {founder} film content answering objections (behind the scenes, warehouse) and react to {creator} and in-house content, especially new objections from comments not yet addressed. Founder videos are best for objections and credibility.
items.why: Founder videos are best for objections and credibility.

items.title: Editing is simple: real B-roll, clean captions, quick cuts
items.text: Keep editing simple: real B-roll, clean TikTok/Instagram-style captions, quick cuts, small visual nuggets, sound effects, and music only if it fits (none in truly organic or in-situation content). Native-feeling edits keep it from looking like an ad.
items.why: Native-feeling edits keep it from looking like an ad.

items.title: A brief is a hypothesis; loop learnings back
items.text: Treat every brief as a hypothesis: after deploy, check spend, hooks and layout to see whether it worked and why, then loop the learnings back to {creator}s. Test, understand, then scale.
items.why: Test then understand, then scale.

items.title: Weekly delivery of new creatives in one clean folder
items.text: Get a weekly delivery of new creatives as downloaded files plus a link in one clean folder, so the {media buyer} can upload straight to the ad account. Speed to the account is speed to scale.
items.why: Speed to the account is speed to scale.

items.title: Bolt a reaction onto a proven video structure
items.text: Bolt a fresh opening (e.g. the {founder} green-screened reacting to a {creator} clip) onto a proven video structure (pick up the product, unbox, demo). You reuse the proven story and only add a new start.
items.why: You reuse the proven story and add a fresh opening.
items.when: making new variations of a proven video

items.title: Put the sauce back: keep hooks short and culture-specific
items.text: Keep hooks short and culture-specific; tell {creator}s when a line they said mid-video is the hook and to open on it. Use comedy at the very top of funnel, then education, then bottom-funnel offers.
items.why: Comedy transcends and gets people together.
items.when: creator feedback and funnel content mix

items.title: Hand editors an organized event shoot with a viewing order
items.text: After a big shoot or event, sort footage by type (POV, interviews, B-roll, scripted intro) and give the {editor} a viewing order: which clips are cleanest to cut first and where real B-roll goes under the script. A clear map lets editors cut many pieces fast.
items.why: A clear map lets editors cut many pieces fast.

items.title: Use the analysis tool on organic videos to find hooks and key elements
items.text: Save organic videos that work, upload several at once to a video-analysis AI tool to pull scenes, transcript, hooks and key elements, then feed that to a writing model to craft a new video. A working organic video is the bedrock to build from.
items.why: Analyzing a working organic video gives you a bedrock to build from.
items.when: turning organic swipes into new scripts

items.title: Reuse a script by swapping the authority figure
items.text: Reuse a working script by swapping the authority figure: keep the script and replace the speaker with whoever fits ({founder}, a real expert, or a known character). Authority is a swappable slot.
items.why: Authority is a swappable slot.

items.title: Speed and accuracy beat polish
items.text: Speed and accuracy beat polish: in one case 9 videos were edited in about 2 hours, three scroll-stopper variations of one were launched overnight, and they spent right away. Follow headline, scroll stopper, caption, lead and body, and cut the fluff.
items.why: Fast and correct beats beautiful.

items.title: Segment customers into cohorts and give cashback by cohort
items.text: Build a view of customer LTV and repeat rate, segment customers into cohorts (one-time, one-time high value, returning, loyal, VIP) and give tiered cashback credit (in one example 5/10/10/15/20%) to push each group up a level.
items.why: Knowing what each group does lets you incentivize the next step.
items.when: retention program for a store with repeat buyers

items.title: Email calendar baseline: daily sends and segmented content
items.text: Run a daily email and SMS calendar with at least two sends a day as a baseline, more to specific segments, and a daily email to non-customers on why to become one. Flows end after one pass, so ongoing follow-ups win the sale.
items.why: Follow-up and reminders land the buy when one message resonates.

items.title: Move a brief through the board after it is written
items.text: Keep work statuses true to reality: once a brief is done, move it from idea to creating on the brief board, assign the {creator} and send them the link. Statuses keep everyone on the same page.
items.why: Statuses keep every person on the same page.

items.title: Study who is actually in your customer base
items.text: Find out who your highest-value customers actually are (e.g. athletes, executives, doctors, military) and use them as real status signals across email, ads, social and landing pages. Real customers are the best proof and show who you are talking to.
items.why: Real customers make the best proof, and tell you who you are talking to.

items.title: Write to the high-value man: respect his time, no deceit
items.text: Write to the high-value customer the way he sees himself: he dislikes wasted time and deceit, trusts recommendations and likes clean experiences, so use top-in-class, motivational language with useful insights, not spam.
items.why: Tone should match who he sees himself as.
items.when: copy for a premium or status-driven {avatar}

items.title: Pull real-time culture into your messaging
items.text: Feed real-time culture (Reddit, news, what customers are thinking about) into messaging so copy joins today's conversation; respect all cultures and avoid political negativity. A conversation leads to the sale.
items.why: Joining the conversation first earns the sale.

items.title: Use the AI baseline, then add your best work
items.text: Use AI dashboard output as baseline thinking, not verbatim, so your time goes to adding value, your own voice notes and market conversations. AI does the repetitive baseline; humans add insight.
items.why: AI does the repetitive baseline, humans add the insight.

items.title: Send every new customer to a portal that answers how to use it
items.text: Send every new customer to a portal that answers how to use the product (guides, routines, a streak tracker, community, reviews). Customers who know how to use it get results and stay.
items.why: Customers who know how to use it get results and stay.

items.title: Keep one core message across all touch points
items.text: Keep one core message across every touch point (customer service, email, ads, organic, packaging), held in a brand bible. Consistency builds belief and trust.
items.why: Consistency builds belief and trust.

items.title: Map the flows so you can diagnose a revenue dip
items.text: Map each email flow (welcome, browse abandon, cart abandon, post-purchase) so a revenue dip can be traced; in one case a welcome series starved because the {media buyer} turned off top-of-funnel ads. Upstream and downstream are connected.
items.why: Everything upstream and downstream is connected.

items.title: Message delays before they complain
items.text: When orders are delayed or on pre-order, trigger proactive updates to that segment (at the warehouse, shipped) instead of waiting for complaints. Tell people before they get angry.
items.why: Tell people before they get angry.

items.title: Sell status: loyalty tiers, leaderboards, store credit
items.text: Sell status with game mechanics: loyalty tiers, leaderboards, hall of fame, streaks verified with new photos, visible store credit in emails, and invitations. Gamification drives repeat purchase and community.
items.when: loyalty and retention for a status-driven {avatar}

items.title: Real human signals beat fabricated polish
items.text: Real human signals (the right clothes, a detail like a nice watch, genuine words from your own story) show taste and authenticity; put real care in so the work does not read as generic. As fake content spreads, real connection is the advantage.
items.why: As fake content spreads, real connection is the advantage.

items.title: Make Instagram feed thumbnails interesting
items.text: Give every Instagram post a thumbnail with a headline and an interesting scene, not a person caught mid-sentence, and check how it looks in the grid. Only interesting tiles get the click.
items.why: When someone scrolls the feed, only an interesting tile gets the click.

items.title: Read an email report by awareness level
items.text: Read email reports by awareness level: culture and lifestyle emails are upper funnel and will not make the most money; revenue comes from problem-solution, product-aware and most-aware emails.
items.why: Different stages liquidate at different points.

items.title: A weak email to a cold list still builds the list
items.text: A weak email sent to cold leads and first-time buyers still has value: in one case a flop still made $208 and opens that would not have existed, warming the list for later.
items.why: Cherry-picking re-engaged people has value beyond that send.
items.when: sending to cold or unengaged segments

items.title: Use report patterns to decide what to film next
items.text: Use report patterns to decide what to make next: when certain problem-topic emails worked, push related video into the same segment and add customer stories. Results show where to feed more of the same.
items.why: Results show where to feed more of the same.
items.when: planning content from email or ad results

items.title: Ask why it worked before every new piece
items.text: Before every new piece, go back to what worked and why you think it worked; each new piece should improve on a reason, not be a random idea. Anchoring in 'why' gives better shots on goal.
items.why: Anchoring in why gives better shots on goal.

items.title: Keep a proven script structure, update references
items.text: Keep a proven VSL structure and refresh its references with recall moments the audience knows (popular shows, famous sports moments). Familiar references make the point easy to take in.
items.why: Familiar recall moments make the point easy to take in.

items.title: Show real authority; price objection hooks are short-lived
items.text: Founder-story ads work by showing real authority: step by step how the {founder} solved the problem, with before and afters. Price-objection hooks work but are short-lived; proof is what converts a first-time viewer.
items.why: Authority converts strangers into buyers.

items.title: No top-of-funnel ads means CPA spikes
items.text: If the top-spending ads are all low-funnel creative, CPA spikes because nothing feeds the funnel; ad frequency tells you where an ad sits. Bottom-funnel ads need new people to work on.
items.why: Bottom funnel ads need new people to work on.
items.when: Meta paid social, diagnosing rising CPA

items.title: Relaunching many old ads at once makes CPA volatile
items.text: When CPA jumps, ask what changed first, such as turning many old ads back on at once; a mix of old high-spend ads and new ones is volatile and needs time to stabilize.
items.why: Know what you changed before reacting to a spike.
items.when: Meta paid social, after major account changes

items.title: Keep stable older VSLs running while new assets prove out
items.text: Keep older VSLs with stable CPA running as the account's bedrock while you keep fishing for new top-of-funnel assets to take over; do not go all bottom-funnel.
items.why: Stability protects the account while testing.
items.when: Meta paid social, during creative testing

items.title: Do not turn off the top-of-funnel ads that hold blended CPA
items.text: Do not turn off the prospecting ads that hold blended CPA; in one case two of them kept blended CPA near $75 and close to front-end break-even, and when they were turned off only high-frequency retargeting and offer ads remained and CPA spiked.
items.why: Without a stable base, the account becomes unstable.

items.title: Turn back on what worked until new creative proves itself
items.text: Turn back on proven top-of-funnel ads and the best bottom-funnel partnership ad, upload new ads, and let new creative earn spend against them. Never turn off proven ads without a replacement.
items.why: No fresh asset can scale yet.
items.when: Meta paid social, when no new asset can scale yet

items.title: Stop frequent toggling; judge after letting ads run
items.text: Stop toggling many ads on and off, which creates anomalies; in one case turning off only obvious low performers in week one and letting the rest run improved blended CPA. Fewer, deliberate changes give clearer reads.
items.why: Fewer, deliberate changes give clearer reads.

items.title: Spot an untouched angle from reviews and expert conversations
items.text: Reread reviews and talk with domain experts to spot under-served problems your product solves (in one case a sub-problem specific to one skin type), then brief a mini VSL on why existing solutions fail for that group. Under-served problems in your reviews are open lanes.
items.why: Under-served problems in your reviews are open lanes.

items.title: Use review words for statics and ad language
items.text: Pull specific phrases from reviews about a new angle and use them in statics and video ads. Customers' own words convert.
items.why: Their words convert.

items.title: Test a new landing page, compare spend to downstream revenue
items.text: When testing a new landing page, send it a share of traffic and compare spend to downstream revenue per page; in one test the new page returned $1,300 on $1,500 spend while the main page returned $2,600 on $1,200.
items.why: Same traffic, different pages, clear numbers.
items.when: landing page tests on paid traffic

items.title: Turn off without emotion when the data is clear
items.text: When data on real spend shows an ad you expected to win is underperforming, turn it off without emotion and double down on the winner. Ego is expensive.
items.why: Ego is expensive; data should decide quickly.

items.title: Own your funnel code so you can change pages yourself
items.text: Get your funnel and store theme code onto your own machine so you can change pages yourself with an AI coding tool instead of waiting weeks or paying per page. Slow feedback loops kill testing, and the owner should control the pages.
items.why: Waiting on others kills feedback loops, and the owner should control the pages.

items.title: Never change the live page directly; test on a branch first
items.text: Never change a live page directly: make the change on a separate copy, preview it with a test order, and only then make it live. Live pages move money.
items.why: A wrong live change costs sales immediately.

items.title: Plan first and check AI page changes before launch
items.text: Have the AI plan before changing a money page, then check what it actually changed and run a test checkout; in one person's experience AI edits introduced bugs 60-70% of the time.
items.why: AI edits on funnels need verification.

items.title: Walk the funnel numbers step by step
items.text: Write down each funnel step's numbers (visitors, offer page, checkout, orders, upsell/downsell takers, device and traffic source) to find where people drop; in one example 8,506 visitors became 3,494 on the offer page, 727 at checkout and 377 orders (about 4%).
items.why: You find the leak by seeing where people drop.

items.title: Double check AI math before trusting it
items.text: Use AI to organize numbers, but recalculate the key math yourself (e.g. orders divided by visitors) before deciding. AI can be wrong on numbers.
items.why: AI can be wrong on numbers.

items.title: Match the page type to what the buyer already knows
items.text: Match the page type to what the buyer already knows: problem- and product-aware buyers should go to a direct offer page with before and afters, while an unaware story advertorial that never names the problem may leave money on the table. Test problem-aware or solution-aware pages for them.
items.why: The page has to match the buyer's awareness.
items.when: choosing landing page type by audience awareness

items.title: Reverse engineer a competitor advertorial with a more direct angle
items.text: Reverse engineer a competitor's story-based advertorial and adapt its structure with a more direct angle that names the exact fear of the {avatar} (her frustration, how she hides the problem, the products that hurt her, and the mechanism).
items.why: A page that names the exact fear hits harder.

items.title: Cast spokespeople that match the audience
items.text: Cast spokespeople who look like the {avatar} you are selling to, and pair that face with an authority figure to be believable. People trust someone who looks like them.
items.why: People trust someone who looks like them.
items.when: casting for ads and pages aimed at a specific demographic

items.title: Skin-of-color angle: the fear of products that bleach
items.text: When the {avatar} already buys products in the category, the angle is often their fear of being harmed by products not made for them (in one case, fear of skin bleaching among women with darker skin). The real objection is past bad experiences, not whether to buy.
items.why: The real objection is not whether to buy but being burned by earlier products.
items.when: angle-finding in categories with underserved buyer groups

items.title: Send volume: daily baseline plus extra campaigns
items.text: Raise email volume to about one campaign a day as a baseline plus extra event and social-based sends (in one case going from 33 to 60+ a month). The audience only degrades when offers are pushed hard without context and strong creative.
items.why: More relevant sends mean more revenue as long as the creative is strong.

items.title: Use auto opt-in and a free gift to grow the list
items.text: Grow the email list with low friction and a good gift: in one case an auto opt-in in the acquisition funnel plus a pop-up offering a free small item made list growth jump.
items.why: A good offer plus low friction grows the list.

items.title: Use a heat map and a click-through variation to remove friction
items.text: Put a heat map on the page, then test a variation that removes friction (e.g. a click goes straight to checkout); in one test this lifted conversion and AOV by about 28%. Document the result.
items.why: Friction removal is a measurable test.

items.title: Test two pages in the same email
items.text: Split test the main offer page against an urgency/closing page inside emails; a closing-style page may work better for warm retention traffic while the main page suits top-of-funnel traffic.
items.why: Warm versus cold traffic want different pages.

items.title: Clean consistent reports; press what worked yesterday
items.text: Keep reports clean and consistent, and when a campaign drives sizeable revenue, send a follow-up the same day instead of leaving drafts unsent. Momentum fades if you wait on what is working.
items.why: Momentum fades if you wait on winning sends.

items.title: Break the list into five segments and measure each
items.text: Break the list into segments (leads, one-time, high-value one-time, returning, loyal, VIP) and track each one's volume, LTV and purchase frequency to see where drop-offs happen and adjust offer language. Use the broad engaged segment for content and tighter segments for offers.
items.why: Surgical sending needs segment-level data.

items.title: Get a weekly report from the team, then refine next month's calendar
items.text: Get a weekly report from the retention team (revenue by week, top campaigns, outliers, sends, learnings), feed it into your planning tool, refine next month's marketing calendar and send it back. In one example the projection was $130K and the result $117K; the loop is what grows revenue.
items.why: Reports without action are wasted; the loop is what grows revenue.

items.title: Know the economics before judging a subscription
items.text: Before judging a subscription, work out its economics: time between purchases, what goes in it, estimated churn, and when to time refills to prevent churn. Gross and contribution margin need ad spend, revenue and cost of goods; without margins you cannot tell if growth is profitable.
items.why: Without margins you cannot tell if growth is profitable.
items.when: designing or evaluating a subscription program

items.title: Seasonal brands need a back end
items.text: A seasonal {brand} with no email or SMS only sells in its peak; nurture customers all year with email and a little ad spend so the next peak is bigger (possibly 2x). Existing customers are the cheapest revenue between peaks.
items.why: Existing customers are the cheapest revenue between peaks.

items.title: Cohort analysis finds the bundle that leads to high lifetime value
items.text: Run a cohort analysis on all customer orders (in one case about 105,000 customers, up to 15 orders deep) to find which bundle leads to the highest-LTV cohort and whether refill timing matches the natural buying cycle, then push buyers onto that bundle.
items.why: Knowing what high-LTV customers buy tells you what to push.

items.title: Check why people unsubscribe and come back
items.text: Check how many subscription cancellers come back; in one case about 15% did, which signaled refills were too frequent. Adjust timing instead of assuming they are lost.
items.why: Behavior data tells you what to fix.

items.title: Split test a skip-the-scroll button
items.text: Test a first button that skips the scroll and goes straight to checkout (in one test conversion rose about 25%), then add sections below for people who come back to read. Buyers arrive emotional, click the first button, then reassure themselves.
items.why: Buyers are emotional on arrival and reassure themselves after.

items.title: Read customer service sentiment to find what to answer in ads
items.text: Run sentiment analysis on comments and support tickets to surface confusion (e.g. pre-order questions or 'are you going out of business'), then write support macros and adjust front-end messaging to the true story. Support questions are your next objection list.
items.why: Support questions are your next objection list.

items.title: Subscription on the front end kills conversion when it is unclear
items.text: Remove a front-end subscription option if it confuses buyers, since confusion kills conversion; reintroduce it later only through incremental tests with clear communication.
items.why: Test, don't push; clarity first.

items.title: Check the AI calendar for hallucinations before sending
items.text: Check every AI-built marketing calendar for hallucinated offers and correct them against the real current {offer} before the team sends. AI plans can invent offers.
items.why: AI plans can invent offers.

items.title: Increase AOV with an order bump and a pay-over-time option
items.text: Raise front-end AOV with small page additions: an FAQ, an order bump for an accessory, and a buy-now-pay-later option (in one case AOV reached about $73).
items.why: Small page additions lift order value.

items.title: Warm-traffic page vs cold-traffic page
items.text: Pages perform differently by traffic temperature: if a page works for warm traffic but not cold, embed its best section on the main page. Analyze each page's ROAS, structure, strengths and weaknesses.
items.why: Page performance differs by audience temperature.
items.when: landing page analysis across warm and cold traffic

items.title: Connect Drive and the brand files first
items.text: Before any production work, connect the shared drive and the shared skill library inside your AI editing workspace, and bring the {brand} folders into your own drive with shortcuts. Briefs and assets are pulled from the drive, so a broken connection stops every job.
items.why: Briefs and assets are pulled straight from the drive, so a broken connection stops every job.
items.when: setting up an AI-assisted editing workspace

items.title: Test the drive connection with a quick ask
items.text: After connecting, test with a quick ask in a new chat (e.g. 'pull up the brand drive'); if it lists the folders, setup works. A one-line test catches a bad connection before a real brief.
items.why: A one-line test catches a bad connection before you start a real brief.

items.title: Start a job with 'pull in brief' and the number
items.text: Start each editing job in a new session by naming the brief to pull in; the AI downloads the files and starts assembling. With briefs and assets stored in one drive, nobody hunts for files by hand.
items.why: Briefs, images and videos all sit in the drive, so you never hunt for files by hand.

items.title: Check the pull and remove slop before editing
items.text: After pulling a brief's files, check everything, delete weak or sloppy AI clips and re-roll any that need it before editing. Bad clips that reach the sequence cost the most to fix later.
items.why: Bad AI clips that reach the sequence cost the most to fix later.

items.title: Paste the folder link if it grabs the wrong folder
items.text: If an AI tool opens the wrong drive folder from a description, paste the direct folder link instead; a link goes to the exact place every time.
items.why: A direct link goes to the exact place every time.

items.title: Review every baseline scene together first
items.text: Review all of a brief's baseline scenes together with the inspiration video and check they make sense as one ad before sequencing. Side-by-side review shows gaps single clips hide.
items.why: Judging scenes side by side shows gaps that single clips hide.

items.title: Sequence only after the scenes look right
items.text: Work in order: review scenes, confirm they look good, sequence them, then edit. Editing unapproved scenes means redoing the cut.
items.why: Editing on top of unapproved scenes means redoing the cut.

items.title: Ask the helper to refresh the shared library
items.text: Regularly tell your AI tool to pull the shared skill library and look for updates, especially when you have not heard from the team, so you always work with the latest rules and prompts.
items.why: You always work with the latest rules and prompts.
items.when: teams sharing AI skills and prompts

items.title: Use the B-roll generator skill for weird B-roll
items.text: If B-roll looks off, regenerate it from the brief with a dedicated B-roll generation skill, so new clips stay consistent with the ad.
items.why: Regenerating from the brief keeps new clips consistent with the ad.

items.title: Expect briefs to arrive in the drive, not a sheet
items.text: Deliver each brief in the drive with all its images, videos and baseline scenes so the {editor} can do the whole job without opening a spreadsheet. One home for the brief removes back-and-forth over missing files.
items.why: One home for the brief removes the back-and-forth over missing files.

items.title: Lead with 'be the best you', not hiding age
items.text: For mature customers, position products as bringing out their best rather than covering up or reversing age; in interviews they said they expect to age and want it to be healthy, not erased.
items.why: Mature customers said they expect to age and want it healthy, not erased.

items.title: Make the glow the promise for older women
items.text: For older women, make healthy glow, hydration and elasticity the promise instead of looking 20; customers in their 60s said they want aging that is healthy and beautiful.
items.why: It matches how the buyer actually describes what she wants.

items.title: Name hyperpigmentation as a top body concern
items.text: When several customers raise the same concern unprompted in interviews (in one case dark spots from past sun exposure on arms and chest), treat it as a proven pain point and test hooks on it.
items.why: Several customers raised it unprompted, so it is a proven pain point.

items.title: Use dryness and crepey skin as body hooks
items.text: Use repeated complaints that customers say nothing solves yet (in one case dry, crepey skin that no product kept hydrated long term) as hooks, and show the {hero product} filling that gap.
items.why: Lasting hydration is a gap customers say nothing fills yet.

items.title: Customers treat skin by what it needs that day
items.text: Some customers choose products day by day based on what their skin needs; frame the {hero product} as a tool for a specific need, not an all-in-one, to fit how they already think about routines.
items.why: Fits the way they already think about routines.

items.title: Show scrub as removing sunscreen buildup
items.text: Use concrete use cases customers describe (in one case a strong scrub valued for removing heavy waterproof sunscreen) to make the benefit real.
items.why: A real situation makes the benefit concrete.

items.title: Offer a gentler version for sensitive skin
items.text: When customers warn a strong formula may be too harsh for sensitive or thinner skin, flag a gentler option and avoid promising the same experience to everyone, so you do not over-sell to the wrong skin type.
items.why: It avoids over-selling to the wrong skin type.

items.title: Show the after-rinse glow, then a follow-up
items.text: If the {hero product}'s visible after-use effect fades (in one case a post-scrub glow), pair it with a follow-up product that holds the result; this supports a bundle and a routine story.
items.why: This supports the bundle and the routine story.

items.title: Test a scrub-plus-tint idea
items.text: Log product ideas that come from real customer use moments (in one case a scrub with a hint of self-tan so the glow lasts) and pass them to the product team to test.
items.why: It came from a real use moment, so it is worth testing.

items.title: Scent and package get praised, value gets attacked
items.text: Know which claims land and which need a defense: in one case customers praised scent and packaging but attacked price and amount, so use the praised traits as proof points and answer value directly.
items.why: Know which claims land and which need a defense.

items.title: Keep fragrance light, not perfumey
items.text: Describe scent the way customers want it; in one case they wanted a light natural fragrance, so copy should say light and fresh, never heavy or perfumed.
items.why: Matches what they said they want.

items.title: Answer the price objection by showing per-use value
items.text: Answer price-per-ounce objections by showing value per use: how little you need each time and how long one unit lasts. In one case a customer compared a small premium tube to a large cheap body wash and called it poor value.
items.why: Value per use is the objection to beat on pages and in ads.
items.when: premium products compared to bulk alternatives

items.title: Tell people to apply on wet skin in the shower
items.text: Show the correct way to use the {hero product} in ads and pages; in one case customers who applied a scrub to dry skin wasted half a tube, while wet skin worked. Wrong use leads to waste and bad reviews.
items.why: Wrong use leads to waste and a bad review.
items.when: products with a specific application method

items.title: Show it fitting a real shower routine
items.text: Script the product into the routine the way customers really do it (in one case scrubbing in the shower while conditioner sits), because they will not add a separate step. Ads that match real routines feel believable.
items.why: Ads that match the real routine feel believable.

items.title: Pitch value and ease together
items.text: Pitch value and ease together; in one interview a buyer said her test is value and ease (easy to dispense, easy to cover the whole area), so stress ease of use along with the result.
items.why: Ease mattered as much as the ingredients.

items.title: Flag tube packaging that falls over in showers
items.text: Pass real-use packaging faults customers report (in one case a tube that falls over in the shower and is hard to squeeze when emptying) to the packaging owner, and avoid shots that show the fault.
items.why: A fault viewers will hit in real use can sink the review.

items.title: Do not film product dispensing struggles
items.text: Cut footage that shows customers struggling with the product (e.g. squeezing the last bit out of a tube); visible struggle plants an objection customers already have.
items.why: Visible struggle plants the objection customers already worried about.

items.title: Frame it as a body treatment, not a wash
items.text: Position a premium product as a targeted treatment with clear amount-per-use guidance rather than an everyday commodity, so it avoids a head-to-head with cheap bulk products.
items.why: It avoids a head-to-head with cheap bulk products.

items.title: Mine competitor routines for what buyers use
items.text: Ask customers what they currently use religiously and why it wins before writing the angle; their favorite product shows you what to beat.
items.why: Their winning product shows what to beat.

items.title: Ask the target-market question in every session
items.text: Make sure every ad names a clear buyer (in one case women focused on dark spots); a named {avatar} makes copy and targeting sharper.
items.why: A named buyer makes copy and targeting sharper.

items.title: Check the batch before blaming the formula
items.text: When a new sample smells or feels different, ask for batch details before blaming a formula change; in one case it traced to a new batch of a raw ingredient.
items.why: Small ingredient batches change feel and scent.

items.title: Compare new samples against what is selling
items.text: Test new samples side by side against the product currently on sale, with several people judging; in one case two people noticed an off note one person would have missed.
items.why: A blind side-by-side catches what one nose misses.

items.title: Ask for the grain size spec of production salt
items.text: Get the supplier's production spec for key raw materials (in one case scrub grain size, about 40-60 mesh) and make all future samples to that spec, or samples will not match production.
items.why: Samples made to a different grain will not match production.

items.title: Find the scrub's leak risk before choosing a jar
items.text: Check leak risk before choosing packaging: oil-rich formulas can seep from jars even with a foil seal, while tubes hold. A messy opening is acceptable; a leak in shipping is not, because it means refunds and bad reviews.
items.why: A leaking shipment is a refund and a bad review.

items.title: Sell a jar option in the scrub range
items.text: When buyers and professional partners ask for larger sizes or a different format (in one case a large jar for spa partners), ask the factory for a sealed version that does not leak.
items.why: A jar option serves buyers and professional channels.

items.title: Call the product messy to open, not leaking
items.text: Set clear pass/fail rules for packaging (in one case: residue under the lid is acceptable, any leak before opening fails). Clear lines speed up packaging decisions.
items.why: Clear pass/fail rules speed up packaging choices.

items.title: Plan packaging tests before ordering the mold
items.text: Plan packaging machine tests before ordering the mold; in one case a new tube needed a ~200-piece machine run on specific tooling that could only happen after ordering. Late discovery of a bad pack costs weeks.
items.why: Late discovery of a bad tube costs weeks.

items.title: Allow four weeks for mold and machine test
items.text: Allow about 3-4 weeks after order for a new mold plus machine test and set launch dates around it, so you do not promise dates the factory cannot hit.
items.why: It prevents promising launch dates the factory can not hit.

items.title: Use machine-test tubes as launch samples
items.text: Ask to keep the good units from a packaging machine-test run (in one case about 250 pieces) as internal pre-launch samples, expecting some scrap while the mold is tuned.
items.why: Free usable samples before launch.

items.title: Know the standard 3.5-month compatibility test
items.text: Know your manufacturer's standard compatibility test length (in one case 3.5 months) and that a low-risk classic formula may ship after about a month with a signed waiver; when time is tight, launch online with a small first run. Choose speed versus certainty on purpose.
items.why: It lets you choose speed versus certainty on purpose.

items.title: Ask for the tested sample, not just any sample
items.text: Ask the factory for the exact units that were tested, made and filled with the batch, as the final check that what you sell matches what was tested.
items.why: What was tested must match what you sell.

items.title: Match tube tests to the final formula
items.text: Before filling pre-made packaging, confirm the formula being tested and filled is the latest version, not the old one; filling the wrong formula wastes the packaging run.
items.why: Filling the wrong formula wastes the packaging run.

items.title: Keep the older stock and formula as backup
items.text: Keep old stock and the current formula as a backup while testing a new formula, so you can keep selling and avoid a stockout during the change.
items.why: A fallback prevents a stockout during changes.

items.title: Remove risky ingredients but keep the feel
items.text: When removing risky ingredients, check the new version against the original sample's feel, not just compliance; customers notice even small feel changes.
items.why: Customers noticed even small feel changes.

items.title: Run formulation talks in a direct chat
items.text: Run formulation feedback in one direct chat with only the product people, and keep orders and finance in a separate thread, so the right people see feedback immediately.
items.why: The right people see feedback immediately.

items.title: Judge body cream on feel at fifteen minutes
items.text: Judge a cream's feel over time, not just at application; in one case a lighter formula felt less moisturizing at first but moisturized by 15-20 minutes, with no sticky feel. Pitch clear sensory benefits like fast-absorbing and non-sticky.
items.why: It is a clear sensory benefit to show.

items.title: Sell the first-use feeling for face scrub
items.text: Sell the honest first-use feeling (comfortable, brighter, hydrated after rinsing) and do not promise fast removal of long-term problems like spots; overpromising week-one results breaks trust.
items.why: Overpromising on week-one results breaks trust.

items.title: Choose the scrub that feels like a scrub
items.text: Pick the sample that feels like what the product is called (in one case the face scrub that felt like a real scrub, not a foaming cleanser).
items.why: The product must feel like what it is called.

items.title: Lead the face scrub with its Thai actives
items.text: Lead a line extension with the same key ingredients that already carry the {hero product}'s story, tying the new product to what is working, and say benefits build over time.
items.why: It ties the face line to the story already working for the body.

items.title: Pick the face oil on texture and scent
items.text: Rate product samples on texture, scent and color separately; in one case samples differing only in fragrance amount also felt different. Splitting the ratings shows what to fix.
items.why: Splitting the ratings shows what to fix.

items.title: Position face oil as an add-on, not a hero
items.text: Set each product's role: sell a supporting product as a pairing with the main products, not as a standalone fix, to avoid overclaiming.
items.why: Setting the role avoids overclaiming.

items.title: Ask what a sample is made of, not a name
items.text: Ask exactly which form of an ingredient a sample uses (e.g. oil vs extract), not just its name, because forms act differently on skin and change claims.
items.why: Specific forms change claims and skin reactions.

items.title: Fit three actives into the firming cream
items.text: Test a new formula's base without fragrance first so the team can judge it, then add scent; position it by its function with the brand's signature natural ingredients.
items.why: Settle the base before scent.

items.title: Plan a day cream beside the night cream
items.text: When testers find a product fits one use (e.g. a thick cream feels like a night cream), plan a companion product for the other use (a lighter day cream); two products make a routine and raise order value.
items.why: Two products make a routine and raise order value.

items.title: Build a brightening serum to match the scrub
items.text: Build the next product to pair with the {hero product} (in one case a brightening serum to match a scrub), sold alone or together; a routine gives you a bundle to sell.
items.why: A routine gives a bundle to sell.

items.title: Give each product one Thai ingredient
items.text: Set a line-wide formulation rule that keeps the {brand} story true (in one case at least one signature regional ingredient in every product, mixed with other proven ingredients).
items.why: It protects the brand story across the line.

items.title: Check whether the factory can make masks
items.text: Check whether your manufacturer already makes an adjacent best-selling category (in one case masks) that fits your positioning; it adds a category beyond the current range.
items.why: A mask adds a category beyond scrubs.

items.title: Scrub packs: tell buyers size clearly
items.text: Label sizes clearly so buyers know how long each lasts; size confusion feeds value complaints.
items.why: Size confusion fed the value complaint.

items.title: Launch one product first
items.text: Launch one product first: the most mature and most on-story one, holding others back, so a single product ships faster.
items.why: Focus gets a product to market faster.
items.when: launching a new brand or line

items.title: Test instant effect and long-term effect separately
items.text: Test and claim instant effects (how it feels right after use) separately from long-term results; honest claims must separate the two.
items.why: Honest claims must separate immediate from lasting results.

items.title: Do not push scrub harder for whiter skin
items.text: Do not make a physical exfoliant stronger to chase a bigger result like brighter skin; over-scrubbing irritates and leads to bad reviews. Real results come from treatment products.
items.why: Over-scrubbing causes harm and bad reviews.

items.title: Match the original sample's natural scent
items.text: Match new batches to the approved original sample on make-or-break traits (in one case scent, with about 95% similarity as the goal), since a tester rejected a perfumey change.
items.why: Scent was the biggest dislike and a make-or-break feature.

items.title: Describe scent as Thai-natural
items.text: Describe a scent in the specific regional style it belongs to (the {brand}'s origin style of 'natural'), because 'natural' means different things in different markets; it sets the right expectation on pages.
items.why: It sets the right expectation on pages.

items.title: Match color to the approved sample
items.text: Match batch color to the approved sample, since color is the first thing a viewer sees; in one case the factory could lighten a too-dark batch by adjusting its colorant.
items.why: Color is the first thing a viewer sees.

items.title: Feels natural beats being fully natural
items.text: Aim for a natural feel rather than claiming 100% natural; a harmless non-natural component is fine if it keeps the look, but never claim all-natural unless it is true.
items.why: Do not claim all-natural unless true.

items.title: Show the product spreading with a little water
items.text: Show a visible, demonstrable benefit in demos (in one case how the product spreads smoothly, especially with a little water) and use the method that shows it best.
items.why: Spread is a visible, demonstrable benefit.

items.title: Get grain size between too fine and too coarse
items.text: When tuning a sample, prioritize what affects the user most; in one case grain size was already close and spread mattered more.
items.why: Prioritise what affects the user most.

items.title: Sourcing special salt grain needs bulk orders
items.text: Special raw-material specs can carry large minimum orders (in one case several tons for a custom salt grain); ask the supplier for the minimum and cost before committing.
items.why: A large minimum order changes the decision.

items.title: Set priorities for the next sample
items.text: Give the factory ranked priorities for the next sample (in one case scent, color and spread first, grain second) so it does not chase small items.
items.why: Ranked priorities stop the factory chasing small items.

items.title: Collect all feedback before sending it
items.text: Collect all testers' feedback and send the manufacturer one consolidated update before requesting new samples; one request avoids rework.
items.why: One consolidated request avoids rework.

items.title: Plan sample timing around the holiday
items.text: Plan sample batches around supplier holidays (in one case suppliers slowed from late January) and book the review meeting right after; holiday shutdowns move launch dates.
items.why: Holiday shutdowns move launch dates.

items.title: Make small batch samples for fans to try
items.text: Make a small batch of trial-size samples (in one case 50-100 small units, needing about a kilo of material) to send to fans for feedback; early fan feedback guides the next change.
items.why: Early fan feedback guides the next change.

items.title: Start tube artwork early, test later
items.text: Share packaging specs early so the designer can start artwork, but hold final design decisions until you have held the real packaging quality in hand, to avoid wasted design.
items.why: Handling the real quality avoids wasted design.

items.title: Decide on a gift box separately
items.text: Decide on extras like a multi-piece gift box separately from the launch; packaging for a single launch product is simpler.
items.why: Packaging for a single launch product is simpler.

items.title: Run founder story ads before building a UGC creator pile
items.text: When paid social is breaking even or losing, shoot {founder} story ads first instead of ordering a batch of {creator} videos and hoping one works. In one case a founder at about $10,000 total revenue the year before moved to about $800-1,000 a day on Facebook after the first founder shoot.
items.why: The founder's own voice got sales right away where the account had not been profitable.
items.when: early-stage brands with unprofitable paid social

items.title: Use the founder's proven videos to brief creators on angles
items.text: Have the {founder} record first to find which angles sell, then use those winning founder videos to brief {creator}s on what to say and which angle to run. Creators sent out without a proven voice just guess.
items.why: Creators sent out without a proven voice just guess; the founder's winning angles give them something to copy.

items.title: Film the founder's own problem-to-result journey as raw organic
items.text: Film the {founder}'s own journey from the problem to the result as raw, unpolished organic video. In one case raw bathroom videos documenting a founder clearing his own problem sold right away and scaled a line to about $1M in roughly six months.
items.why: Unpolished proof of the real problem being solved sold immediately.
items.when: founders who personally had the problem the product solves

items.title: Clear patent risk and own the product before scaling
items.text: Clear patent and IP risk and own your product before scaling. In one case a product hit about $1M in six months, then a cease and desist stopped sales for about a year while the founder built an owned product, which took about four more months to get profitable.
items.why: An IP claim can shut off a winning product overnight and cost a year.
items.when: before scaling a product you do not own outright

items.title: Raise standards and build systems as revenue climbs
items.text: As revenue climbs, raise standards and keep the detailed daily routine instead of relaxing, and build the team and systems under the growth. Complacency shows up in results months after the routine slips (in one case about six months later).
items.why: Complacency shows up in results months after the routine slips.

items.title: Build loyalty, community and LTV, not just profitable acquisition
items.text: Profitable paid acquisition alone is not a business; build systems plus loyalty, community and good LTV so customers do more than buy once. Only a real base beyond one-off purchases pays for a team and supports an exit.
items.why: Only a real base beyond one-off purchases can pay for a team and support an exit.
items.when: any DTC brand at any revenue level

items.title: Document every sales objection and write a reversal for each
items.text: Use a straight selling framework: name the problem in words the customer understands, build interest, send them to the store, then document every objection they raise and write a reversal for each. That turns selling into a repeatable framework.
items.why: Once objections are written down and reversed, selling becomes a repeatable framework rather than guesswork.

items.title: Name the mental problem behind the physical one
items.text: For every product, name the mental problem under the physical one and how it shapes the {avatar}'s worldview (in one example, a teen with acne feeling ugly and avoiding people), and speak to it: we've been through this, this was made for you. The felt experience is what makes an ad land.
items.why: The felt experience is what the customer can't fully put into words, so naming it makes the ad land.

items.title: Start with a product already selling and reverse-engineer its videos
items.text: To start, find a product already selling on TikTok Shop or Amazon, reverse-engineer its viral videos into batches of 10-20, and launch on a basic website. Proven demand and proven videos take the guesswork out of a first launch.
items.why: Proven demand and proven videos take the guesswork out of the first launch.
items.when: first product launch for a new seller

items.title: Use free-plus-shipping with a post-purchase upsell to get started
items.text: If a first launch does not take off, switch to a free-plus-shipping {offer} with a post-purchase upsell (in one example $50 was quoted for shipping). It makes some money and teaches how the funnel works.
items.why: It makes a little money and teaches how the funnel works even before the brand is big.
items.when: early-stage funnels that are not converting

items.title: Master competitor research, direct-response copy and team replication
items.text: Master three skills: competitor research (what they do and how your product differs), direct-response copywriting for ads and landing pages alike, and operations that replicate your skills across a team.
items.why: These three apply to every part of the business, from ads to landers to scale.

items.title: Give every VA a written weekly assignment and accountability board
items.text: Give every VA written weekly assignments on an accountability board (e.g. 10 ads this week for a named product) and measure against it. Without oversight, quality and turnaround slip after the first batch.
items.why: With no oversight anyone slacks, so the first five great ads turn into slow, weaker work.
items.when: managing VAs and remote creative staff

items.title: Track each editor's ad spend against what you pay them
items.text: Give every role a quality metric and a quantity metric; track each {editor} (copy and editing separately) on the ad spend their ads earn versus their pay. In one team the best editors cost about 3% of their ad spend, with no commission.
items.why: Spend on an editor's ads is the clearest measure of whether their work wins.
