items.title: Put 'free' and today-only discount in the page header
items.text: Put 'free' and a today-only discount in the sales page header bar (e.g. 'free shipping plus 50% off today only'). 'Free' is the most powerful word in marketing and today-only adds urgency.
items.why: Free is called the most powerful word in marketing, and today-only adds urgency.

items.title: Add zero-margin digital bonuses and free extras to raise value
items.text: Raise perceived value with zero-margin-cost bonuses (digital guides, ebooks) and free add-ons on multi-unit orders, then restate the total value against the price.
items.why: Zero-cost or 100%-margin bonuses raise perceived value without cutting margin.

items.title: Design packaging for 'plop value' on the counter
items.text: Design packaging for 'plop value': premium packaging that looks worth the price when set on the counter, and show what's in the box piece by piece. A plain box makes a premium product feel cheap.
items.why: A product arriving in a plain brown box feels cheap; beautiful packaging confirms the price was worth it.

items.title: Default the bundle picker to two units with per-unit savings
items.text: On checkout, default the bundle picker to the 2-pack with a per-unit price lower than buying one, plus a countdown timer, a stock counter tied to real inventory, a pre-applied coupon and visible contact details. Defaulting to two raises AOV; real scarcity and contact info build urgency and legitimacy.
items.why: Defaulting to two raises order value, and real scarcity plus visible contact info builds urgency and legitimacy.

items.title: Add order bumps; over 20% of buyers take one
items.text: Add order bumps on checkout (e.g. a $19.95 self-underwritten protection plan, expedited shipping); in one funnel over 20% of buyers took one of three bumps. Bumps add margin and can lift overall conversion.
items.why: Even a simple bump is an easy way to add margin, and bumps also lift overall conversion rate.

items.title: Never pre-select order bumps
items.text: Never pre-select order bumps; leave them unchecked so customers opt in. Consumer-protection regulators go after pre-selected bumps, especially at volume.
items.why: Consumer-protection agencies tear through pre-selected bumps, especially once you do volume.

items.title: Put a linked terms and privacy line above the checkout button
items.text: Directly above the checkout button add small text saying that by clicking the buyer agrees to the terms of service and privacy policy, both linked and opening in a separate page or modal. It builds confidence, protects against class-action suits, and does not appear to hurt conversion.
items.why: It gives buyers confidence and protects the merchant from class-action attorneys who hunt for pages without it; it does not appear to hurt conversion.

items.title: Make upsell one 'more of the same' with a reason
items.text: Make the first one-time upsell after a single-unit purchase 'more of the same' with a reason: a short video confirming the buyer made a great choice, then a concrete reason to buy a second unit, an extra discount and free shipping, with a 3-step progress bar and a 'do not hit back' note.
items.why: Reinforcing the decision and giving a concrete reason to buy more lifts take rate; a short step count makes the end feel close.

items.title: Keep all upsells inside the original transaction
items.text: Run post-purchase upsells inside the original transaction in one session, not as separate charges; one merchant cut chargebacks from over 5% to about 0.8%. Separate charges give one customer several chances to charge back.
items.why: Separate upsell charges give one customer two or three chances to charge back, exposing the merchant account.

items.title: Build continuity into a one-time product with a consumable upsell
items.text: Turn a one-time product into recurring revenue by offering a low-ticket consumable on subscription as an upsell, framed as solving the next problem the {hero product} leaves (in one example heat patches at about $60/month for a device).
items.why: It turns a one-time purchase into recurring revenue.

items.title: Add a community membership upsell framed as a welcome gift
items.text: Offer an expert community membership (experts in a group, weekly webinars) as a later upsell, framed as a buyers-only welcome gift with a 30-day trial then a monthly fee (in one example $97/month, about $100/month added recurring revenue per taker).
items.why: It adds about $100/month recurring revenue per taker on top of the consumable continuity.
items.when: upsell flows for health or wellness products

items.title: Benchmark upsell take rates and day-zero customer value
items.text: Benchmark upsell take rates and day-zero customer value; one reviewed funnel showed upsell one at 13.1% vs 18.5% in a split test, upsell two 8.4%, upsell three 7.2%, and average day-zero value of $270. A high day-zero value lets you spend more to acquire each customer.
items.why: A high day-zero value lets you spend a lot more to acquire each customer.

items.title: Keep a full contact and policy footer on every sales page
items.text: End every sales and upsell page with a footer carrying support email, phone, terms and return policy, not just FAQs. Without it people doubt the company is legitimate and conversion drops.
items.why: Without the footer people doubt the company is legitimate and conversion rate drops.

items.title: Route upsells by what is already in the cart
items.text: Route upsells by what is already in the cart: a one-unit buyer gets 'buy a second at a discount', a two-pack buyer gets a different offer. Order dynamic upsells from highest to lowest dollar value before the thank-you page.
items.why: A static upsell wastes the slot; someone who bought two does not need two more.

items.title: Build downsells for every declined upsell
items.text: Build a downsell for every declined upsell: if a buyer says no to an offer, show a discounted version (e.g. two more at a lower price) before moving to the next offer. A no at full price can be a yes at a lower one.
items.why: A no to the full offer can still be a yes at a lower price.

items.title: Use the thank-you page and confirmation email for one more ask
items.text: Use the thank-you page and order confirmation email for one more ask (a booked call, a last bump, community and onboarding links); in one funnel the thank-you page call booking logged 1,096 submits. Right after buying, customers are primed to act.
items.why: Right after buying, the customer is primed to take more action, and you don't know if they will come back.

items.title: Put support email and phone up front in post-purchase emails
items.text: Put support email and phone right at the top of order confirmation and follow-up emails and say plainly that buyers can reach out. Visible support builds confidence and pre-empts chargebacks and returns.
items.why: Being front and center about support builds confidence and pre-empts chargebacks and returns.

items.title: Trade a free gift for customer video testimonials
items.text: Ask buyers for written or video testimonials (or interview them on a call) and send them something free in return; use that UGC across ads and sales pages. Customers saying it works goes further than the brand saying it.
items.why: Customers telling the world the product works goes much further than the brand saying it.

items.title: Copy a winning funnel's flow, never its copy or proof
items.text: Buy through successful funnels yourself and map the whole flow (advertorial, sales page, checkout, upsells, thank-you page) to replicate it, but write your own copy and use your own images and testimonials. Copying someone else's copy and proof is only a short-term play.
items.why: The flow is a proven process; ripping someone's copy and real customer feedback is only a short-term play.

items.title: Build single-product landing pages for top sellers
items.text: Give top-selling products their own single-product landing page and funnel for targeted ads; in one comparison storefronts converted around 2.1-2.2% versus 20-30% for single-product pages.
items.why: A focused page for one product always converts far higher than a store with many products.

items.title: Find a subscription angle even for non-subscription products
items.text: Find a subscription angle even for non-subscription products, such as a small monthly membership (e.g. about $9.99/month for 20% off every purchase) or seasonal/region-specific bundles. Without any subscription you need heavy volume and strong email/SMS repurchase.
items.why: Recurring revenue becomes substantial over time and most companies leave it on the table.

items.title: Use a sub-one-second, single-page, mobile-first checkout
items.text: Use a single-page, mobile-first checkout that loads in under one second, then a couple of upsells; 70-80% of buyers are on mobile. One claim cited: every three seconds of load loses 40% of buyers, and multi-step checkouts kill conversion.
items.why: For every three seconds of load you lose 40% of buyers, and multi-step checkouts kill conversion.

items.title: Spread payment processing across several merchant accounts
items.text: Spread payment processing across several merchant accounts and check true blended rates (an advertised 2.9% can end up near 6% plus 30 cents). Processors can shut accounts after risk reviews, so spreading volume spreads the risk.
items.why: Processors can shut accounts down after risk reviews; spreading volume spreads the liability.

items.title: Split-test pages four ways, then split again off the winner
items.text: Split-test pages four ways (control plus three variants), cut underperformers by click-through and conversion, then build three new variants off the winner and repeat. It reaches an optimized page in one or two rounds, faster than A/B tests.
items.why: It reaches an optimized page in one or two rounds, far faster than A/B testing.

items.title: Kill active ads with AOV under $60 first
items.text: In the highest-spending campaign, filter last-7-day active ads by AOV and turn off every ad under a set floor (in one account $60); low-AOV ads are being credited with subscription or low-value sales, not new customers.
items.why: Low-AOV ads are not scaling or prospecting and just waste spend.
items.when: Meta paid social weekly kill pass

items.title: Give every ad seven days before judging it
items.text: Give every ad at least seven days before judging it; filter by creation date and leave anything newer out of the kill pass so ads have time to learn.
items.why: Every ad needs time to breathe and learn.

items.title: Cut duds without waiting for a turnaround
items.text: Once ads meet the kill criteria, turn them all off in one pass instead of waiting for a turnaround; in one pass 20 ads that spent $2,700 in a week were cut, and that money moved to better-performing ads.
items.why: The money isn't just saved; it gets reallocated to better-performing ads.

items.title: Kill ads spending 3x target CPA with ROAS under 1
items.text: Second kill pass: turn off ads that spent at least three times target CPA in the last 7 days with ROAS below 1, and double-check low spenders that slipped through. In one walkthrough this caught about $5,500 of wasted spend.
items.why: In the walkthrough this caught about $5,500 of wasted spend.

items.title: Fast spend with bad CPA still gets turned off
items.text: An ad that picks up spend fast is a good sign, but if its CPA is bad, turn it off even before seven days when the data is clear (in one example $90-140 cost per purchase). Spending on assets that take spend but aren't profitable hurts the business.
items.why: Spending money on assets that take spend but are not profitable is bad for the business.

items.title: Feed kill-pass learnings back to the editor
items.text: Feed kill-pass learnings back to the {editor}: when a type of ad keeps dying (in one case bottom-funnel discount ads), tell them to stop making it.
items.why: That is the learning the kill pass produces.

items.title: Keep long-running ads with proven history
items.text: Zoom out to 30 days before cutting; an ad with a long track record (in one case over a year) and slightly positive return stays on after a weak week. True historical data outweighs one bad week.
items.why: True historical data outweighs one bad week.

items.title: Don't touch your top spender
items.text: When cutting high-CPA ads with negative ROAS (in one pass, over $65 CPA in 14 days), leave the top spender alone if it is technically profitable; it is usually the one doing the prospecting.
items.why: The top spender is usually the one doing the prospecting.

items.title: Judge prospecting campaigns on the blended business
items.text: Judge story-based prospecting campaigns that bring true net-new audiences on the blended business; they can run higher CPAs (about $60 blended in one account) when ROAS is also higher, but still kill their low-AOV ads and ads with no conversions past the timeline.
items.why: Top-of-funnel ads have a different CPA threshold; what matters is the blended result.

items.title: Look at AOV and CPA, not 'it's making money'
items.text: Do not be fooled by an ad that looks profitable; check AOV and CPA. Turn off ads with no conversions or spend well past launch, high CPCs, or fatigue with negative return; in one account this pruning cut the ad count roughly in half.
items.why: Ads fatigue and die off; pruning this way cut the account roughly in half.

items.title: Find the last-mile tracking number for customers
items.text: For orders shipped cross-border from overseas, look up the last-mile tracking number and courier from the international carrier's number so customers can see the domestic tracking history; in one store over 80% of revenue was domestic orders fulfilled from overseas.
items.why: Most revenue (80%+) is US orders fulfilled from China, and customers may need the US tracking history.

items.title: File finished edits in Pending Posting, then by archetype
items.text: File finished graphics and videos in a 'pending posting' folder, and once posted, move them into folders by content archetype, so the team keeps a reference library of everything that has gone out.
items.why: It keeps a reference library of everything that has gone out.

items.title: Pull brand and raw assets from the Creative Assets folders
items.text: Keep all creative inputs in one known folder structure: brand (fonts, logos, palettes, packaging), raw content and {creator} footage, ideas and the optimization log, polished branded video, and copy.
items.why: Everything needed to produce content lives in one known structure.

items.title: Bank the top-spending ad per angle with a Drive link
items.text: After testing, bank the ad that spent the most in the last 30 days for each angle with a link to the file, building a backlog of best ads of all time to draw on when new creative is needed.
items.why: A backlog of best ads of all time shows what has worked and keeps working when new creative is needed.

items.title: Turn each banked winner into new concepts in the angle
items.text: Once a winner is identified, log new concepts as iterations or expansions of that same angle and test them. The process is test, identify winners, make more like them and expand within the angle.
items.why: The process is test, identify winners, then make more like them and expand within the angle.

items.title: Update Notion pages through Claude, removing redundancy
items.text: Bring new research to an AI model with the existing wiki page, have it flag redundant information, propose removals and rewrite, then push the update straight into the wiki. Research dropped in chat never becomes actionable; pages stay current instead of bloated.
items.why: Research that just gets downloaded or dropped in Slack never becomes actionable; pages stay current instead of bloated.

items.title: Test new creative as flexible ads in one ad set
items.text: Test new creative in one campaign with one testing ad set: for each new concept duplicate an existing flexible ad, swap in the new creative and copy, rather than building a new ad set. Flexible ads do dynamic-creative-style testing and simplify the account.
items.why: Flexible ads do dynamic-creative style testing at the ad level, which simplifies the account.

items.title: Upload and launch all new ads every Friday
items.text: Upload and launch all new ads on one fixed day each week instead of scheduling set launch times; launch time does not really matter to the platform.
items.why: Launch time does not really matter to the platform; scheduling was only for humans tracking time.

items.title: Run a weekly stop loss on high-CPA ads
items.text: Run a weekly stop-loss rule: pause any ad in the control ad set that spent at least a set amount in 7 days with a 14-day CPA over target (in one account $500 spend and $60 CPA), plus a fail-safe pausing new ads with no sales at a spend cap (in one account $150). Ads run as long as possible while clear losers drop automatically.
items.why: Ads get to run as long as possible while clear losers are removed automatically.

items.title: Run one Meta campaign per business objective, not per segment
items.text: Run one Meta campaign per business objective (one per {offer} or product) with all customer segments inside it, rather than separate prospecting, remarketing and retargeting campaigns. Meta's algorithm now wants consolidated campaigns and lets creative do the separating.
items.why: Meta's algorithm now wants consolidated campaigns and lets the creative do the separating.

items.title: Set one affordable daily budget per campaign, allocated by CPA
items.text: Give each business-objective campaign one daily budget you can afford and, when Meta is the core channel, allocate the marketing budget there based on CPA.
items.why: Meta is the main ad platform, so the marketing budget should sit in one house and follow cost per acquisition.

items.title: Split ad sets by creative archetype; duplicate one per new creator
items.text: Inside the campaign, give each creative archetype its own ad set ({founder} stories, product benefits, experts, influencer UGC, comedy, {avatar} messaging tests); when a new {creator} delivers, duplicate an ad set and load only their videos. You can test archetypes while the system keeps spending.
items.why: This lets you test new archetypes while the overall system keeps spending the way Meta wants.

items.title: Treat creative as the targeting that reaches new audiences
items.text: Treat creative as the targeting: Meta decides who sees an ad from the content itself, so new content types reach new people. In one account, ads without the {founder} took 30-something percent of an $8K campaign's spend, diversifying the ad library.
items.why: Meta shows each person the content that fits them, so new content types are how you reach new people.
items.when: Meta paid social, reaching new audiences

items.title: Brief more of a category whose ads win, to beat its best
items.text: Group ads into categories, read which categories get the spend and best results, and brief more videos of a working category with the goal of beating that category's best ad.
items.why: Category-level reads show what is prioritized and where new variations have the best odds.

items.title: Make ads look like the buyer's feed, not one long format
items.text: Make ads look like the {avatar}'s actual feed (e.g. around 30-second funny pieces with different people) rather than relying on one long format, and think like a media company: paid Meta is the organic algorithm with dollars behind it. Setup is data entry; content is the work that wins.
items.why: Campaign setup is data entry; the real work that wins is studying what people watch and making great content for it.

items.title: Open videos with a hard-to-read paragraph to hold viewers
items.text: One tactic heard from another operator: open a video with a short paragraph in a hard-to-read font so people stop and take time to read it, buying the extra seconds of attention the feed demands.
items.why: Forcing viewers to read buys the extra few seconds of attention that the feed now demands.

items.title: Watch AI-heavy ads for clicks without conversions
items.text: Be suspicious of heavily AI-made videos for a premium {brand}: they can hold the same click numbers while conversions drop, because they pull a lower-spending crowd. Position creative for buyers with money.
items.why: Ads that pull a lower-spending crowd look fine on clicks but lose at checkout.
items.when: premium or luxury brands using AI creative

items.title: Have editors cut real footage before reaching for AI
items.text: When an {editor} leans too hard on AI visuals, have them dial it back and use the {brand}'s real footage first (the {founder} at the factory, customers using the product). Too much AI dilutes an engaging ad.
items.why: Too much AI dilutes an engaging ad; real footage is the authentic material the brand already owns.

items.title: Add a sticky add-to-cart so buyers can skip the page
items.text: On long offer or presale pages, add a fast way to buy: a sticky add-to-cart or 'check availability' button, or one that jumps to the offer. Some visitors are ready now and shouldn't have to read the whole page.
items.why: Some visitors are ready to buy now and should not have to click through the whole funnel.

items.title: Presale page must pass about 40% through to the offer
items.text: Before putting a presale advertorial in front of the offer page, do the math on click-through; in one case roughly 40% of visitors needed to reach the offer page for conversion rates to still work. A presale page only pays if enough people get through it.
items.why: A presale page educates and frames the buyer, which can raise conversion, but only pays if enough people get through it.
items.when: adding a presale page to a funnel

items.title: Write offer page copy straight from customer reviews
items.text: Write offer page copy straight from customer reviews and feedback forms: the problem, what fixing it leads to, social proof, the {hero product} and the guarantee. Don't make the copy up.
items.why: Customer words are what maximize conversion rate for the offer.

items.title: Spell out subscription price and cadence so it can't be misread
items.text: Read the subscription section as a fast-scrolling buyer would and spell out price and cadence so it can't be misread (e.g. 'refilled every 30 days for $14.99 per bottle', not a line that reads like a one-time price). Someone should never finish the page unaware it is a subscription.
items.why: Someone could read the whole page and still not know it is a subscription.

items.title: Tell plan buyers results take 90 days, above the timeline
items.text: Right above the results timeline on the plan page, tell buyers that full results take a set period and they should stay on the plan at least that long. In the example, full results took 90 days (the skin renewal cycle is about 30 days), so the minimum was three months.
items.why: It explains why the plan keeps shipping and justifies staying past the first month.
items.when: subscription or multi-month plan product pages, near the results timeline

items.title: Optimize headline, hero image, offer and price first
items.text: When reviewing a page, put most of the work into the top: the headline, the hero image, the {offer}, the price and the buttons. Then check a visitor can tell what happens when they press the button.
items.why: From performance experience this top section is the most important part of the page.
items.when: landing page and product page reviews

items.title: Cast creators the age you want to buy
items.text: Compare who appears in your content with who you want to buy, and cast {creator}s of the age you want to reach. In one case the buyer base averaged 35+ and nobody under 25 was in the content; younger buyers start spending on the category around 24-25.
items.why: Buyers skew toward the people they see in the ads.
items.when: creator casting when trying to reach a new age group

items.title: Adapt the winning founder script to customers from new groups
items.text: To open a new demographic pocket, take the proven {founder} script and adapt it for real customers from that group, for example a Latino customer speaking Spanish, keeping the same script. A base from one group caps reach.
items.why: A core base of one group caps reach; creatives featuring other groups expand into the rest of the population.
items.when: paid social, after a founder script is proven, expanding to new demographics

items.title: Cut ad language that tells other groups it isn't for them
items.text: Cut descriptors that exclude viewers (for example a specific skin tone) when you want the ad to reach beyond the core group. Anyone who doesn't match decides instantly the product is not for them.
items.why: Viewers who don't match the descriptor instantly decide the product is not for them.
items.when: ad scripts and copy when expanding beyond the core audience

items.title: Keep creative in-house; agencies don't close the feedback loop
items.text: Staff the marketing arm in-house with a creative strategist, a {media buyer} and a social media manager instead of handing creative to agencies. Agencies were tried and did not close the feedback loop between content and results.
items.why: Agencies were tried and were not efficient because they do not truly close the feedback loop.

items.title: Track every creative from capture to CPA, then rebrief winners
items.text: Track every creative from capture to paid CPA: what was made or received from {creator}s, whether it needs an {editor}, where it was posted, organic and paid metrics. Take the lowest-CPA pieces that got real spend back to briefing for more scripts and variations, then film again; untracked footage gets lost (one case: footage sat unused for a year).
items.why: Footage that sat unused for a year shows pieces get lost without tracking; the loop is what makes the flywheel turn.
items.when: running a creative pipeline across organic and paid

items.title: Post organic daily at the same time; recut best into 60s
items.text: To start getting organic results, post one video every day at the same time, around 60 seconds, recutting your best existing pieces into 60-second versions. This was advice relayed from a full-organic operator, whose own best posts ran six to seven seconds.
items.why: Advice relayed from a full-organic account operator about doom-scroll attention spans.

items.title: Use cheap fast offshore editors, but oversee them
items.text: Cheap offshore {editor}s (in one case about $1,000/month in the Philippines) can turn two or three videos at a time from a script plus found footage and produced a scaling winner within two months. They bring no creativity, so someone must oversee them.
items.why: They are fast and cheap, but the output follows only the script given.
items.when: scaling video editing volume on a budget

items.title: Swap top performers between organic and paid
items.text: Put top paid content on social with dollars behind it, and hand the top organic posts to the {media buyer} to test as ads, even if a post doesn't look like a standalone ad. What worked in one channel often carries into the other.
items.why: Something about a post that did well organically can carry into paid, and vice versa.
items.when: brands running both organic social and paid social

items.title: Assign one operator to chase every node weekly
items.text: Put one operator in charge of the day-to-day who checks every step weekly: did it get posted, did we try the new angles, why are videos held up, are we behind. Back it with clear task tracking; without it, {founder}-driven bursts followed by lulls make output swing.
items.why: Founder-driven bursts of 20 videos followed by lulls make output swing; consistent tracking keeps it steady.
items.when: content and creative operations with several people

items.title: Buy inventory for the seasonal spike month
items.text: Plan inventory around the seasonal spike month: know when the seasonal ads run and buy extra stock for that specific month rather than averaging across the quarter. In one case a gift holiday drove a June spike, so extra stock was bought for June only.
items.why: A quarterly average hides the spike and leads to stockouts or overbuying.
items.when: inventory planning for products with a seasonal sales spike

items.title: Cap new subscribers for 90 days and measure the effect
items.text: Before turning subscriptions fully on, cap new subscribers for a fixed window and watch the effect on the business and inventory; raise the cap only if the numbers stay healthy. In one case the cap was 3,000 subscribers for 90 days, with 4,000-5,000 as the next step.
items.why: Scaling subscriptions without a cap can outrun inventory.
items.when: launching or scaling a subscription program

items.title: Put 80% of focus on the core that drives revenue
items.text: Put about 80% of focus on the core that already drives revenue (closing the ad flywheel, reaching new markets through creatives with different nationalities and comedians) and cap new products at about 20% of attention. In one case a clear path to $10-20M existed without new products.
items.why: A clear path to $10-20M exists without new products, which dilute focus.
items.when: prioritizing growth when the core product has room to scale

items.title: Use see-through bottles so customers see when to reorder
items.text: Use see-through packaging so customers can see how much product is left; seeing it run low is an internal trigger to reorder. In one case, the repeat customer rate rose on its own after the switch, without a subscription.
items.why: Seeing the product run low is an internal trigger to buy more.

items.title: Search Reddit for what the market believes about the problem
items.text: Search Reddit for the problem to learn what the market believes about it, then build products and messaging that answer that belief. In one case many younger men said the category was marketing nonsense and asked about a pill instead.
items.why: It would be ignorant as a business owner not to understand what the market believes.
items.when: market research before product or messaging work

items.title: Make every post personal, conversational, or funny
items.text: Speak as the {avatar}'s older brother or best friend, not a brand. Every piece of content (support emails, comment replies, social posts) should be personal: ask or answer a question, spark conversation, or make people laugh.
items.why: The goal is to be as authentic as possible, the way you would talk with family.
items.when: brand voice across social, support and comments

items.title: Read the customer brain doc before creating any content
items.text: Before creating any content, read the customer brain document: what the {avatar} wants and dislikes, limiting beliefs, motivations, inspiring case studies, what they love, and their problems. It gives a clear picture of who you are speaking to.
items.why: It paints a clear picture of who you are speaking to so content makes a subconscious connection.

items.title: Pair the physical problem with a subconscious problem in each topic
items.text: Build every content topic from a physical problem plus a subconscious one, then a relatable story where {hero product} solves both. Keep the physical problem fixed and vary the subconscious one to make new angles (example: forehead acne plus low confidence approaching women). You are selling the inner outcome, not the product.
items.why: People solve inner problems with products; you are selling confidence, not skincare.
items.when: angle and topic generation for content

items.title: Start with long-form video, then cut it into every format
items.text: Start content as long-form video, then break it into short-form videos, thumbnails, infographic images and written pieces. Video can be broken into every other format.
items.why: Video is digestible and engaging and can be broken into every other content format.

items.title: Make content evergreen but seasonal; promos only for launches
items.text: Make about 99% of content evergreen but relevant to the time of year (example: dry skin in winter) so it can be reused for years. Keep the ~1% promotional content for launches and seasonal promotions, framed broadly, because promo content can only be used once.
items.why: Promotional content can only be used once; evergreen content can be repurposed.

items.title: Post only what a friend would laugh at and share
items.text: Every social post must be native to its platform, unpolished and authentic: something you could send a friend and they would laugh or learn from. Posts that look like ads look out of place; short videos can be reused across short-video platforms and as ads.
items.why: Content that looks like an ad or is over-polished looks out of place; shareable content is what makes social pop.

items.title: Use owned channels to inform, not sell
items.text: On owned channels, inform rather than sell: send useful information and updates by email and link to a video, blog or value page that carries the buy link. In one case an email announcing a full product explainer video, with the buy link in the video description, sold very well.
items.why: Informing builds involvement, and sales follow off the back end.

items.title: Text non-buyers a personal update with a product video
items.text: Write texts like personal messages to friends. Example: to people who clicked but didn't buy, send 'our {hero product} orders are starting to deliver, check out this quick video' with the product page linked from the video.
items.why: Texts keep the brand top of mind in decisions without being salesy.
items.when: SMS to abandoned-cart or non-buyer lists

items.title: Write blog posts like cited Wikipedia entries
items.text: Write each blog post like a cited Wikipedia entry that concretely answers one question, with sources at the bottom and a call to action to a product, then distribute it by email and text. Detailed, sourced content builds authority.
items.why: Detailed, sourced content establishes the brand as an authority.

items.title: Treat ads as amplification of content that already sells
items.text: Treat ads as amplification of content that already sells: fill them with the best native-looking UGC from {creator}s who reviewed the product, made for each channel. Once a piece tests well in ads, post it organically and boost it again; in one case a short-video channel generated orders with no ads.
items.why: Product and content should sell without ad dollars (TikTok generated orders with no ads); ads only amplify.

items.title: Send a weekly newsletter plus plain-text connection emails
items.text: Run a weekly polished newsletter with images, plus plain-text connection emails: first-name personalization, few or no images, like a personal note, used for check-ins and reminders.
items.why: Connection emails feel personal and avoid distracting elements.

items.title: Run whitelisted ads from creator handles alongside branded ads
items.text: Get access to {creator}s' pages and posts and run budget from their handles to the {brand} site (whitelisting), and mix this with branded ads run from the {brand}'s own account. The mix is what allows scaling.
items.why: Mixing whitelisted and branded content is what allows scaling.
items.when: scaling paid social with creator content

items.title: Create original content on TikTok first, then cascade it
items.text: Make original content on TikTok first and engage the community there, because it gives the fastest market feedback. Then cascade it into Instagram reels, info posts, UGC, results and memes; Facebook gets leftovers only; YouTube waits.
items.why: TikTok gives the quickest feedback from the market.

items.title: Make content that answers: is this a cool dude I trust?
items.text: Don't polish; make content that is in the culture, entertains and connects, so viewers decide they like and trust the person. Then let email and text make the revenue off the back end. People care more about whether they trust the person than about the product.
items.why: People care more about whether they like the person than about the product, especially men buying skincare.
items.when: organic content, especially in categories where the buyer is skeptical of the category

items.title: Fix CPA spikes by feeding the account more ads
items.text: Watch new-customer CPA as the controllable metric. Turn off ads the platform suddenly overspends on, but fix the root cause by launching more ads so the account has somewhere to spend. In one case an ad hit about $500 CPA within hours and the fix was a batch of about 35 new ads.
items.why: Whack-a-mole on bad ads does not fix an account struggling to find where to spend money.
items.when: Meta paid social when CPA spikes

items.title: Keep proven spenders as backup if a new batch stalls
items.text: If new-customer CPA hasn't moved by mid-week after launching a batch, turn back on ads that previously sustained top-tier spend (in one case $5-10K) even if their CPA had risen. Ads that proved they can carry spend beat ads that can't.
items.why: Ads that have proven they can sustain spend are better than ads that cannot carry it.
items.when: Meta paid social, when a new creative batch stalls

items.title: Send creatives a weekly video on last week's ad results
items.text: Every week, record a short video walking through how last week's launched ads performed and post it in the creative team's channel, so they see which ads gained spend and which didn't.
items.why: The creative team needs to see which ads gained spend and which did not.
items.when: weekly creative feedback loop between media buying and creative

items.title: Answer every ad comment, handling objections and adding humor
items.text: Be active in ad comments: answer questions and objections, and make people laugh so others reply. Comments are where objections surface and much indirect selling happens; on platforms whose comments don't reach the help desk, reply inside the ads manager.
items.why: Comments are where objections surface and much indirect selling happens; engagement lifts conversion rate.
items.when: paid social while ads are live

items.title: Be a friend on social; be professional in support email
items.text: On social, talk to people like friends; in support email, when a customer has a specific product issue, be more buttoned-up and professional while still natural and kind.
items.why: Each channel carries a different kind of conversation.
items.when: brand voice across social vs customer support

items.title: Use Triple Whale as source of truth across ad platforms
items.text: When running ads on several platforms, use one third-party attribution tool (in one case Triple Whale) as the source of truth for sales, because each platform claims credit for the same sales.
items.why: Each platform tries to take credit for the same sales.

items.title: Iterate on the winning creator's persona in new scenes
items.text: When a UGC {creator} who matches the target persona wins, iterate with that same persona in new scenes, openings and situations. In one case a 50+ man with a clear product intro hit a 35-40% hook rate, so new versions showed him in the gym, being asked what he uses, or with friends his age.
items.why: The persona has proven it hooks the audience and trains the algorithm well.
items.when: paid social, after a creator persona wins

items.title: Speak to one person and their problem, not generic product
items.text: Avoid generic product ads; make each ad speak to one person and that person's problem. Product catalog ads can work but failed for this {brand}.
items.why: Specific ads feel authentic and personally placed; generic ones reach nobody deeply enough to buy.

items.title: Answer every comment and email with a real reply
items.text: Answer customer comments and emails on every platform quickly and with a real reply that starts a conversation, not just a thumbs-up emoji (except for very basic comments).
items.why: Every reply is a chance to treat customers like family and start a conversation.

items.title: Offer a cheaper product when a customer says it's expensive
items.text: When someone says a product is too expensive, recommend a lower-cost product that solves the same problem. Make it as easy as possible for people to buy.
items.why: Make it as easy as possible for people to buy and solve their problem.
items.when: support, comments and sales replies for brands with more than one price point

items.title: Track CSAT, response time, resolution time and messages per ticket
items.text: Measure customer experience on CSAT (0-5), first response time, resolution time and messages per ticket, keeping the last three as low as possible. Fix problems at the source by updating site info and reply templates and flagging when more support staff are needed.
items.why: These numbers show whether customers are actually being made happy quickly and easily.

items.title: Log every experiment with hypothesis, metric and result
items.text: Log every test in a master sheet: business function, date, optimization objective, hypothesis, deliverable, metric targeted, analysis and next steps, and mark each result positive, neutral or negative. It turns creativity into numbers over time.
items.why: It quantifies creativity and shows what works and what doesn't over time.

items.title: Balance improvement effort across all four business functions
items.text: Track improvement effort across content creation, performance marketing, website management and customer experience, and raise whichever is lagging so all four stay level. They only move the business when they move together.
items.why: The functions only improve the business when they move together.
items.when: planning improvement work across the business

items.title: Bring an analyzed idea with a roadmap to the bi-weekly meeting
items.text: Each team member analyzes their own function and brings an idea plus an implementation roadmap and needed resources to a regular (in one case bi-weekly) meeting. If it is judged high-impact, it goes on the plan and they own it.
items.why: Improvements to marketing efficiency and customer experience create profit, and everyone is a key contributor.

items.title: Build every creator video on scroll stopper, entertain, educate, CTA
items.text: Performance creative is native, organic-looking feed video with a clear problem and solution, such as a before-and-after. Every piece carries a scroll stopper, entertainment, education and a call to action, and should have organic viral potential as is.
items.why: Content that looks like an ad or feels salesy gets picked up and ignored; content people would share earns attention.

items.title: Call out the skin problem in the first seconds, several versions
items.text: Name the pain point first, then show how {hero product} solves it, and make several versions of the first couple of seconds where the problem is called out. For a first-of-its-kind product, naming problem and solution removes most of the confusion (estimated at about 80%).
items.why: A first-of-its-kind product raises questions; naming the problem and solution removes about 80% of that confusion.
items.when: video ad openings, especially for new or unfamiliar products

items.title: Give creators six content types to film
items.text: Ask {creator}s for six content types: problem-solution before-and-afters, unboxings, how-to tutorials on one problem with a tip and demo, day-in-the-life routines, three-reasons-why lists, and original skits. On TikTok, film tutorials as video replies to existing comments.
items.why: Each type is native to the feed and lets the product show up where it makes sense instead of as a hard sell.
items.when: briefing creators for organic and paid content

items.title: Make skits off current events; remake sounds in your own voice
items.text: Make skits that ride current events and exist purely to entertain, with the product only where it fits and no hard CTA. Never use copyrighted audio; hum or re-voice sounds yourself so the post can be run as an ad.
items.why: Entertaining posts stand out on the feed, and re-voiced audio avoids copyright problems when the post is run as an ad.
items.when: organic skit content that may later run as ads

items.title: Collect the video testimonial after use, not at unboxing
items.text: An unboxing first impression is fine, but require a separate video testimonial after the {creator} has used the product for a while, and encourage them to document results over the following months. Real-use testimonials are what convince buyers.
items.why: A testimonial after real use gives a legitimate experience that shapes how buyers see the product.
items.when: creator deliverables for products with results over time

items.title: Deliver raw and edited files to a per-creator Drive folder
items.text: {creator}s drop raw and edited files in their own shared folder, sorted by topic, and save anything already posted to TikTok without the watermark first (a free tool works) so it can run on other platforms.
items.why: Sorted, watermark-free files can be reused across platforms without back-and-forth.

items.title: Get Instagram collab invites and TikTok Spark authorization on every post
items.text: On every {creator} post, get an Instagram collaborator invite and TikTok Spark Ads authorization with the code sent to the {brand}. It handles disclosure up front and lets the {brand} put budget behind the creator's handle.
items.why: It handles the disclosure and legal side up front and lets the brand put budget behind the creator's handle.
items.when: creator posts that may be boosted as ads

items.title: Open every ad on a weird but relevant clip
items.text: Open every ad on a weird or unique clip tied to the ad (examples: shaving half your head, extreme close-ups, squeezing product all over your hand on purpose), so the viewer reacts 'what did he just do?' and keeps watching.
items.why: The viewer reacts with 'what did this guy just do?' and keeps watching.

items.title: Add a voiceover so a real person carries the story
items.text: Add a voiceover, recorded while filming or as a separate memo, so a real person carries a storyline viewers can follow; music goes under it later. It also makes captions easier to write.
items.why: A voice puts a real person behind the video and makes captions easier to write.

items.title: Shoot phone video at 1080p 30fps, never 4K
items.text: Shoot phone video at 1080p 30fps, never 4K, because social platforms compress everything. Use good lighting, a clean set that matches the angle, clean audio, a centered subject and a tripod if shaky.
items.why: Social platforms compress everything, so 4K adds nothing.

items.title: Deliver it like a recommendation to a friend, not a commercial
items.text: Deliver it like a recommendation to a friend, not a commercial: real emotion, your own voice; treat any script as a guideline and redo takes until it doesn't sound like an ad.
items.why: Viewers tune out anything that sounds like a commercial.

items.title: Caption every video centered, native-style, in Proxima Nova Semibold
items.text: Caption every video so it makes sense with sound off, with text centered around the subject and product, never covering the face or product, in platform-native styles (bubble blocks, outlined text, speed-read). One {brand} used Proxima Nova Semibold, the TikTok font, when editing on a computer.
items.why: Captions lift engagement and comprehension with sound off, and centered text survives repurposing across placements.

items.title: Lead with visuals; let copy only guide them
items.text: Treat video and photos as the {brand}'s most important asset and make them realistic and personal; copy only guides the visual. People read far less than they used to.
items.why: People read far less than they used to, so the visual has to stop and sell.
items.when: creative direction across ads and site

items.title: Define the brand look as two reference brands combined
items.text: Give {creator}s a one-line brand reference made of two familiar brands combined (in one case: Apple's design with Supreme's culture, exclusivity and perceived value). It sets a distinct vibe everyone can aim at without copying competitors.
items.why: A blend of two familiar brands sets a distinct vibe everyone can aim at without copying competitors.
items.when: briefing creators and designers on brand look

items.title: Drop any design that doesn't load fast or convert
items.text: Pair high-end looks with conversion: if a design element isn't functional or doesn't load fast, don't use it on the site or in ads.
items.why: Design that doesn't load or function brings no dollar back.

items.title: Make product photos explain benefit and use instantly
items.text: Make product photos explain the benefit, use case or features instantly by showing the product in context, pair products in shots to plant the add-on purchase, and show accessories in use. Product photos live mainly on product pages and in emails.
items.why: Context paints the picture of using the product, and pairings plant the add-on purchase.
items.when: product photography for product pages and email

items.title: Shoot lifestyle images with the product in the customer's real moment
items.text: Shoot lifestyle images of the product inside the customer's real setting, showing a benefit or use case; some background is fine but the product stays the focus. They are the most versatile asset (pages, emails, ads, social) because people picture themselves in the same spot.
items.why: People put themselves in the same position when they see the product in their own context.

items.title: Make video read without words and cut it on the beat
items.text: Every video should explain the scene with no words or captions needed (captions only guide), be cut to the beat of the music, and include people and use cases, not just product. One {brand} used hard-hitting boom-bap, jazz and lo-fi beats to match its culture.
items.why: Video is what gains and nurtures attention before the viewer knows what is happening.
items.when: video editing for ads and social

items.title: Let ads win the click; let the landing page sell
items.text: Ads win the eyeball, the click and the branded impression; the website and landing page do the selling, laid out top to bottom by AIDA (attention, interest, desire, action) and ending with a call to action.
items.why: The landing page is where purchase intent actually happens.
items.when: splitting the job between ads and landing pages

items.title: Design pages mobile-first and keep the subject dead center
items.text: Design pages mobile-first and fast, because most traffic comes from phones via social ads (80%+ in one case). Design vertical, and even when filming wide keep the subject and key element dead center.
items.why: Most visitors arrive on a phone straight from a social ad.
items.when: site design and visual assets for social traffic

items.title: Order the product page: result headline, demo, proof, box, FAQ, reviews
items.text: Order the product page: a headline stating the result and time (example: a clear result in one minute) over a standout product shot, then image and video of how it works, the main value prop against the usual alternative, how to use it, the difference, what's in the box, FAQ, results and reviews. A visitor should get it without reading the text blocks.
items.why: A visitor gets what the product does even without reading the text blocks.

items.title: Sell what the product does for buyers, not price
items.text: Like Apple's product pages, sell the experience and outcome so the buyer can picture themselves in it; don't lead with price or functions. People buy what the product will do for them.
items.why: People buy what the product will do for them.

items.title: Wrap the product inside a numbered listicle on an adjacent topic
items.text: Open a pre-sell on a topic the {avatar} already cares about, promise a numbered list in the first seconds, and slot {hero product} in as one item. Example: '7 signs she doesn't like you', with acne as sign 3. The audience stays for the topic and meets the product as part of the value.
items.why: The audience stays for the topic and meets the product as part of the value, not as an ad.

items.title: Hold viewers with open loops and a mid-video recap
items.text: Hold viewers with open loops and a recap: say the first items are the worst, label later items as ones where they still have a chance, recap the list so far, and tell them to stick around for the rest.
items.why: Open loops and recaps keep viewers watching through and past the product section.

items.title: Bridge to the product with study-backed numbers
items.text: Bridge to the product with cited studies and specific numbers that size the problem, then promise what fixing it adds up to. In one example, three studied problems were each scored on a 1-7 attractiveness scale (one cost 1.8 points, another 1.4) and fixing all three was framed as +4 points.
items.why: Specific studies and numbers make the problem feel real and the fix worth acting on.

items.title: Demo cleansing on orange peels: brush versus hand
items.text: Demonstrate the product side by side against the usual alternative on a stand-in surface, then close on time-per-day and a discount link. In one example dirt-and-oil was rubbed into two orange peels as pores, one cleaned with a brush (10,000 vibrations a minute) and one by hand, showing hands just move dirt around.
items.why: The side-by-side shows hands just move dirt around while the brush pulls it out.
items.when: demo videos for products that beat a common habit

items.title: Replace the long FAQ with a searchable help center
items.text: Replace a long FAQ with a searchable help center on its own subdomain, with article categories (tracking, products, shipping and returns, billing, account, popular questions), a self-service chat for refunds and tracking, and a contact link, linked from the footer.
items.why: Customers ask the same questions repeatedly, and one central place simplifies customer service.

items.title: Answer tickets by pasting the matching help article link
items.text: Write help articles with step-by-step instructions and a how-to video so agents can paste the article link into tickets, and show related products on each article. It speeds replies and keeps selling as the line grows.
items.why: It speeds replies and keeps selling more product as the line grows.

items.title: Cover products, delivery and core skin problems in the help center
items.text: Write help-center articles on each main product (benefits, features, use, ingredients, instructions), on delivery (fulfillment, billing, notifications, refunds, replacements, exchanges) and on the core problems the {avatar} has. Answering every question builds authority and trust.
items.why: Answering every question builds authority, keeps the brand top of mind and creates a content moat that earns trust.

items.title: List questions in a sheet from existing sources, dedupe, then build
items.text: Start a sheet of topics and questions answered from what already exists: the current FAQ, product science material, research notes and studies, product details and review Q&A. Remove duplicates, build the help center, and keep adding over time.
items.why: The information already exists; it only needs organizing, and it can grow iteratively.

items.title: Run an always-on customer and lead survey
items.text: Run an always-on customer survey: what gut instinct made you buy over others, what problem you wanted solved, what was unique about buying from us, what you liked most, what word describes you, how the product makes you feel, what annoyed you about alternatives, what you'd change. Ask leads why they were interested and why they didn't buy, then distill answers into one doc.
items.why: After a year of answers you know the customer at a fundamental level and can speak in their terms.

items.title: Scrape comments on top ads and export reviews for angle mining
items.text: Have a VA scrape comments from your top video ads of all time and export reviews (about 800 in one case) into sheets, then run them through AI to find new angles and ads. Comments show exactly what the community says when it sees your content.
items.why: Comments show exactly what the community says when they see your content.
items.when: angle research from existing ads and reviews

items.title: Fill every funnel stage; brief the stage that's under-indexed in spend
items.text: Make content for every awareness stage: unaware ({founder} story, how it's made), problem aware, solution aware (social proof, ease of use, guarantees), product aware (features, differentiation) and retention/advocacy. Check where spend is going and brief videos and statics for the stage that is under-indexed.
items.why: Covering each stage captures every part of the customer journey instead of only top of funnel.

items.title: Spend 80% on new concepts, 20% on iterations
items.text: Spend about 80% of creative time on brand-new concepts that reach new audiences or {avatar}s (same problem, different person), and about 20% iterating on winners: new scroll stoppers and headlines with the rest of the video unchanged.
items.why: New concepts find new buyers; iterations extend proven ones cheaply.
items.when: creative production mix for paid social

items.title: Write new 10-30 second leads onto proven VSL bodies
items.text: Make most new ads as new leads: swap the first 10-30 seconds and bolt them onto a VSL already proven to work (for example a {founder} story or social proof VSL). Make a brand-new VSL only for a different market or problem.
items.why: It tests new openings fast while keeping the body that already converts.
items.when: paid video, once a VSL body is proven

items.title: Lead with transformation, humor and misconception angles
items.text: Lead with the angles proven in the account; in one account these were true lifestyle before-and-after transformation, candid humor, and busting a misconception about the usual fix.
items.why: These angles have already performed best in the account.

items.title: Script ads: hook, story, education, product, mechanism, proof, offer, CTA
items.text: Script ads in this order: hook, storyline, education or usefulness, introduce the product, unique mechanism, proof it works, an {offer} to transform themselves, and a call to act now.
items.why: It follows simple marketing principles and has been the best-working structure.

items.title: Test new concepts in dynamic creative before moving to control
items.text: Run every new concept through a dynamic creative test so the platform finds the best video and copy combination, then move only that single winning combination into the control ad set. Keep media buying simple and lean on the platform.
items.why: Knowing the winning combination gives confidence when it goes into control.

items.title: Duplicate the last DCT ad set and name it date-DCT-angle-concept-actor
items.text: Duplicate the last creative-test ad set to keep the standard settings, and name each one by date, test type, angle, concept and the actor or message (e.g. men over 40), so each test reads at a glance.
items.why: Duplicating keeps the standardized settings, and the naming shows what each test is at a glance.

items.title: Launch tests Mondays at 12am, two weeks apart
items.text: Start each new creative test on a Monday at 12am, two weeks after the last one, with no end date, unless a critical test means shifting others. Each test needs at least two weeks to show whether it gets spend.
items.why: Each test needs at least two weeks to show whether it gets spend.

items.title: Target broad; exclude customers only in test ad sets
items.text: Exclude the customer list in test ad sets only; the control ad set excludes nothing. Keep targeting broad (in one case all US men 18-65+) with automatic placements so the platform finds buyers.
items.why: Keeping targeting broad and standard lets the platform find buyers.
items.when: Meta testing and control ad set targeting

items.title: Wait two weeks and $500 spend before graduating a test
items.text: Let each creative test run at least two weeks and ideally spend at least $500 before moving anything into control; earlier reads aren't reliable.
items.why: Earlier reads are not reliable enough to replace a control.
items.when: Meta creative testing, before graduating a winner

items.title: Answer skeptic comments with humor, a small-team voice, and risk reversal
items.text: Answer skeptical comments with humor so they know a real person is replying, say you're a small team, and remove risk: full money back, plus the real return rate. In one case only 4% returned (a 96% success rate), which turned a skeptic into 'maybe I'll try it'.
items.why: Acknowledging the doubt and showing there is nothing to lose turned a skeptic into 'maybe I'll try it out'.

items.title: Answer 'overpriced' by refusing to be a commodity
items.text: When a commenter calls the product overpriced, refuse to be a commodity: point to the real cost to make, import and ship, contrast the cheap knockoff (how long it lasts, its quality), and stress results and the science, while acknowledging they have options. Show a real person behind the {brand}.
items.why: The commenter is judging it as a commodity; a real person and real results change the comparison.
items.when: replying to price objections in ad comments for premium-priced products

items.title: Turn repeated comment objections into new products and offers
items.text: Track beliefs that keep showing up in comments and answer them at the business level, for example by building a product that meets the objection and leading with it as another top-of-funnel product. In one case the belief was that diet and hormones cause the problem, so a supplement was built.
items.why: Meeting the market where its beliefs are is how you break through.
items.when: product and offer planning from repeated objections

items.title: Reply clearly to grow threads, then turn beliefs into top-of-funnel ads
items.text: Reply to comments by acknowledging the person and answering clearly to keep the thread going. Then turn the belief from the thread into a fresh top-of-funnel ad and carry it into emails, texts, landing pages and the FAQ; more people hold that belief than care about the {founder} story.
items.why: Clear replies multiply comments and show what the market believes, and more people hold that belief than care about the founder story.

items.title: Open the weekly report with new-customer CPA, then MER
items.text: Open the weekly paid report with new-customer CPA, the number the buyer controls most, then MER. Recompute without the days before new ads took spend to see the real trend; in one case CPA went from $100-116 to $77-91, down 23% to about $85 with pre-launch days removed, at an MER of about 1.8.
items.why: New-customer CPA is the number the buyer controls most.

items.title: Never switch off top spenders; beat them with new creative
items.text: Never switch off top-spending top-of-funnel ads; leave them on and let new creative take spend from them. In one case turning off a top spender destabilized the account and raised CPA, and turning it back on stabilized the campaign.
items.why: Turning off a top spender destabilized the account and lifted CPA.

items.title: Let a launch settle a week, then trim high-frequency weak retargeting
items.text: Wait about a week after launching a batch to see where spend lands, then cut ads not carrying spend, especially high-frequency retargeting ads that are inefficient mid-funnel.
items.why: Those ads aren't doing heavy lifting and trimming them gains efficiency.
items.when: Meta paid social, a week after a new batch launches

items.title: Relaunch best retargeting ads as holiday sale campaigns
items.text: For a holiday promotion, relaunch your best mid- and bottom-funnel retargeting ads as sale campaigns, turn off the ones doing little, and raise budget through the week. In one case most promo conversions came from those proven ads and the promo was net positive.
items.why: Most promotion conversions came from those proven retargeting ads, and the promo campaign was net positive.
items.when: paid social during short holiday promotions

items.title: Judge test CPA in Triple Whale and watch blended CPA
items.text: Judge test CPA in a third-party attribution tool (in one case Triple Whale) rather than the ad platform, because the pixel double-counts through the funnel, and always check blended CPA for how the business is doing.
items.why: Funnel tracking muddies Facebook's numbers.
items.when: Meta creative testing with multi-step funnels

items.title: Graduate tests with real spend and CPA below average
items.text: Move a test into control only when it has spent a decent amount and its CPA is below the account average. In one case the target was under $50: a $37 test graduated and a $61 one was weaker. Discount reads taken while out of stock, when CPA spikes.
items.why: Spend plus below-average CPA shows the ad can beat the current control.

items.title: Move the winning combination as the existing post ID
items.text: Move the winning dynamic-test combination into control as the existing post: preview the test ad to find the winning video-copy combo and its post, then in control duplicate a recent ad, choose 'use existing post', select that post ID, paste the URL parameters and rename it. This keeps the exact combination and its engagement.
items.why: Using the exact post keeps the combination Facebook picked and its engagement.
items.when: Meta, moving a dynamic creative test winner into control

items.title: Keep four to six ads live in control; queue extra winners
items.text: Keep four to six active ads in the control ad set depending on spend. If it's full, mark the new winner pending and switch it on when an ad dies by the automated rules; park iterations of a working control until it dies, since they rarely beat a control that is still working.
items.why: Iterations rarely beat a control that is still working, given how the algorithm learns.

items.title: Cut ad budgets when Amazon stock runs out
items.text: Cut ad budgets when the product is out of stock on a major marketplace, because those shoppers won't buy elsewhere and colder audiences care even less; better, never go out of stock there. In one case Amazon was about 25% of sales, and that week spent $59K for about $80K revenue.
items.why: Ads keep spending while a quarter of the sales channel can't convert.
items.when: paid media for brands that also sell on Amazon or another marketplace

items.title: Cut leaky ads the moment they're out of KPI
items.text: Kill ads that are out of KPI or show no potential after a few days to a week, or after 36 hours if CPA is far off (in one case $150). It isn't emotional: in one case cutting from about 300 active ads to about 50 took weekly spend from $59K to $39K on the same $80K revenue.
items.why: Leaky ads waste thousands; cut spend flows to the best ads anyway. It is not emotional.

items.title: Drop automation tools that cost more than their decisions
items.text: Cancel automation tools that cost more than the decisions they make. In one case a rules tool cost $1,300 to make one decision a day that a {media buyer} could make.
items.why: The cost isn't justified by what it does.

items.title: Sell skin supplements as the internal fix after topicals failed
items.text: Sell an ingestible as the internal fix for people whose topical products failed, using a visual hook of the visible problem, instead of claiming it directly fixes the problem. So many people have tried many topical products that the internal angle lands easier.
items.why: So many people have tried loads of skin products and seen them fail.
items.when: advertising supplements tied to a visible problem

items.title: Keep a strong non-converting hook; rebuild the body
items.text: When a video has a strong hook but doesn't convert or hold, keep the hook and rebuild the body: brief {creator}s to copy only the first three to five seconds and build different bodies on proven angles and objections. In one case an affiliate TikTok Shop video hit a 50% hook rate with no conversions.
items.why: The hook is proven; the body is what lost the viewer.
items.when: video ads with high hook rate and low hold or conversion

items.title: Tag every test with angle, pain point, test type and notes
items.text: In the creative testing tracker, mark each ad live or winner, its general and specific angle or pain point, the test type and notes, and feed that back to the creative team. Test landing pages one at a time so you know which one is working.
items.why: Detailed tags turn tests into feedback that makes better ads.

items.title: Cut weak ads and give a struggling campaign the weekend
items.text: Before killing a struggling campaign, cut its weakest ads and give it the weekend; if it holds, raise budget. In one case a campaign dropped from about $100 CPA to $60-73 with two ads carrying spend.
items.why: The campaign recovered once the dragging ads were off.
items.when: Meta campaign that is close to being killed

items.title: Accept negative first-order profit on top spenders if account CPA holds
items.text: Allow top spenders negative first-order profit while they bring in new customers and overall account CPA is falling; watch them and get more aggressive only if they creep up.
items.why: New customers matter more than each ad's first-order profit when the account is healthy.
items.when: Meta paid social when the account is healthy

items.title: Send the Monday report, then launch the week's ad batch
items.text: Each Monday send the paid media report (net profit headline, CPA trend per campaign, top ads linked), launch the week's ad batch right after, and ask the team what to add or remove from the report. A fixed weekly rhythm keeps creative flowing.
items.why: A fixed weekly rhythm keeps new creative flowing and the report useful.

items.title: Sell the bundle by the per-unit price
items.text: Show the lowest per-unit price ('as low as $X each') and make it reachable only through the bundle, framed as one for you, a backup, and gifts. It pushes buyers to the bigger bundle and raises average order value.
items.why: It pushes people to the bigger bundle, which raises average order value on the front end.
items.when: bundle offers on product and landing pages

items.title: A 'starting at' price in the ad lifts click-through
items.text: Put the lowest possible price in the ad ('get {hero product} for as low as $X') when the value behind it is real, then check which version took spend. In one case low-price ads got higher click-through and took most spend versus plain '30% off' creative.
items.why: The low-price ads got higher click-through and took the majority of spend versus plain '30% off' creative.
items.when: paid ads with bundle or tiered pricing

items.title: Make the offer ultra clean and clear for partners
items.text: Whenever you hand creative to affiliates or {creator}s, make sure they know exactly what the {offer} is and that it reads in one glance; the pricing strategy only works in their content if the offer is clear.
items.why: A clear offer is what lets the pricing strategy actually work in other people's content.

items.title: Pair every new angle with the mechanism that proves it
items.text: When research gives you a new angle, write down how the product solves the root cause (the mechanism) and put it in the brief, so partners use the same hook-plus-mechanism logic. The mechanism makes the product feel unique and gives people a reason to believe the hook.
items.why: The mechanism makes the product feel unique in the market and gives people a reason to believe the hook.

items.title: Always keep testing, even when something works
items.text: Keep testing new angles alongside winners and keep watching what spends; a new angle that suddenly starts spending is a signal to build on. Winners, especially seasonal ones, fade.
items.why: The seasonal winner will fade. New angles keep the brand ahead.

items.title: Don't over-credit a win during a peak season
items.text: Don't over-credit a win during a peak season, when almost anything sells better. Note the season when judging what works, and look for what holds up outside it.
items.why: Being in the right place at the right time inflates results.
items.when: reading results during holidays or peak seasons

items.title: US shoppers are jaded, so show you know what they've already seen
items.text: Before writing for the US market, study the claims and ads shoppers have already been burned by, then position as an authority who understands what they tried. US shoppers have seen the boldest claims many times and assume it's fake unless you prove you know their history.
items.why: Americans have seen the boldest claims many times. If you don't prove you understand their history they assume it's fake.
items.when: copy and positioning for US consumers in crowded categories

items.title: Find where the customer talks and borrow their words
items.text: Find where the {avatar} actually talks online (in one case men talked on Reddit) and how they phrase things, then translate that language into the creative, landing page, {offer} and funnel.
items.why: What they say and see online is how you should speak back to them in each medium.

items.title: Customer conversations beat desk research
items.text: Talk to real customers and listen to how they describe the problem; use online research to confirm and expand those conversations, not replace them.
items.why: The actual conversations are the most valuable input you get.

items.title: Study competitor funnels and the category leader's offers
items.text: Pull up the funnels of competitors doing huge volume and the best-known brand in the category, and study how they structure offers (BOGO, clear value). Copy the offer structure, not their product; their offers show what the shopper responds to.
items.why: Their offers show the psychology of the shopper and what they respond to.

items.title: Reposition the offer against what they tried before
items.text: Frame the {offer} around what the shopper has already tried and failed with, and show a high full-price anchor next to a lower real price. You can't sell on form and function alone. In one case this moved device AOV from $69.99 to $98 and funnel AOV past $130.
items.why: You can't sell on form and function alone. Pricing and offer psychology get people over the hump.

items.title: Test a broken page in incognito and mobile view, then escalate
items.text: When a landing page looks wrong, check it in an incognito window, check the other landing pages, and check mobile view in the browser's inspector, then flag it to the team as urgent; paid traffic is burning money on it every minute.
items.why: Paid media traffic goes to these pages, so a broken page burns ad spend every minute.

items.title: Run the eye-level test against competitors
items.text: Put your content next to competitors' and be honest about who looks better at a glance. If a cheaper competitor's content beats yours, adjust, because shoppers will pick it.
items.why: If a cheap knockoff looks better than you, shoppers will pick it.
items.when: creative and page reviews against competitors

items.title: Give creative feedback slide by slide, objectively
items.text: Review a brief slide by slide with specific, objective notes on what is wrong and why, push back where needed, and invite the designer to push back too.
items.why: Specific, objective notes get the brief fixed faster than general reactions.

items.title: Brand look: a middle ground between brand and direct response
items.text: Aim the {brand} look at a middle ground between branded and direct response: in one test, the full detailed brand look hurt landing pages, and a flatter, scannable version in the brand colors worked. It must be easy to scan and buy while still feeling like the {brand}.
items.why: It has to be easy to scan and buy while still feeling like the brand.
items.when: landing page and ad visual design

items.title: Lighten product and ad imagery
items.text: Use lighter, brighter product and ad images and mix dark and light depictions; avoid dark colors against white text or black text on dark backgrounds. Dark images hide the mechanism and are hard to read.
items.why: Dark images hide the mechanism and are hard on the eyes. Competitors' bright images are easy to read.

items.title: Buy the cheap knockoff and compare it with your hands
items.text: Buy the cheap competing products, hold them next to yours, and find the real physical differences you can prove, then show them. Those differences position {hero product} as the best option.
items.why: The differences are what position your product as the best option for sensitive skin.

items.title: Back each claim with a document you can produce
items.text: Keep documentation for each product claim and lead with it; knockoffs won't have the paperwork, so a provable claim can't be copied.
items.why: A claim you can prove cannot be copied by the cheap competitors.
items.when: product claims in crowded or knockoff-heavy categories

items.title: Lead with customer before-and-afters, unedited
items.text: Lead with real customer before-and-afters, unedited, and show a range of results, not only the best ones. It is real proof of the improvement.
items.why: It is the core differentiator and it is real proof of the improvement.

items.title: One image, one feature, one benefit
items.text: Give each product image one feature or benefit and little text; split images that cram in several features. Competitors who separate everything read crystal clear.
items.why: Competitors separate everything and make it crystal clear. Stuffed images are hard to read.

items.title: Only claim what is true on the listing
items.text: Check every callout against the real product before it ships, and claim only what is true. In one case the body was waterproof but the charging port was not, so the image must not say the product is.
items.why: False claims create refunds and trust problems.

items.title: Show who the product is for with diverse before-and-afters
items.text: Show before-and-afters across races and problem types, and label the {founder} photo as the founder, so the product doesn't read as for one group only. In one case people kept asking whether it was only for one group.
items.why: People ask whether it is only for black men. Showing a mix makes clear who the brand serves.
items.when: brands perceived as serving a single group

items.title: Show the mechanism with CGI instead of a guy rubbing his face
items.text: Show how the product works with CGI of the mechanism rather than just someone using it; a person using it doesn't explain an invisible mechanism.
items.why: A man rubbing it on his face does not explain sonic vibration. The CGI does.
items.when: products whose mechanism isn't visible in normal use

items.title: Check the customer research before using a word like 'glow'
items.text: Check the customer research before using a word; use the words the {avatar} uses for the problem. In one case a beauty word ('glow') was dropped for the words the audience actually used.
