items.why: The word has to match how the avatar talks about the problem.

items.title: Keep packaging imagery true to the real box
items.text: Keep packaging images true to the box the customer actually receives; never depict a box that won't ship.
items.why: What's pictured must match what ships.
items.when: packaging imagery on ads and pages

items.title: Explain why their past fixes failed, in the headline logic
items.text: Write the page so the reader sees why every previous product failed: the problem wasn't the products, it was something they couldn't reach (in one case 'a depth problem'). Then the new mechanism is the missing piece, and they stop blaming themselves.
items.why: It keeps them from blaming themselves or their past products and makes the new solution make sense.
items.when: landing pages for buyers who have tried other fixes

items.title: Turn research into the page headline
items.text: Turn the strongest true research finding into the page headline, then use the body to explain it in plain steps. Only publish claims you have verified; a true, surprising finding hooks people who've tried everything.
items.why: A true, surprising finding hooks people who've tried everything.

items.title: Stack the offer: guarantee, free month, store credit
items.text: Close the page with a full {offer} stack: product bundle, a free first month of an add-on, a 90-day guarantee, and store credit for sending in results, explained plainly. Piling on real value makes the decision easy and lowers risk.
items.why: Piling on real value makes the buy decision easy and lowers risk.

items.title: Show a demo video and a close that calls for a choice
items.text: Include a side-by-side demo ({hero product} versus the usual way) and end with a plain choice: keep doing what you're doing, or fix the root cause.
items.why: The demo makes the difference visible and the close forces a decision.

items.title: Judge cheap-traffic image ads on CPC and CTR, then blended profit
items.text: Judge cheap-traffic image test ads on CPC and CTR first; weak CPA on small spend is fine if the traffic keeps the blended business profitable. In one case realistic AI images got an 11-cent CPC and blended efficiency stayed profitable.
items.why: Realistic AI images got an 11 cent CPC and exploded traffic, and the blended efficiency stayed profitable.
items.when: paid social image ads used to drive top-of-funnel traffic

items.title: Turn research into an avatar image with the problem and angle in it
items.text: Turn research into an image that shows three things: a specific {avatar} in a specific moment, the problem visible on them, and the angle. The avatar plus the visible problem makes viewers stop and wonder.
items.why: The avatar plus the visible problem makes the viewer stop and wonder.

items.title: Test with stills first, then build video on what wins
items.text: Test an {avatar} and angle with static images first; if it is engaging, go deeper on that avatar, refine the angle, then write storyboards and video ads. It's the cheapest way to validate before spending on video.
items.why: It is the cheapest way to validate before you spend on video.

items.title: Don't stop making conversion video ads
items.text: Keep making regular conversion video ads while cheap image ads fill the top of the funnel; the image ads drive traffic but not strong return on their own.
items.why: The image ads are great traffic but not great return on their own.

items.title: Keep graphic content ad-safe
items.text: Keep ads platform-safe: no blood or overly graphic content in the ad; put the grossest material on the landing page instead.
items.why: Too-gross content risks platform rejection.
items.when: ads about gross or graphic problems

items.title: Click through your own funnel's selections and back button
items.text: Click through your own funnel's product-selection steps for every product: one option is always selected, it can't be deselected, and the choice stays after pressing back. Losing a selection mid-checkout breaks orders.
items.why: Losing a selection mid-checkout breaks orders.
items.when: funnel QA before and after launches

items.title: Standardize pages: only the problem language changes
items.text: Once testing shows what works, lock the page sections, copy structure, images and {offer}; for a new market or problem, change only the words describing the problem (and maybe colors). Pages go out fast and stay consistent.
items.why: Nothing has to be built from scratch, so pages go out fast and stay consistent.
items.when: scaling landing pages across problems or markets

items.title: The reusable section stack of a sales page
items.text: Reuse the same ordered section stack on every sales page: headline, subheadline, social proof, before-and-afters, product demo, unique mechanism, {founder}, expert videos, a rotating brag bar, customer videos, product callouts, free gift, {offer}, testimonials. Keep the subheadline to a clean line break.
items.why: Reusing the exact same sections keeps every page clear and the language the same.

items.title: One problem-specific page per core problem
items.text: Build one page per core problem the product solves and send problem-specific ads only to the matching page, so the ad and page speak to the exact same problem.
items.why: The ad and the page speak to the same exact problem, so the experience is relevant.
items.when: products that solve several distinct problems

items.title: A general homepage links to the problem pages
items.text: Make the general page a high-level overview (reviews, timelines, the science, one picture per problem) that links each problem to its specific page, and use it for search and retargeting. It needs less education because people click through to their problem.
items.why: Less education on the general page because people who want more can click to their specific problem.
items.when: site structure with multiple problem pages

items.title: Problem-aware pages bring people in; the general page reaches unaware
items.text: Send most traffic through problem-aware pages, because that typically works; use a broader page showing how it works, the problems and the results to reach unaware and solution-aware people who don't believe the category works.
items.why: Most men know what skincare is but don't believe it works, so you show how.
items.when: routing paid traffic by awareness stage

items.title: If you spot something not standardized, fix it
items.text: When you see a color or element that differs from the page standard, bring it back in line instead of leaving it.
items.why: Little inconsistencies keep popping up and the pages should stay clean and crisp.

items.title: Product page template: one-time vs subscribe plus cross-sell
items.text: Use one product page template (name, subheadline, bullets, price, {offer}) for every product; subscription products add a one-time vs subscribe choice and a cross-sell of {hero product}. The same structure makes pages fast to make.
items.why: Same structure on every page means the pages are fast to make.

items.title: Template the upsell so new products just drop in
items.text: Use one templated upsell flow and customer portal so a new product just drops in and shows as a simple separate store. It's simple for the customer and fast for the team.
items.why: It's simple for the customer and quick for the team.
items.when: post-purchase upsells as the product line grows

items.title: Aim to get one 'yes', then split test biweekly
items.text: The upsell sequence's goal is to get the buyer to add one thing, because one yes leads to more. Run a baseline sequence and split-test order and prices about every two weeks, watching take rate.
items.why: Once they say yes once, they are likely to say yes to more.

items.title: Lead with the most direct cross-sell, shown clearly
items.text: Lead the upsells with the most direct cross-sell (an accessory for the product just bought), shown clearly on a clean background with a few value props, and use the same approach for every upsell. The buyer is in a buying mindset, so be ultra clear on what they get.
items.why: They just got a bunch of free stuff and are in a buying mindset, so be ultra clear on what they get.

items.title: Default to the one-time, one-bottle option
items.text: Preselect the one-time, single-unit option on upsells so yes is one tap, make the bigger bundle or subscription easy to switch to, and place buttons for right-thumb use. In one case take rates were much higher on one-time because the customer wouldn't subscribe to something untried.
items.why: Take rates are higher on one-time because this customer doesn't subscribe to something he hasn't tried.
items.when: upsell pages for customers who haven't tried the product

items.title: Order bump data: 30% attach rate on the supplement
items.text: Use real attach-rate data to decide what to offer where. In one case a supplement as a checkout order bump on subscription got a 30% attach rate, which proved demand, so it was then offered as a one-time upsell.
items.why: Use real attach-rate data to decide what to offer where.
items.when: deciding order bump vs upsell placement

items.title: Set subscription frequency from how often people really use it
items.text: Set the default subscription frequency from how often people really use the product, not 30 days by default, and check the data between purchases. In one case 30 days caused heavy churn because buyers didn't use it daily, so 60 days (or a 45-day test) was set.
items.why: Guys don't use it daily, so 30 days means insane churn.

items.title: Write upsell copy in the customers' own review language
items.text: Write upsell copy from customers' own review quotes; if the product has no reviews yet, reuse relevant reviews from {hero product}. It removes doubt because it's what customers actually say.
items.why: There's no question whether it will work, because it's literally what customers say.

items.title: Compare an agency quote to doing it in-house
items.text: Before signing an agency contract, compare its price with what the same deliverable costs in-house or from a freelancer, and use standard rates with your people. In one case an agency quoted $12K for 10 street interviews the team already made at scale.

items.title: AI-built pages still need a designer and the real code
items.text: Pages made with AI still need a landing page designer (in one case about $150 a page) to design them, then front-end code, and the team should work from the platform's own code so it can swap pieces in and out.
items.why: Having the base code lets the team make updates and swap pieces in and out.

items.title: Research TikTok Shop with a data tool before choosing products
items.text: Use a data tool to study TikTok Shop top products before choosing what to sell: what moves (in one case roughly 100K units in 30 days), at what price, and who makes the content. Many top products are one cheap core product, and both price and content need to be clear.
items.why: It tells you if the category has an opportunity and what price and content it needs.

items.title: Compete on value when you're pricier: free add-on plus higher commission
items.text: When you are pricier than the competition, compete on value: include a free product with {hero product} and pay {creator}s higher commission so they push the value.
items.why: You can't win on price, so incentivize on value.
items.when: TikTok Shop or affiliate selling against cheaper competitors

items.title: Hand editors raw founder video plus labeled B-roll
items.text: When handing raw talking-to-camera {founder} video to an {editor}, label the main video, where the B-roll is and which clips are hooks for a specific ad, and ask them to cut it natural and clean into clippable points. One long raw video can become several clips.
items.why: Each long raw video can become several clips if the key points are easy to find.

items.title: Put offers, products and pricing in one offer bank
items.text: Keep every {offer}, price, product detail and live campaign in one database (an offer bank) everyone can open, so everybody works from the same real information.
items.why: So everybody works from the same real information.
items.when: team operations across marketing and support

items.title: Check every idea against what the consumer cares about
items.text: Check every cultural-calendar idea (sporting events, holidays, religious observances) against one question: is this what our consumers care about and connect with? If yes, make content, emails, SMS and offers for it.
items.why: Translating real conversations into the brand keeps it relevant.

items.title: One customer service playbook everyone speaks from
items.text: Keep one customer service playbook with the voice, products, how to use them, common questions and objections, fixes, how to log bad products and how to escalate, and have everyone answer from it so tickets hand off cleanly and support scales.
items.why: When everyone speaks from the same place, tickets hand off cleanly and it scales.

items.title: Know the live offers before you talk to a customer
items.text: Check the live offer list (what's running, prices, timelines) before replying to a customer, so you can say exactly which offer is in play.
items.why: You have to communicate exactly what's happening.

items.title: Make support feel like a conversation, not a transaction
items.text: Make support feel like a conversation, not a transaction: add a human touch from what the customer follows in culture, then handle the issue.
items.why: The goal is real connection, not just service.

items.title: Cross-sell proactively in support
items.text: In support, look at what the customer bought and what they're missing, recommend it with the live {offer}, and tell them how to get the best result. Proactive, concierge-level help brings people back.
items.why: Concierge-level help makes the experience addictive and brings people back.
items.when: customer support with a multi-product line

items.title: Check your year of data for flat revenue and under-sending
items.text: Pull a year of email campaign data and look for months where send volume doesn't match demand. In one case Q4 was flat and only six emails went out in 24 days of February, when Q4 should have had three to four times more campaigns.
items.why: Q4 should have had three to four times more campaigns, so revenue was left on the table.

items.title: Judge by campaign revenue and send about one a day
items.text: Decide email volume from campaign revenue, not flow revenue; if each campaign earns (in one case about $1,500), send much more, aiming at about one a day and finding where it fatigues.
items.why: Each additional campaign earns, so under-sending is leaving revenue.

items.title: Don't let unsubscribes alone stop you from sending
items.text: Don't let rising unsubscribes alone stop you sending, as long as ads add net new leads every day. Keep spam low by mixing engaging content (social, conversation) with offers and sending to relevant segments.
items.why: It is only spam if you hit people with nothing but offers.
items.when: high-frequency email programs fed by paid lead flow

items.title: Give every task a due date so it shows up in my day
items.text: Give every assigned task a due date, because undated tasks don't show in the assignee's task view and get missed.
items.why: He runs his life out of Asana and needs to see work at a high level as it fills in during the week.
items.when: task management tools such as Asana

items.title: Keep production in production, distribution in distribution
items.text: Keep production and distribution separate on the board: research, briefs, creation, edits and creative loops in production; the paid social section only for handing finished content to the {media buyer} and uploads. It keeps counts (briefs, edits, live, completed) easy to track.
items.why: Some content is also used organically and it keeps counts (briefs, edits, live, completed) easy to track.

items.title: Move cards forward when you hand work off
items.text: Move a card forward the moment work is handed off (idea to creating or editing once it reaches the {creator}, designer or {editor}); the board only tells the truth if cards sit in their real stage.
items.why: The board only tells the truth if cards sit in the stage they are really in.

items.title: Search your customer list for notable people as proof
items.text: Search the customer list for athletes, doctors and other notable buyers, verify them from the raw list, and use them as real authority. Real status proof connects the {brand} to culture without making anything up.
items.why: It's real, so you can connect the brand to culture and status without making anything up.

items.title: Start emails from the conversation people are already having
items.text: Start emails from a conversation the {avatar} is already having (a game last night) instead of a generic topic, then cross over to the product. Real cultural moments give many shots on goal without over-sending.
items.why: You connect with something they already know and think about, then sell.

items.title: Keep email bodies as HTML so you can add variables, and check AI errors
items.text: Keep email bodies as HTML so you can insert variables (such as the customer's store credit and a ready gift code) before pasting into the email platform, and read AI drafts for mistakes. In one case the AI added a 60-day guarantee that didn't exist.
items.why: Personal variables make every send more useful, and the AI is not 100% there.

items.title: Shoot long videos in wide and tall
items.text: Produce every VSL in both 16:9 wide and 9:16 tall, so it works on YouTube and the landing page as well as organic and ads.
items.why: So it works on YouTube and the website landing page as well as organic and ads.

items.title: Coach first-time talent while shooting, then edit hard
items.text: First-time on-camera experts may be low energy and need many takes; coach them while shooting and have the {editor} cut hard so the video matches the energy and detail of your other anchor videos. Anchor videos have to be ultra on point.
items.why: These videos are anchors, so they have to be ultra on point.
items.when: filming experts or first-time talent for anchor videos

items.title: Swipe an authority video, then rewrite it for your product
items.text: Save an authority video that stands out (for example a doctor speaking about a problem nobody talks about), rewrite its script for {brand} and {hero product}, and hand the {editor} the new script as a mini VSL. It combines authority, insight, the problem and the product in one piece.
items.why: It combines authority, insight and the product in one clean piece.

items.title: Authority edits: bright, clean, real B-roll
items.text: Edit authority videos bright and clean with the best-quality real B-roll; avoid AI visuals unless showing a scientific demonstration. Caption style matters little; authority needs real footage.
items.why: Authority needs real footage, not AI.

items.title: Give designers the Pantone and hex for each product color
items.text: Keep one page with each product color's Pantone and hex code and send it to whoever makes colored assets, so they have everything before launch.
items.why: They have everything needed in one place before launch.
items.when: products sold in several colors, before launch

items.title: Preview a change before you merge it, especially checkout
items.text: Before merging a site change, open its checks and look at the page preview; if you can't see it, ask instead of merging blind, especially on checkout, which is easy to break.

items.title: Find unfulfilled orders with a saved filter
items.text: In the store's orders list, save a filter for unfulfilled orders, skip the canceled (struck-through) ones, fulfill the rest, then pause the product until it's back in stock. In one case many subscriber orders had piled up unfulfilled.
items.why: A lot of subscriber orders had piled up unfulfilled.
items.when: store order backlogs during stock problems

items.title: Turn team questions into a living quick-answers page
items.text: Turn the team's support questions into a living quick-answers section on the customer service page, and connect the help desk so it learns what customers say. The page improves over time.
items.why: It makes customer experience dynamic and improving.

items.title: Make the retention goal moving single-product buyers onto the full set ({hero product} plus its companion…
items.text: Make the retention goal moving single-product buyers onto the full set ({hero product} plus its companion products). In one case set cohorts had the highest LTV, highest AOV and most consistent reorders.
items.why: Data shows set buyers come back more and their AOV is higher.
items.when: brands with a hero product plus companion consumables

items.title: Set refill cadence from real buying behavior
items.text: Set refill cadence from cohort data on real buying behavior, not a default 30 days: buyers who run out later cancel when stock piles up. In one case (100,000 data points, 5 cohorts, 15 orders deep) most churn came from 30-day rebills, so single items moved to about 45 days and sets to about 75.
items.why: Men run out later than 30 days and cancel if they have too much.

items.title: Free sampling does not build retention
items.text: Don't give products away free to build retention; customers have to buy and invest to value the product. In one case free sampling led to no higher retention at all.
items.why: Free samples did not lead to higher retention at all last year.

items.title: Educate first: a short diagnostic quiz at the top of the funnel
items.text: Educate first: add a short diagnostic quiz at the top of the funnel (in one case three questions: the problem, the person's type, what they've tried) that gives a personalized guide and {offer}, and make the welcome flow explain the full routine. The highest-LTV customers are educated; one-time device buyers didn't come back.
items.why: The highest-LTV customers are educated. One-time device buyers never come back.
items.when: top of funnel and welcome flows for routine-based products

items.title: Set the subscription cadence by what they pick
items.text: Set subscription cadence by what the buyer picks; in one case one item got a 45-day cadence and several items got 90 days, matching the behavior in the data. Build the {offer} to adjust to behavior.
items.why: That is typically the behavior shown in the data.

items.title: Raise second-purchase rate first
items.text: Raise the second-purchase rate first; if it rises, third purchase and LTV follow. In one case the goal was moving repeat rate from about 20% toward 50% with companion products in both flows and campaigns.
items.why: If second purchase rises, third purchase and LTV follow.

items.title: Acquire with a low price, then grow value on the back end
items.text: Acquire with a lower price for velocity, backed by strong messaging and added value, then grow value on the back end. In one case the targets were $250-300 LTV and a 50% returning customer rate.
items.when: front-end pricing for products with strong back-end

items.title: If opens are fine and clicks are low, fix the email image
items.text: If email opens are fine but clicks are low, fix the creative inside the email: make the image match the message and be clickable, and drop old stock images.
items.why: Messaging and creative inside the email decide who clicks.
items.when: email performance with good open rate and weak CTR

items.title: Make the email image fit the story, even playfully
items.text: Make every email image fit the story, even playfully: for a game-day email, show the product in place of the ball; for an on-the-go email, show it in the bag. An email about a topic with no picture of that topic is a miss.
items.why: An email about basketball with no basketball picture is a miss.

items.title: Keep an inventory sheet with sell-out dates
items.text: Keep an inventory sheet with on-hand stock and projected sell-out dates from the current sales rate, and spot gaps early (in one case a product was a week from selling out).
items.why: So you can fill gaps and buy accurately instead of running out.

items.title: Judge ads on your real funnel, not Meta-attributed numbers
items.text: Judge ads on your own store numbers through the real funnel (ROAS, spend, purchases, AOV), not on what the ad platform attributes.
items.why: You get a clear number on everything.

items.title: Sort ads into winners, workhorses, underperformers and losers
items.text: Rank every ad on spend and return into winners, workhorses, underperformers and losers; between ads with similar spend, make more of the one with higher ROAS. In one case a new ad at $500 spend, 18 purchases, $27 CPA and 2.4 ROAS was a good early signal.
items.why: You save money by cutting losers and know what to make more of.

items.title: Feed winning videos to an analyzer and tie results to elements
items.text: Run winning videos through a video-analysis tool to pull out why they worked, tie that to the ad's numbers, and use it for the next content roadmap, headlines and variations. It replaces a strategist's manual breakdown.
items.why: It replaces a creative strategist's manual breakdown.
items.when: creative analysis of winning video ads

items.title: Compare two landing pages and combine the strengths
items.text: For two landing pages that ran in the same week, list what was strong and weak on each, use the higher-spend page as the base, and merge them into one stronger page; also note which pages didn't work.
items.why: You can see all of this in real time and improve efficiency.

items.title: Scale founder content from real comments
items.text: Scale {founder} content from real comments: make founder ads about business updates, customer experiences and results, and turn each week's comments into comment-reply videos.
items.why: Founder content scales when it's fed by real-time customer language.

items.title: Turn customer review videos into ads in batches
items.text: Turn customer review videos into ads in batches: filter reviews with media, download and extract the videos, let AI pick the production-ready ones from the caption, then make the ads. Real customers describing their experience is all the format needs.
items.why: Real customers talking about their experience is all the ad format needs.

items.title: Teach the AI your ranking logic, then bank the learnings
items.text: If AI ranks ads wrong, give it your logic (what counts as a workhorse, top of funnel, winner); then have it analyze winning videos, bank the learnings and use them as rules for the next creatives.
items.why: Giving it the logic is how the analysis gets right and repeatable.

items.title: You must know what to do to program a business
items.text: AI agents can do media buying, copy and variations, but you must know what the business needs to direct them; the tool only helps if you know what to ask.
items.why: The tool only helps if you know what to ask it.

items.title: Map the whole customer journey from real cohort data
items.text: Pull every customer and order, build cohorts, and get clear percentages for what makes people come back or leave; base every flow on that map.
items.why: You then know who the customer is, how they speak and what they do next.

items.title: Audit old flows and fix them layer by layer
items.text: Audit existing email flows: count them, find the ones making no money or holding outdated emails, and update them one flow at a time, week by week, in the current {brand} voice. In one case most of 40-plus flows made no money.
items.why: Outdated flows and old agency emails drag down the experience.

items.title: Check in on flow progress on a regular call
items.text: Hold a weekly or biweekly check-in on new flows and their language, catching typos and inconsistencies before anything goes live.
items.why: You only want it live when it's truly dialed in.

items.title: Set-buyers come back and keep buying
items.text: When buyers of the full set return and keep buying it, build a post-purchase upsell so more first-time buyers get the set. In one case about 33% of set buyers came back and 80% of them kept buying the set.
items.why: It is a repeat-purchase vehicle with a relatively high AOV.
items.when: brands with a bundle that drives repeat purchase

items.title: Every email needs an intent and a place to send them
items.text: Give every email and SMS clear intent: what you just did, what others like you did, what you need to know, and where to go, linking to a portal or page where they can act. 'Check it out' emails move nobody.
items.why: Emails that only say 'check it out' don't move anyone.

items.title: Build a language bank from reviews and feedback
items.text: Build a language bank from all reviews and feedback forms (leads, customers, returners, refunders), sorted by stage, and use customers' real words lightly cleaned up instead of writing copy. Real language builds believability.
items.why: Real customer language is the basis of everything and builds believability.

items.title: Ask the AI to pick the review most likely to win the click
items.text: Paste the email you're about to send plus relevant reviews into an AI project and ask which review is most likely to win the click or build trust, to choose fast and accurately.
items.why: You get out quickly and accurately.

items.title: Split test simple HTML emails against design-heavy ones
items.text: Split-test simple HTML emails against design-heavy ones, and lean toward simple HTML; design-heavy emails are slow to update, and fast updates matter more than looking perfect.
items.why: Fast updates matter more than looking perfect, and new images can be generated.

items.title: Spell out the task and the end state for a contractor
items.text: When handing a build to a contractor, state the baseline, the exact end state (for example a real editable theme with the new page as the actual home page), and ask them to flag anything that isn't possible. Otherwise you get one page you can't change.
items.why: Otherwise you only end up with one page that can't be changed.

items.title: Answer the questions customers are asking
items.text: When customers worry about orders, subscriptions and refunds, publish one clear update answering each question, own mistakes plainly, and say how to get a refund. Transparency avoids bad blood.
items.why: Transparency means no bad blood and customers know what to expect.

items.title: A key product selling out can break your bundles
items.text: Know which SKUs your bundles depend on and watch their stock: in one case one product selling out broke both the main set and the main bundle, two key revenue drivers at once.
items.why: Two main revenue drivers disappeared at once.

items.title: Get access to the page code instead of waiting on a vendor
items.text: Get access to the site's code repository so you can change pages yourself (for example with an AI coding tool) the same day, with changes arriving as requests you review and merge, instead of waiting on a vendor.
items.why: You can make updates the same day, without asking the vendor each time.
items.when: sites run by a platform vendor

items.title: Check where the price really lives before changing it
items.text: Before changing a price, find where it really lives: a price in the page HTML may not change checkout, which can be set by campaign packages or hard-coded. Troubleshoot until you know which one to change.
items.why: The front-end price and the checkout price can disagree.

items.title: Judge marketing as an ecosystem, not only Meta
items.text: Judge marketing as an ecosystem, not on Meta alone: subscription acquisition, email flows, lead capture, storefront bundles, campaigns and seasonal moments all add to the return, and back-end revenue can make less efficient ad spend a good trade.
items.why: Back-end revenue pads inefficient ad spend, so the whole thing can still be a good trade.

items.title: Everything a customer gives you feeds ads, email and pages
items.text: Treat everything a customer gives you (a review, a comment, a launch, an ingredient question) as new material for ads, emails, landing pages, the FAQ and comment-reply content. Don't let it sit in silos; aggregated context makes marketing and AI systems better.
items.why: The more context you aggregate, the better the marketing gets, and AI systems can be built around it.

items.title: Segment the list into buckets with a goal each
items.text: Segment the list into buckets (leads, one-time customers, returning, loyal, VIP subscribers, engaged), give each a goal, and move customers to the next bucket as they hit it, for predictable customer journeys.
items.why: It creates predictable customer journeys.

items.title: Test offers against each other and measure contribution margin
items.text: Test offers against each other (for example 25% off vs 10%, 20%, a free product, a bundle) and judge them by gross contribution margin in real dollars, not sales volume.
items.why: The best offer is the one that earns the most dollars, which a plain discount often isn't.

items.title: Build offers as bundles and value stacks, not hero-product discounts
items.text: Build offers that raise AOV or LTV, as bundles and value stacks (for example a bundle with a free accessory and a preselected subscription with a small discount), rather than discounting {hero product}.
items.why: Discounting a premium hero product isn't the best path, and bundles put people on a higher LTV route.

items.title: Buying the full set on first order nearly doubles returns
items.text: Design offers to make people come back, not just to lower CPA. In one case buyers whose first order included the device plus its companion products returned at 33%, versus 17% for device-only.
items.why: A lower CPA can look good while the customer never returns.

items.title: Map offers to the right segment
items.text: Match each {offer} to the segment it makes sense for; don't upsell a companion product to someone who never bought the main product, or an accessory to someone with no product.
items.why: The offer has to make sense for what they already have, or take rate falls.
items.when: email and upsell offers by segment

items.title: Three email types and two styles
items.text: Plan emails as three types (education, narrative, offer) in two styles (designed and rich text), pull angles from customer feedback, and rotate through angles, archetypes and offers so the business feels alive.
items.why: Rotating angles, archetypes and offers keeps the business feeling alive, like a car brand that sells the same cars in new colors.

items.title: Get seasonal context by searching TikTok
items.text: Get seasonal context by searching TikTok for what people say about the upcoming season in your category (essentials, activities, destinations), and put it into emails and ads.
items.why: It makes the brand feel real and more than just a product.

items.title: Connect store and email data to model first-to-fourth purchase and LTV
items.text: Connect store and email platform data in one backend so you can see every profile's order count, time between purchases, AOV and LTV (in one case 100,000-plus profiles) and model first-to-fourth purchase behavior.
items.why: You know what they will do, how much they'll spend and when.

items.title: A private store app gives you the API key
items.text: To connect a tool to your store, create a custom app in the store's developer dashboard, generate an API key and plug it into the tool; that's all it takes.
items.why: It is not as complicated as it looks.
items.when: connecting tools to a Shopify-type store

items.title: Treat AI-built dashboards as useful, not perfect
items.text: AI-built analytics dashboards are useful but not perfectly accurate; in one case one built for under $1,000 surfaced new angles and customer profiles. Bring in a real developer when you need more.

items.title: Plan quarter first, then month, with owners and recurring tasks
items.text: Plan by quarter first, then month, with sections for customer service, content, email, funnels, inventory and product; give each item an owner, link the working files, and use recurring Monday tasks for repeating work.
items.why: It keeps repeatable work getting done every week.
items.when: business planning in a task tool

items.title: Get ad-account access through Business Manager partner access
items.text: To get ad account access, ask the owner to add your Business Manager as a partner on their assets instead of sharing logins; it protects their account from being shut down when you work in it.
items.why: It protects their account from going down if you log in and work in it.
items.when: agency or contractor access to Meta ad accounts

items.title: Tell customers the truth early, it protects the brand
items.text: When something goes wrong, tell customers plainly and early, before the story spreads; silence hurts reputation more, and honesty can bring customers to help.
items.why: Honest communication limits reputation damage and brought help from customers.

items.title: Subscribers are what keep the store alive on day one
items.text: Subscriptions keep revenue alive when acquisition stops: in one case, when the store reopened, first-day orders were mostly subscriptions and organic. Focus on acquiring subscribers and getting rebill timing right.
items.why: Without the subscriptions there would have been no first-day revenue.

items.title: Turn expert research into flows, then hand to the build team
items.text: Turn an expert's analysis plus your customer data into a concrete flow plan and hand it to whoever builds the flows, so the back end is clean before new traffic arrives.
items.why: New traffic lands on a back end that is ready to retain it.

items.title: Pay clippers on views and stock up organic content
items.text: Film lots of content ahead of time and have an editing team paid on views clip it into organic posts, keeping the organic machine running without fixed cost.
items.why: It keeps an organic content machine running without fixed cost.

items.title: Give whoever runs inventory and finance real experience
items.text: Put an experienced operator on inventory, fulfillment and finance, plus a finance check that you're buying enough but not too much; don't leave them unchecked while the {founder} focuses on growth. In one case an inexperienced manager caused trouble that was too late to fix.

items.title: Turn what you just did into a skill by telling Claude
items.text: After finishing a task, tell the AI to create a skill from what you just did, or paste in an old SOP or recording transcript to turn into steps, then refine it over time. Skills are plain language.
items.why: Skills are just natural language, so explaining it as if talking to a person works.
items.when: capturing repeatable work with AI assistants

items.title: Share skills across the team and give each skill variables
items.text: Share skills from a team folder or team account, and make brand specifics (which account to open, KPIs) variables so the same skill works for every {brand}.
items.why: Skills are local files, and many were written around one business, so they need to be generalized.
items.when: AI skills across several brands or teammates

items.title: Keep personal and team AI accounts separate
items.text: Keep personal and team AI accounts separate (personal chats in your own, shared projects and skills in the team's), and give each person only what their role needs.
items.why: Mixing personal finances with work chats is a risk, and extra access distracts people.

items.title: Get inspired by the content you already have
items.text: Get creative ideas from content you already own: browse existing content and customer UGC, test raw real images (such as a real unboxing review) in feed and stories, combine elements into new creatives, and watch the placement report.
items.why: Raw customer images work well for promotions and your database has plenty.

items.title: Archive every post about the brand automatically
items.text: Use a tool that automatically archives every post anyone makes about the {brand}, and use those posts as the base for bottom-funnel creative.
items.why: Real customer content makes the easiest bottom-funnel ads.

items.title: Let teammates explore new tools first, with direction
items.text: When a new AI tool appears, have a teammate spend a couple of days exploring it with your exact test brief; they may get about 80% of what you would and save the {founder}'s hours.
items.why: It keeps the founder from spending six hours on every test.

items.title: Rebuild a page by pasting its source into Claude
items.text: To learn from a page, copy its page source (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) into an AI coding tool and ask it to recreate it, then fix missing pieces section by section.
items.why: It gets nearly one-to-one, and you adjust the rest by describing it.

items.title: Screenshot each section and describe what you want
items.text: If there's no design file, screenshot each section, describe exactly what should happen (such as a scroll interaction), and let the AI build it; clear description is what makes it work.
items.why: The AI follows well when you define it clearly.

items.title: Put a Claude-built page into Shopify as a page template
items.text: To put an AI-built page live on Shopify, add a new page template in the theme code, paste the code, save, create a page that uses that template, and preview it before sending traffic.
items.why: It is how a page made in Claude becomes a live page.

items.title: Iterate tweak by tweak, with images from the store files
items.text: Upload images to the store's file library, give the AI the links and say where each goes, ask for separate mobile and desktop versions, and keep iterating tweak by tweak until it's on point.
items.why: Letting Claude place images avoids messy tags, and repeated tweaks get it on point.

items.title: Use AI to wireframe a better page than the current one
items.text: Vibe-code a quick version of your page ideas with AI, even without a designer, to see the lay of the land before investing.
items.why: It shows the brand and the better landing page idea fast.

items.title: Pull sales by product from the store, then cross-check by hand
items.text: Use an AI store connection to pull sales since a date by product and variant (singles, multi-packs, sets), then validate it with a manual export.
items.why: Quick AI numbers are a starting point that a person should validate.

items.title: Read the product stack to decide what to restock
items.text: Watch which products sell through fastest and why, and restock by sell-through plus how the product fits the funnel. In one case a follow-up product outsold a newer one because the main problem leaves a secondary problem, so it sold as an add-on to the main funnel.
items.why: Sell-through plus how it fits the funnel tells you what to buy next.

items.title: Idea to sent email in 30 minutes: research, pick, send
items.text: Get an email out in about 30 minutes: pick a cultural moment, have AI research what the {avatar} says about it on Reddit, generate image variations, choose the best as the email image, and have AI write the copy with the {offer}.
items.why: It takes about 30 minutes to get an email out without design.

items.title: Keep sending the email format that consistently earns
items.text: Keep sending the email format that consistently earns (in one case a little over $1,000 each send) and send fewer heavily salesy versions; a repeat performer beats something new each time.
items.why: Format that works repeatedly beats trying something new each time.

items.title: Split the research step from the writing step
items.text: Split AI work into components: do the research step first, then feed it into a separate writing step, instead of asking for everything at once.

items.title: Let the AI save the character as a skill
items.text: Use an AI tool that learns as you create to save a skill for how a recurring character looks, with reference images of the character and supporting cast, so every asset in that format stays consistent.
items.why: It auto-updates the skill and memory as you work.

items.title: AI is good for visual drafts, weaker for the final build
items.text: AI is good for analyzing pages and copy and for visual drafts (assets, sections, a mini quiz funnel), but weaker at the final build; unique designs still need a developer.
items.why: The assets weren't final and the implementation wasn't the strongest.

items.title: Hand off a brand as a package: playbooks, offers, SOPs, courses
items.text: Hand off a {brand} as one package: support playbook, how LTV works, the offer bank, creative strategy, editing SOP, brand assets, a {creator} onboarding course, and the strategy documents, so the team can review how it ran.
items.why: Everything on how the brand ran is in one place and can be reviewed by the team.
items.when: handing a brand to a new owner or team

items.title: Customer language and customer intelligence are the key skills
items.text: Of the AI skills, the heavy hitters are {founder} authenticity, customer language and customer intelligence, because they tie every output to the customer's words and data. Put your page HTML into a skill to produce new pages.
items.why: They tie every piece of output back to the customer's words and data.

items.title: Run the page factory from avatar sheet and language bank
items.text: Run the page-building skill with the {avatar} workbook, the customer language bank and the {offer}, and ask for the page you need; it diagnoses the funnel stage, picks the sub-avatar and builds a first draft grounded in real customer language.
items.why: It produces a first shot grounded in real customer language.

items.title: Don't one-shot a page: correct the brand style and the copy
items.text: Don't one-shot an AI page: give it the real current page and past designs to fix brand style, then check the copy's sophistication and awareness level against the {avatar} sheet, which AI skips. Your eye for vibe and conversion design finishes it.
items.why: You need your eye for the vibe and conversion design knowledge to finish it.

items.title: A built page gets you about 80% there in an hour
items.text: An AI-built page gets about 80% of the way in an hour, versus an agency costing four to five thousand dollars and three weeks. Finish it by rewriting copy into real speech, showing a short list of core ingredients with a button for the full list, and adding video, social proof, a sticky add-to-cart and risk reversal.
items.why: It would cost an agency four or five thousand dollars and three weeks.

items.title: The page types the factory can make for one avatar
items.text: From one {avatar}'s research you can make an offer page, a listicle ('seven things nobody tells you about [problem] after [age]') or a mini game based on what that avatar actually plays. Directional accuracy is enough for a first version.
items.why: Directional accuracy is enough for a first version.
items.when: AI page generation for an avatar

items.title: Send traffic to an offer page before building pre-sells
items.text: Find ad reach and the winning message first, point traffic at a core-{avatar} offer page and read conversion rate; build sub-avatar pages and pre-sells later. If an offer page can't convert, a pre-sell won't save it.
items.why: If you can't convert on an offer page, a pre-sell won't save it.

items.title: Walk the buyer's path to build the page in order
items.text: Build the page in the order of the buyer's thoughts: the video shows the problem and a transformation, then on the page she wants validation, so show before-and-afters, what's inside, how it works, others using it, price, risk reversal, then questions.
items.why: A page follows the thoughts of the person arriving.

items.title: Ingredient mechanism matters more than a clever story here
items.text: Let research decide which mechanism to highlight; for one audience an ingredient-stack mechanism mattered more than a unique way to explain it.
items.why: What the research shows should drive the mechanism you highlight.

items.title: A too-branded page cut conversion, so simplify
items.text: Applying a high-end brand look (fancy buttons) to landing pages dropped click-through and conversion; keep the brand colors with light touches but simplify to a direct-response structure.
items.why: Conversion fell when it went too far into brand vibe.

items.title: For a demonstrable product, pre-sells didn't pay off
items.text: For a straightforward, demonstrable product where buyers see a before and after, offer pages beat pre-sells; in one case only one pre-sell performed and it didn't scale, because buyers only cared about using it and seeing the result.
items.why: Men only cared about rubbing it on the face and seeing the before and after.
items.when: funnels for products with visible before-and-after results

items.title: Use realistic images and customer videos as baselines
items.text: Use real images and customer and practitioner videos as baselines, and generate ultra-realistic images to extend them, rather than polished designed pieces; realistic UGC-style content is what to lean on.
items.why: Realistic UGC-style content is what to lean on now.

items.title: One platform where anyone can make a brand email without knowing the skills
items.text: Build one operating platform with segments, live campaigns, offers, customer language and a dynamic calendar, so a teammate picks a segment and email type and gets a baseline draft from customer language with the skills running in the background.
items.why: The skill work runs in the background so the person doesn't have to think about it.

items.title: Breakthroughs come from the market's content plus the market's words
items.text: Breakthroughs come from fundamentals: read the customers' current words (Reddit), watch the content they watch, combine those formats with that language, then execute well. Swiping and agents mostly fill the funnel but don't move the needle.
items.why: Swiping and agents mostly fill the funnel but don't move the needle.

items.title: Don't swipe your way to a leap
items.text: Swiped formats and other brands' ideas keep the funnel full, but the real jump comes from new formats built on fresh customer research. Everyone copies everyone, and the follower gets caught.
items.why: Everybody is copying everybody, and the follower gets caught.
items.when: creative strategy, when deciding where the next big lift will come from

items.title: Make sure clippers' content is usable before you scale it
items.text: When content posted by clippers takes off, confirm {brand} actually has the rights to use it (not a fake influencer or a {creator} you don't work with) before scaling it; then reuse what worked (e.g. the better-looking people and the AI carousel look) and compound. A breakout you can't legally reuse can't be scaled.
items.why: A breakout you can't legally reuse can't be scaled.
items.when: organic clipping programs, when a clipped post breaks out

items.title: Design landing pages so the developer isn't the bottleneck
items.text: When turning an AI landing page draft into code, simplify layouts that are hard to build: drop fiddly elements like arrows, let the before-and-after lead, keep text as support. Sliders and compressed GIFs are fine; complex containers and spacing waste developer time.
items.why: Complex containers and spacing take dev time you can avoid by designing for it.
items.when: landing page design handed from AI draft to a developer

items.title: Pile on social proof until it's undeniable
items.text: Load the page with social proof until it is undeniable: a carousel of featured reviews with a short summary of each, then the {offer} box, then the review widget. Overloading proof is fine; the aim is to show people use and love {hero product}.
items.why: The aim is to make it undeniable that people use and love the product.

items.title: Be transparent about ingredients even when leaning natural
items.text: If the page leans natural and highlights a few core ingredients (four botanicals in the example), still add a click-through to the full ingredient list and a clear list in the {offer} box, and tone down before-and-afters so you don't oversell. Otherwise people assume those are the only ingredients.
items.why: People will assume those are the only ingredients and it's not fully natural.
items.when: landing pages for ingredient-led products with a natural positioning

items.title: Check AI-generated numbers and add the founder call-out
items.text: After an AI writes a page draft, check and correct its numbers and headline copy yourself, and add a small {founder} call-out if the message includes one. AI copy contains wrong numbers.
items.why: AI copy contained incorrect numbers.
items.when: any AI-drafted page or copy before it goes live

items.title: Learn the tool in real time and record it for others
items.text: When you need a new tool skill, follow a tutorial step by step, do each step yourself and record your screen as you go; if stuck, ask the AI assistant to do the step. Learning in real time keeps you from getting stuck, and the recording trains the next person.
items.why: If you don't learn in real time you get stuck, and the recording helps the next person.
items.when: team members picking up a new technical tool

items.title: Write a readme that tells every agent what the project is for
items.text: Keep a readme with the high-level purpose of the project and of each agent, and tell the AI to read it first each session. Agents need the director's vision, rules and skills before they work, and you stop re-explaining context.
items.why: Agents need the director's vision and the rules and skills before they work.
items.when: running AI agent projects across many sessions

items.title: Feed the system your direction continuously and retire old info
items.text: The director sets the vision up front and keeps feeding the AI system direction through transcripts and recordings, updating in real time and retiring old information while keeping a baseline of what works and what doesn't. That makes a self-learning system that compounds.
items.why: This builds a self-learning system that compounds.
items.when: maintaining an AI agent system over time

items.title: Start the system from how you actually work
items.text: Start an AI system from how the {founder} actually works: give it their strengths assessment and recorded chat sessions so it knows what to do, what not to do and where they need help. The agents then work the way the director works.
items.why: The agents then work the way the director works.
items.when: setting up a personal or team AI agent system

items.title: Put an orchestrator at the top, with a human deciding direction
items.text: Put an orchestrator agent above the others that works directly with a human director who makes the key decisions. Agents still need direction from someone with real-world context, because the work serves real people.
items.why: Digital work still serves real people, so human discretion sets where it goes.

items.title: Make brand-specific details variables so one system serves every brand
items.text: Strip brand-specific details out of skills and agents and make them variables, so the system can be duplicated per {brand}, take on new accounts and keep its own feedback loop for each. Turn everything known about a brand into working variables.
items.why: Real-time duplication per brand lets you make better decisions. It's really a product that you build a brand perception around.
items.when: building AI tools meant to serve more than one brand

items.title: Run a loop: create, analyze, ideate, refine
items.text: Run a tight loop of creation, analysis, ideation and refinement so each loop gets smaller and output gets faster, with the goal kept clear: profit. The tighter the loop, the more outlier performance you produce.
items.why: The tighter the loop, the more outlier performance you can produce.
items.when: any creative or marketing production system

items.title: Think like an architect: layers, relevance, frequency, priority
items.text: When asking an AI to build something, think as an architect, not a worker: specify layers of information ranked by relevance, frequency and impact, and have it list the gaps in its own build first.
items.why: You are building Legos in layers, not working as a worker.
items.when: directing AI to build systems or tools

items.title: Turn an offer page into a design system to speed wireframes
items.text: Load {brand}'s offer page, emails, logos and sections into a design tool as a design system so copy turns into on-brand wireframes fast. Note that moving the result into Figma isn't automatic.
items.why: It expedites turning copy into wireframes you can build any asset from.
items.when: speeding up wireframes for pages and emails

items.title: Plan the email automation: calendar, text, review, design
items.text: Automate email production as a chain: check the marketing calendar for the next email, write the text for review, run it through the design system to make a few wireframe options based on existing emails, then notify the reviewer in chat. With triggers set, each hand-off can be automated.
items.why: With triggers set up you can automate each hand-off.
items.when: email production with a marketing calendar and design system

items.title: Visualize a long workflow so you can see what each step produces
items.text: When a workflow is a long list of written steps (30-odd in the example), turn it into a visual view that shows what each step actually outputs. Steps mean little until you can see what they produce.
items.why: Without seeing the output of each step it doesn't mean much.

items.title: Organize context by core avatar, sub avatar and funnel stage
items.text: For each {brand}, store core {avatar}s, sub-avatars (each defined by one determining factor), swipe references and the customer's language for every funnel stage as files the copy and teardown tools pull from. The tools then always pull the exact context they need.
items.why: The tools continuously pull the exact context they need.
items.when: setting up context for AI copy and teardown tools

items.title: Keep customer language verbatim in a bank
items.text: Keep customer answers word for word in a language bank; never summarize them, especially for copy. An {avatar} profile can be summarized, the language bank cannot. Keep adding questions from customer calls and {creator} feedback. The depth is what makes the writing strong.
items.why: The depth is what makes the writing powerful.

items.title: Match the language stage and the swipe to the audience
items.text: Match the language source and the swipe to the audience's awareness stage: for an unaware audience, use prospects' language and a swipe built for unaware; for a subscriber email, use how subscribers talk, then answer non-subscribers' objections.
items.why: Things fall into the right place without overthinking it.
items.when: writing ads or emails for a specific awareness stage

items.title: Clear the inbox by category using 'move to'
items.text: Clear the inbox by category with 'move to' so mail leaves the main inbox but can still be found, instead of deleting it.
items.why: It keeps the inbox clean without deleting anything.

items.title: Build your own dashboard for content research by avatar
items.text: Build a content research feed organized by {avatar} where one click on an item triggers a teardown that reproduces the creative, so research and teardown live in one place.
items.why: All tools in one place, from research to teardown.

items.title: Begin every session with the same start prompt, and route work through Claude
items.text: Have every team member start each AI session with the same start prompt and keep work in the shared system (shared and private folders, automations); use instant messaging only for sudden communications.
items.why: The daybook now works together, with shared and private folders and automations.
items.when: a team working through a shared AI workspace

items.title: Plan two weeks of marketing ahead, not day to day
items.text: Every two weeks, plan emails, SMS, static ads and video ads together around the month's promotion or seasonal moment, and plan peaks well ahead (e.g. 2 or 3 emails a day around Black Friday). Planning ahead lets you capitalize on moments instead of going day to day.
items.why: It lets you capitalize on moments and stay ahead rather than going day to day.

items.title: One email, one action, one message
items.text: Each email does one thing and carries one message: a big image, a big headline, a subheadline, a button and the core image of the action you want. Social proof is optional; don't overcomplicate it.
items.why: There's no need to overcomplicate the email process.

items.title: Give every email its own concept and moment
items.text: Give every email its own concept by adding a layer of deeper {avatar} and cultural research per email, so none repeat. Email reaches people who already like {brand}, so you can show the brand more uniquely; retention depends on customer behavior and is not one size fits all.
items.why: Retention is not one size fits all and depends on customer behavior.
items.when: email campaigns to existing customers and subscribers

items.title: Build emails from brand sections and a Pinterest mood board
items.text: Lay out emails from {brand}'s own indexed sections and design system, and for imagery gather relevant Pinterest pins for lighting, styling and mood before creating the product pictures. Emails stay consistent but unique, with no Figma step.
items.why: Emails stay similar but unique, and no Figma step is needed.

items.title: Human review at the end: images, typos, links, then feed notes back
items.text: At the end of an automated email line, a person checks images, typos and links in a review page; every note or regenerated image is fed back into the system so it improves, then the email is scheduled.
items.why: The system writes and builds, but a person checks it and teaches it.

items.title: Read the editing SOP alongside the asset index
items.text: Use the editing SOP together with the footage index: the index finds the footage, the SOP says how the edit should be built when the index doesn't answer the question.
items.why: The index finds footage; the SOP tells you how the edit should be built.
items.when: video editing with an indexed asset library

items.title: File returned creator videos by who the creator is
items.text: When a {creator} returns videos, file the batch in the creator content folder under that creator (new folder for a new creator) and note who they are (gender, ethnicity), because the sorting tool organizes footage by who is on screen.
items.why: One consolidated place means the AI tool that cuts up and organizes Drive can find it by who is on screen.
items.when: filing creator deliveries into a shared footage library

items.title: Never trust AI timestamps for where a clip starts - check the question that prompted the answer
items.text: Don't trust AI-suggested cut points for where a clip starts; listen back and start where the question that prompted the answer begins. In the example the AI said 19 seconds and missed the question, so the clip started too late.
items.why: AI picked the core topic but missed the full conversation, so the clip started after the question was asked.
items.when: cutting clips from interviews or podcasts with AI help

items.title: Keep the conversation line order so the podcast format feels real
items.text: Script podcast-style clips as numbered lines in conversation order: the question, the host's answer, the follow-up, then the explanation. Without the setup lines the answer reads as an abrupt monologue and doesn't feel like a podcast.
items.why: Context from the conversation makes it feel like a real podcast; otherwise it is too abrupt.

items.title: Listen to the whole raw recording for small engaging moments
items.text: Don't edit only from summaries; listen through the full raw recording and find the small moments where the explanation gets engaging and organic yourself. Those nuggets are what make the content feel organic.
items.why: Those small nuggets are what make the content feel organic.
items.when: editing long recordings into short content

items.title: Show on screen what is being talked about, using B-roll and generated B-roll
items.text: Show on screen exactly what is being talked about with B-roll, generating it if needed (e.g. crawling bugs when the line is about things in pores; people with the problem when the topic is the problem). Use fresh takes first if truly needed, otherwise generate. Cold traffic is half listening, so a literal visual makes them stop.
items.why: Cold traffic is scrolling and half listening; something visual that stands out makes them stop and watch.
items.when: talking or conversation videos for cold traffic

items.title: Ad = avatar side plus format side
items.text: Treat every ad as two halves: the {avatar} side gives the angle, language and tone; the format side gives the hook, scroll stopper and lead. Both working together make ads that keep working at scale.
items.why: Together they create ads that keep working at scale for a long time.

items.title: The angle is the opener that starts the conversation
items.text: Choose the angle as the way you say hello to this specific {avatar}, researched from what they are going through, not a hard sell. The angle is the most important element because it opens the door; a light opener gets a response.
items.why: The angle is the most important element because it is how you open the door.

items.title: Match the avatar's language, then set the tone
items.text: Write in the words and culture the {avatar} actually uses, found only through research, then set the tone carefully: not too pushy too early, not too weak. Right angle and language with the wrong tone loses trust, and trust is the point of all three.
items.why: Right angle plus language but wrong tone loses trust; the goal of all three is trust.

items.title: Define hook, scroll stopper and lead precisely
items.text: Hook = the written first line; scroll stopper = the visual that shows the hook (in direct response, something visceral showing exactly what the hook says); lead = what continues the conversation after both land. The lead only works if the hook and scroll stopper work first.
items.why: The lead only works if the hook and scroll stopper work first.

items.title: Build trust in the body with shared stories before the product
items.text: After the lead, use the body to build trust through story: say you see them, you went through it too, and what you learned; only then introduce {hero product}. If viewers start asking questions, you have buy-in. It's not about selling.
items.why: Storytelling is the oldest way humans build trust; it is not about selling.
items.when: the body section of video ads and long-form sales videos

items.title: Do not go straight product-problem-offer for most buyers
items.text: For most buyers, don't go straight product-problem-offer; warm them up with narrative first. Long-form with a real body and real authority brings higher-quality customers than a static image with 'buy now', while buyers sold on pure insecurity refund badly.
items.why: Customers who buy off pure insecurity refund badly - 'dollar store buyers'.
items.when: choosing ad structure for cold traffic

items.title: Order of the pitch: root cause, our mechanism, why others fail, results, offer
items.text: Once trust is built, pitch in this order: the real root cause, {brand}'s mechanism, why other mechanisms fail, results and track record, then the {offer} and guarantee. Sales is simple once the story and root cause are done.
items.why: Sales is simple once the story and root cause are done, because you already know objections, features and benefits.
items.when: the selling section of video ads and sales videos

items.title: A brief is just plugging elements together, then asking 'is this the best way to show it?'
items.text: A brief is plugging elements together: do the {avatar} side first, then take the format's structure and write hook, scroll stopper and lead in order, asking each time whether it is the most visceral way to show it. Structure is the skill; once it's set, writing is easy.
items.why: Once the structure is thought through, you can be creative inside it, and briefs get easy.

items.title: Open fast and filled, slow down only when education starts
items.text: Make the opening seconds of a video punch, punch, punch with no dead air, then loosen the cuts once the education part starts. Dead air in the opening loses the most unaware viewers.
items.why: Dead air in the opening loses the viewer from their hypnosis; the opening has to pull in the most unaware audience before you slow down.
items.when: editing pace of short video ads

items.title: The opening line does not mention the problem yet
items.text: Open on a weird, attention-grabbing statement before mentioning the problem at all, so the start hits the widest, most unaware market. The beginning of the video is what opens the market, so it must hit hard.
items.why: The start of the video is what opens up the market, so it has to hit ultra strong.
items.when: video ad openings aimed at cold, unaware audiences

items.title: A slow delivery can be fixed in the edit by cutting between words
items.text: When a line was delivered too slowly or with a stumble, cut the extra and join the good parts so it flows, then note it so delivery improves on the next shoot.
items.why: Edits can rescue a weak take, but he also treats it as feedback for himself.

items.title: Rewrite lines that do not sound like you (AI copywriting tells)
items.text: Cut or rewrite any line that sounds AI-written (e.g. 'honestly...', 'is this really me?') and that the speaker would never say, in the speaker's own voice. AI tells break authenticity.
items.why: It breaks authenticity.
items.when: reviewing AI-written scripts before or after filming

items.title: Cut scripts down when science slows the delivery
items.text: Science sections slow the speaker's delivery, so trim dead air and repeated phrases there and zoom out or change the visual to carry the slower part and keep tempo.
items.why: Explaining complex material makes him slow; the edit has to keep tempo.
items.when: editing educational or mechanism sections of videos

items.title: Put customer B-roll on a line about reaction or proof
items.text: When the script tells how other people responded, lay customer footage over that line so the claim is shown the moment it's made.
items.why: It supports the claim visually at the moment it is made.
items.when: video edits with proof or reaction lines

items.title: Know the sections of a VSL while you cut it
items.text: Read a sales video cut as stages, each with one job: strong lead into story, science showing why others fail and the root cause, proof, features/benefits/how to use, outcome, risk reversal, final price pitch. Naming the stage tells you whether pacing and content fit.
items.why: Naming the stage tells you whether the pacing and content fit.
items.when: editing or reviewing long-form sales videos (VSLs)

items.title: A fresh lead can be bolted onto an existing VSL
items.text: The opening of a long sales video can be a separate fresh lead: build and test the lead on its own, then connect it to the long-form body. The lead pulls attention in and sets up the story.
items.why: The lead sucks attention in and sets up the story that follows.

items.title: Cutting a minute out can make it stronger
items.text: Don't be afraid to remove content for flow; in one sales video, cutting almost a minute and trimming dead air at the start made the story hit harder.
items.why: Speeding the start and trimming dead air made the story hit harder.

items.title: In podcast-style edits, the interviewer's question comes first
items.text: In podcast-style edits, don't open on the answer: show the interviewer's question first, then the answer, or open on a shocking moment, then the question, then the rest. Without the question the answer has no context.
items.why: Without the question there is no context for the answer.

items.title: Show what is being said: bugs, bacteria, real faces
items.text: B-roll must be ultra accurate to what is being said: if the line says bugs and bacteria, show bugs and bacteria, generating it with an image or video tool if needed, and make generated people look real.
items.why: Things must be 'ultra accurate to what's being said'.

items.title: Fill the whole frame with B-roll
items.text: Make B-roll fill the entire frame with the subject large and centered, never small in a corner; a partly filled frame looks bad.
items.why: A small or partly-filled frame looks bad.

items.title: Use a real before image instead of faking a clear-skin shot
items.text: Don't fake a before-and-after by retouching the problem away; use a real photo of the person with the problem as the before and a real photo without it as the after. Real is more believable and easier.
items.why: Real is more believable and easier.

items.title: Demonstrate the device in use, not just in the box
items.text: Show {hero product} being used, not just sitting in the box, so people understand what it does.
items.why: People should understand what is happening, not just see the object.
items.when: product shots in video ads, especially devices

items.title: Captions: bigger, fewer words per line, organic cinematic Instagram style
items.text: Make captions bigger with fewer words per line in an organic, cinematic Instagram style, and keep the same size, color and font through the whole video; don't change it mid-video.
items.why: Reads as organic, and congruent styling keeps it clean.

items.title: Cut to new B-roll every three to four seconds in the key section
items.text: In key story sections, cut to new B-roll about every three to four seconds, and use a visual joke when it helps the metaphor land. Constant visual change keeps people engaged.
items.why: Constant visual change keeps people engaged and the metaphor lands.

items.title: Bleep every curse word so the video can run as an ad
items.text: Bleep every curse word so the video can also run as an ad; don't leave it to how viewers interpret it.
items.why: We want to be able to run these as ads too.
items.when: organic videos that may be run as paid ads

items.title: Show the stores and screens the narration names
items.text: Give each place or thing the narration names its literal picture: a store rack for a store, a real screen recording for an online marketplace, a collage of influencer videos for influencers, struggling before images for 'it doesn't work'. It pulls the viewer along.
items.why: Each phrase gets its literal picture so the viewer is pulled along.

items.title: Do not keep the camera on the speaker the whole time
items.text: Don't keep the camera on the speaker the whole time; alternate between B-roll, the interviewer and the speaker, and use {brand}'s UGC and before-and-after library for proof footage, so there's always something new.
items.why: One engaging piece of content that holds attention the entire time.

items.title: Watch the edit raw to see if you would stop scrolling
items.text: Review the edit raw, as a viewer in the feed, and ask whether you would actually stop scrolling. That is the test the ad has to pass.
items.why: That is the test the ad has to pass.
items.when: final review of any short video ad

items.title: No transition or zoom at the very start
items.text: Start straight on the scroll-stopper clip with no transition or zoom-in, and make what it is clear right away, because the content has to work both as organic and as an ad.
items.why: Much of our content has to work as organic and as an ad, so the start must be immediately clear.

items.title: Cut off the blank screen at the end
items.text: End the video when the speaker finishes; trim the blank frames after.
items.why: No need for dead frames.

items.title: Test short videos fast, then bolt the winners onto the VSL
items.text: Make short, clean videos so they test fast, and when one wins, attach it to the front of the long-form sales video without more editing. Clean shorts make it easy to test many and reuse winners.
items.why: Cutting the shorts clean makes it easy to test different ones faster and reuse winners.
items.when: testing short leads for long-form sales videos

items.title: Variation rule: hold one thing constant, change one thing, make three versions
items.text: Variation rule: edit the original, then make two more versions that change only one thing (e.g. the scroll stopper) while the hook and headline stay, so three originals become nine videos. Changing one variable at a time shows what moves results.
items.why: Changing one variable at a time shows what actually moves results.

items.title: Count the batch before you hand it back
items.text: Count the batch against the plan before handing it back (e.g. three videos times three versions = nine); in one batch only 7 of 9 were delivered.
items.why: His batch had 7 instead of 9.

items.title: Use culture the audience actually follows for the visual joke
items.text: Pull visual jokes from the culture the {avatar} actually follows (e.g. sports stars they know), pairing a familiar figure with the point being made. Comedic, culturally familiar pairings stop the scroll.
items.why: Comedic, culturally familiar pairings are scroll stoppers for this audience.

items.title: We make ads that spend, not social posts
items.text: Build videos to go into the ad account and scale spend, not as social posts; hashtags and posting don't matter. Judge them by spend and sales, not views.
items.why: The goal is selling millions of dollars of product, not going viral.

items.title: Organic vibe plus direct-response fundamentals = the ads that scale
items.text: The ads that scale sit where organic style and vibe overlap with direct-response fundamentals tested on large ad spend (clear problem, structure, social proof). Pure vibe gets views, not sales.
items.why: Viral videos and videos that sell millions are different things.
items.when: short-form video ads for paid social

items.title: Name the problem and why it matters in the script
items.text: Name the problem in the script, then say why someone cares (e.g. a partner's comment and the fear of losing them) so the viewer relates and feels it. If the creative never names the problem, viewers don't understand it.
items.why: Emotions like fear and desire drive the scroll; the problem must be named.

items.title: Add a few lines to a creator's script so the purpose is clear, without making it corny
items.text: Don't rewrite a {creator}'s whole vibe; add a few lines that tie it back to the problem or mechanism and delete lines that feel too ad-like. It stays organic but gains a clear purpose.
items.why: Keeps the organic feel while giving the creative a point.

items.title: Tie even a plain product to a desire
items.text: Tie even a plain product to a desire people want, as big brands do (a grooming brand tying trimming to being more attractive). Mechanism or marketing has to carry the desire.
