items.why: Mechanism or marketing has to carry the desire.

items.title: A strong hook comes from an authentic reason (comment, girl buys you skincare)
items.text: Hooks that spend come from an authentic reason to watch (a viral comment answered, a POV where a partner buys the product, 'I stole my partner's products'). Take an organic hook and give it a direct-response purpose; the hook is what made people watch.
items.why: People watched because of the hook; the rest is a basic demo.
items.when: writing hooks for short-form video ads

items.title: Dial down an ad-sounding script instead of dropping it
items.text: If a script feels too much like an ad (someone listing every product), keep the concept but reframe it as a story so it no longer feels like corny direct response.
items.why: Same concept, but it no longer feels like corny direct response.
items.when: reviewing scripts that read as too salesy

items.title: Read early spend as the signal
items.text: Read early spend as the signal: in one case a new ad spent over $1,300 in five days, while the same {creator}'s earlier videos without a framework got no spend. Real frameworks behind a video are what get spend.
items.why: Real frameworks behind the video are what get spend; a random bathroom video did nothing.
items.when: judging new ads in the first days on paid social

items.title: A viral organic video can sell little; add a direct-response second half
items.text: A viral organic video can sell little; attach a direct-response script to its back half. In one case a video with millions of organic views sold very little, and with the second half added it scaled to about $250K in spend.
items.why: The short version spent a bit; the full version with direct response went the distance.
items.when: turning viral organic videos into paid ads

items.title: Great copy with zero energy still fails - use scripts as the backbone
items.text: Well-written copy with zero energy still fails. Keep delivered scripts as backbones in a database and have the creative strategist run them through the process to add the energy and vibe.
items.why: Objectively great copywriting, but no energy or vibe.
items.when: scripts that read well but lack energy

items.title: One song, many variations, becomes a recognizable sound across videos
items.text: When a song works, make variations of it and use them on the back of all videos so the sound becomes recognizable for {brand}.
items.why: Repeated sound builds recognition; spend was not the point of the first song.
items.when: audio for a brand's video ads

items.title: Not everything needs an editor
items.text: Not everything needs an editor: reviews and reactions can be made on a phone with captions in a simple app, while problem-solution or technical videos with a set process go to {editor}s.
items.why: Fast simple content does not need the full editing line.
items.when: deciding which videos go through the full editing line

items.title: Pull from the shared elements library instead of making everything
items.text: Keep a shared elements library (sound effects, emojis, B-roll, scroll stoppers, memes) and have {editor}s pull from it instead of making everything fresh. It speeds everything up.
items.why: It speeds everything up.

items.title: Add a clean voiceover line to a silent demo, and react to it
items.text: A silent product demo with no words underperformed; cutting the best parts, adding a split-screen before-and-after and one clean voiceover line fixed it, and a reaction version did even better. Make the message explicit and keep innovating on the format.
items.why: Same footage performed better once the message was explicit.
items.when: demo-style video ads that aren't getting results

items.title: Film on a phone, natural light, 4K 30 not 60
items.text: Film on a phone in natural window light at 4K 30fps (not 60), not a studio look; film raw first and edit later so the footage can be reused. It looks authentic, and platforms downgrade the file anyway.
items.why: Authentic, not phony; platforms downgrade the file anyway.

items.title: The product must be named and demonstrated in the video
items.text: High-quality footage is fine, but the video must say plainly what {hero product} is and demonstrate it. In one case the best ad of its type was simply a person saying 'this is {hero product}' and showing the demo; clarity beat polish.
items.why: Clarity beat polish.

items.title: Keep subject and captions inside the 4:5 safe area
items.text: Film 9:16 but keep the subject and captions centered inside a 4:5 area, because Instagram crops tall videos to 4:5; anything cut off high or low won't work.
items.why: Placements crop; you must still see what you show.

items.title: Make it look like it is not an ad
items.text: Make the video look like it isn't an ad: native-looking captions and fonts, a centered subject, simple delivery. Native content is what stops the scroll.
items.why: Native content is what stops the scroll.

items.title: Download creator videos into our Drive the same day
items.text: When a {creator} sends videos by link, download them into {brand}'s own drive the same day (creator folder, new folder for a new creator), then share the folder link and write the brief for the {editor}. Creators sometimes delete content when their drives fill up.
items.why: Creators sometimes delete content when their own drives fill up.

items.title: Talk about the product without ever sounding salesy
items.text: Talk about {hero product} without sounding salesy: say what it is, how it works, the benefit you got and how to get it, and position it by what it does before naming it. Positioning and language give better hooks, retention and watch time.
items.why: Positioning and language give better hooks, retention and watch time.
items.when: scripts for founder or creator video ads

items.title: The job is shifting a belief: skincare works, how you use it doesn't
items.text: The job is shifting a belief, not hard selling: when the {avatar} believes products in the category don't work for them, agree it isn't the products but the method, then show {brand}'s new mechanism. Hard sell only gets people already in market; belief shifting scales.
items.why: Hard sell only gets people already in market; belief shifting scales.
items.when: ads for skeptical audiences who have tried the category

items.title: Touch and use the product until you can explain it simply
items.text: Before writing or filming, hold, use and read about {hero product} until you can explain how it works in plain language; if the delivery sounds scripted, redo it.
items.why: If it sounds scripted or like BS, we will not take it.
items.when: creators, founders or team members filming product content

items.title: Keep the content and the landing page congruent
items.text: Send people to a landing page that says the same thing the video said: the {creator} brings attention, the page carries the matching message. Congruence makes people convert at a higher rate.
items.why: People buy more because it feels natural and consistent.

items.title: Answer the price objection with the mechanism and the audience's own words
items.text: Answer the price objection ('why pay this much?') with why {hero product} works better than what they use now and why current products aren't working, built on what the audience says and thinks; ignore knockoffs and competitors.
items.why: They are skeptical; the answer is the real mechanism.

items.title: Put the script, hooks, and B-roll ideas in the brief and link the research
items.text: A brief should carry the script, hooks and B-roll ideas in one place, plus a link back to the research brief that produced the idea, so the {editor} has everything and the idea trail stays clear.
items.why: The editor needs everything in one place and the idea trail stays clear.

items.title: Ask the AI for a discrete, detailed scene-by-scene breakdown, not a high-level one
items.text: When an AI's ad breakdown is high level, push for discrete detail scene by scene: the actor's demographic, what an on-screen comment says and its platform style, what the product scene shows, the emotion on faces. Those details explain why an ad works at scale.
items.why: These details explain why an ad works at scale.

items.title: Add what the AI cannot know about the customer, then rerun
items.text: Read the AI's ad breakdown against what you know of the customer and add the cultural context it can't see (e.g. details in the setting that suggest the person is married, which adds a motivation), then ask for an updated breakdown.
items.why: AI misses cultural context that we know from our customers.

items.title: Look for the types of creators that fit and recruit more who look like the winner
items.text: Note the type of person in a winning ad (e.g. young, athletic, clean-cut) and recruit more {creator}s who look like them to make similar content.
items.why: If his videos work, others like him can make similar content for us.
items.when: creator sourcing after a winning ad

items.title: When an AI edit loses details, tell it: keep everything else, change only this
items.text: Asking an AI to update its answer can drop details it had; tell it to keep everything else and change only the one thing, and check the new version against the old one.
items.why: He found it missed things after the update.

items.title: Think about how consumers perceive it, not what looks good to the eye
items.text: Before sending a video back, judge how the market will perceive it, not what looks good: for phone-style content use TikTok/CapCut-style captions or plain static text, not polished cinematic ones, because that's what viral content in the feed uses.
items.why: Based on how his market reacts, viral content on Instagram uses TikTok style captions.
items.when: captioning and styling phone-shot video ads

items.title: Do not drop parts of the ad - check the whole script is in the edit
items.text: Check the edit against the full script and footage so no part is dropped (intro, key clips, punchline). Put the complete video together first; you can cut later. Missing pieces make a narrative built to work a certain way feel jagged.
items.why: The narrative was built to work a specific way; missing pieces make it jagged.

items.title: Edit a music-style video to the beat
items.text: Cut a music-style video like a music video, not a YouTube video: line up the track so the beat drop lands on the cut and the visual hit. A beat drop grabs attention.
items.why: A beat drop gets the neck bouncing and gets the viewer's attention.

items.title: Show what the line means: product 3D, dollar signs, not the definition
items.text: Show what a line means rather than its definition: pull the product image from the site and make it a rotating 3D shot; for a money line, show money. Generate visuals with an AI tool if needed.
items.why: Visuals should carry the idea quickly and creatively.
items.when: B-roll for abstract or business lines

items.title: Add motion to transitions; keep the punchline cut
items.text: Add camera-style motion between scenes so the edit doesn't feel static, and never drop the punchline cut in a comedy beat.
items.why: Without motion and the punchline the edit feels flat.

items.title: Do not reuse a copyrighted song
items.text: Don't use someone else's copyrighted song, and don't reuse the same track over and over; use original music.
items.why: It is copyright and repetitive.
items.when: choosing music for videos and ads

items.title: Use the clip with the real juxtaposition as the hook
items.text: Use the clip with a real, unexpected juxtaposition as the hook (someone doing something the viewer doesn't expect from them), and ask 'would I react to this, yes or no?' before editing.
items.why: The juxtaposition is what makes people stop and watch.

items.title: Show people who match the viewer when naming a group
items.text: When the script names a group of people, show clips of the right kind of person for each, including different races, so every viewer sees themselves.
items.why: Make it relevant to whoever is watching.
items.when: B-roll for lines that name audiences

items.title: Use the clips already linked in the brief
items.text: {editor}s should use the footage linked in the brief rather than skipping it; it was linked on purpose.
items.why: They were linked on purpose.

items.title: Start with the interviews when editing an event shoot
items.text: When editing an event shoot with interviews, go through the long interview clips first for clean, quotable nuggets, then add the opening talk, a montage of general B-roll and the closing scripted clip.
items.why: Interviews give direct, clean nuggets to build the edit on.

items.title: Brief the editor with the script and the shape of the video
items.text: Brief the {editor} with the full script, a plain description of the video's shape beat by beat, which clips to skip, and the mood you want (funny, interactive, vibing).
items.why: With the script and structure clear, the editor can make it feel like a music video.

items.title: Every edit needs a hook or headline on top of the scroll stopper
items.text: Every edit needs a bold on-screen hook or headline on top of the scroll stopper (e.g. a 'POV:' line), because a cool opening clip alone doesn't speak to everyone.
items.why: The headline is what the hook then gets into.

items.title: Find 'viral loops' inside the main video and move them to the front
items.text: On the first cut, look inside the main video for 'viral loops' (an interesting standalone line) and move them to the start as extra hook variations; each is a new variation for almost no work.
items.why: Each one is a new variation with almost no extra work.
items.when: making hook variations from existing footage

items.title: Do not over-edit; use open loops and simple text
items.text: Don't over-edit: keep what the phone captured, add simple text, a headline and a clear scroll stopper, use open loops and small visual nuggets (e.g. reversing a move), and skip flashy transitions.
items.why: Maximize attention without over-editing.

items.title: The best hooks look natural, not like an ad
items.text: Direct-response hooks work, but the best hooks and scroll stoppers look natural, not like an ad; look through existing clips for a line that stands on its own.
items.why: His team flagged that hooks were too direct.

items.title: Make net-new creatives by combining two existing assets
items.text: Make net-new creatives by putting a standalone hook clip in front of another strong clip or a long sales video and captioning it; go back through old work for new combinations. Some of the biggest ads came from short engaging videos placed on top of the sales video.
items.why: Some of his biggest ads came from putting short engaging videos on top of the VSL.
items.when: producing new ads from an existing footage bank

items.title: When an ad spends, mine it for more hooks
items.text: When an ad is spending well, treat it as proof the script works and cut more hooks from the same video to run as new versions.
items.why: Proven script plus a new environment is spending, so squeeze more from it.
items.when: after an ad starts getting spend

items.title: Recipe for a variation: copy a hook line to the front, add a comment, keep the rest running
items.text: Simple variation recipe: copy a strong line to the front, leave the original video after it so it closes the loop, add a screenshot of a top comment and a headline, and run it.
items.why: Clean, consistent variations that follow the same principles.

items.title: Pick a hook aimed at people with the real problem
items.text: Pick hooks aimed at people with the real problem (e.g. 'I was really struggling with this, see my before and afters') over price-led hooks, so you attract buyers with real need rather than bargain hunters.
items.why: Built for guys dealing with real skin issues, not just want the cheapest thing.

items.title: Combine a hook with a video only if the two make sense together
items.text: Put a pre-extracted hook on a different video only if the hook and clip make sense together; if not, don't do it.
items.why: The point is to make sure what we put together makes sense.

items.title: Extract topics and hooks from a long shoot up front
items.text: After a long shoot (e.g. a podcast), extract all topics and a hook for each up front (one shoot gave 33 topics and 30 hooks) to build a bank of ready combinations. Not every hook will be good; you only need some to stand out.
items.why: It creates a bank of ready combinations.
items.when: processing long-form shoots into short content

items.title: Add a sound effect and a matching picture at the key word
items.text: At the strongest word, add a sound effect and a picture that proves it (e.g. a real before photo) with a quick zoom. People react to the moment; a curse word reacts well but must be bleeped.
items.why: People react to the moment; the picture proves what is said.
items.when: editing key moments in video ads

items.title: Three headline versions per hook; name the file by hook and version
items.text: Write three headline versions (e.g. 'POV:' style) per hook, and name each file by topic, hook number and version (e.g. topic 2 hook 23 version 1). That's how iteration clips get made from what already exists.
items.why: That is how iteration clips are made from what already exists.

items.title: Opening clip always has a headline
items.text: The opening clip of every edit carries a headline, and any clip that works as a scroll stopper on its own becomes its own variation.
items.why: It makes the video stand out.

items.title: Keep edits consistent so you can isolate what worked
items.text: Keep versions consistent (same assets and styles) so only one thing changes; then you can tell why one got more watch time (e.g. with vs without an actor).
items.why: Consistency lets you isolate the variable.

items.title: Use the brand colors we have, not new ones
items.text: Use {brand}'s actual brand colors in captions and graphics, not a new custom colorway, so assets stay accurate.
items.why: So it is at least accurate.
items.when: captions and graphics on brand videos

items.title: Go deep on every video: make every variation, then let the data pick
items.text: Go deep on every video and load every unique variation you spot, even if it feels like too many; more iterations give the best shot at finding what works, and the data picks.
items.why: Once they are loaded he can see what works.
items.when: producing variations from each new video

items.title: Use store credit balance and segment to personalise emails
items.text: If you know a customer's segment, store credit balance and past purchases, send emails showing their exact credit and recommending products to spend it on, using the email platform's profile variables. It gamifies coming back and raises lifetime value.
items.why: Gamify coming back and raise lifetime value.
items.when: retention emails with a store credit program

items.title: Store credit works through Shopify gift cards at checkout
items.text: In {brand}'s setup, store credit runs through gift cards: the customer enters their email, checks their balance, combines several small cashback gift cards into one fresh gift card and enters it at checkout like a discount code.
items.why: A simple way to combine several small credits into one usable value.

items.title: Split multiple speakers on a 9:16 podcast
items.text: With several people on camera in a podcast, split them in the 9:16 version (e.g. top and bottom) so you can cut dynamically between all of them and it feels like a show.
items.why: The last podcast-style content was not dynamic or entertaining.

items.title: Use an AI chat with the transcript to find hooks, topics and funny lines
items.text: Give the transcript to an AI chat and ask for hooks, topics, scroll stoppers and funny moments with timestamps, then start moving things around; you decide the questions. Let the tools do the grinding so the {editor} can focus on assembling and embellishing.
items.why: Let technology do the grinding so the editor can focus on putting it together and embellishing.

items.title: Add culturally relevant embellishments on top of the clips
items.text: Once clips are pulled, the {editor}'s job is to string them together so they make sense, add culturally relevant touches, and distribute fast at the same quality; speed of distribution is what makes the money once research and shooting are done.
items.why: The research, people and studio work is already done; speed of distribution is what prints money.

items.title: A cornerstone video gets maximum intent and detail
items.text: A cornerstone video like the {founder} story lives everywhere (landing page, social feeds, cut down for short-form and stories, brand heritage page, first video in the post-purchase email), so edit it with maximum intent: clean, clear, consistent, with authority.
items.why: It is the basis of the business and the face of the brand.
items.when: the founder or brand story video

items.title: Use the newest footage and update stale content
items.text: Use the newest footage in the drive (current behind-the-scenes, team, customers, before-and-afters) instead of old material, and check for content that hasn't been updated, so the story stays current.
items.why: Updated content makes the story current.

items.title: Learn from the more sophisticated market, then simplify
items.text: Study a more sophisticated market in the same category closely, take its angles and elements, and simplify them for a less exposed market (the example: translating women's skincare angles for men).
items.why: That is how he cracked some of the men's angles.
items.when: finding angles for an under-marketed audience

items.title: Run the short-form batch first; if it gets no spend, put VSLs on the back
items.text: Launch the batch of short leads first; any that don't get spend get a long sales video attached to the back and are rerun. Make new iterations of the sales video every month. Short leads are different enough on the front to share one sales video.
items.why: Short leads are different enough on the front to put onto the same VSL.
items.when: Meta paid social with short leads and a long-form sales video

items.title: Founder stories always work; put storyline in every lead
items.text: {founder} stories always work; when making new leads for the sales video, make sure they carry a storyline so the viewer feels pulled into the world.
items.why: Story hypnotizes people into buying.
items.when: writing leads for long-form sales videos

items.title: Give loyalty discounts as store credit so the product stays full price
items.text: When customers ask for loyalty discounts, give store credit cash back instead of cutting price, so {hero product} stays full price and they earn something for the next order.
items.why: Gives value to loyal customers without discounting.

items.title: Get the second purchase fast, especially with a consumable
items.text: Get the second purchase as fast as possible: prompt customers to use their credit, recommend based on what they bought, and aim to get a consumable bought so they return a third and fourth time. Third-purchase buyers come back and spend a few hundred.
items.why: Third purchase buyers come back and spend a few hundred.

items.title: Read how a tool is being used by customers before scaling it
items.text: Before scaling a retention tool, look at how customers actually used it (e.g. a 10-order VIP using store credit on a new device plus a refill). A few uses without prompting (three in the example) is a signal to promote it.
items.why: Real orders show how it should be pushed.

items.title: Move finished videos out of Editing so the queue stays accurate
items.text: Move finished videos out of the editing column to done right away so the queue only shows live work.
items.why: Keeps things moving clean and clear.

items.title: Test narratives with statics for click-through before filming
items.text: Test new language and storylines quickly with static ads to read CTR, then film the winners. Clickbait-leaning is fine as long as it isn't illegal or false.
items.why: Test narratives faster.

items.title: Weekend shoots should come with clean briefs to roll off
items.text: Have clean briefs ready before every shoot (spend-backed ideas) so you film a good amount from a list; simple formats can hit.
items.why: He films weekends; briefs make the shoot precise.
items.when: planning founder or creator shoot days

items.title: Upload new images to the platform file area and link them in the code
items.text: To add images to a store page, upload them in the commerce platform's files section, copy the link it gives you and put that link into the page code.
items.why: Images are referenced by link in the code.

items.title: Run scroll-stopper variations in threes
items.text: Run creative variations in threes (e.g. three scroll-stopper versions of the same video).
items.why: It is his standard way of testing.
items.when: testing video variations on paid social

items.title: Creator outreach: expect about 5 percent reply, 2-3 weeks to videos
items.text: In {creator} outreach by DM, expect about a 5% reply rate, so send many and follow up with those who confirm; videos take two to three weeks to come back, so start early, and send a set of products so the unboxing shows the range.
items.why: These numbers set expectations for volume and timing.

items.title: Hire the outreach job to someone who already does it, and give them a template and tracker
items.text: Hand creator outreach to someone who already knows the job, with a baseline outreach template and tracking sheet ready, and train them on how to identify the right {creator}s; check their understanding instead of assuming it.
items.why: Process established; a person who knew how to do it was hired cheaply.

items.title: Judge by net profit, not revenue; look at expenses first
items.text: Judge the business by net profit after everyone and everything is paid, not revenue; look at expenses first and cut those that don't make sense. In the example, expenses, not debt, were eating the revenue.
items.why: Expenses, not debt, were eating the revenue.

items.title: Start every edit in the SOP and the creator folders
items.text: {editor}s start every edit in the editing SOP and the {creator} folders, where before-and-afters and core elements are already linked.
items.why: Everything an editor needs is linked there.
items.when: onboarding editors to a footage library

items.title: Avatar workbook: core avatars, sub-avatars, rules and stages
items.text: Run each {brand}'s data through one standard avatar workbook: positioning and brand resonance, core {avatar}s, then sub-avatars with demographics, rules and stages, simple enough that anyone can load it and start. It makes avatar research repeatable across brands.
items.why: It makes avatar research repeatable across brands.

items.title: Use AI design tools to visualize a page, not to code it
items.text: Use AI design tools to visualize page sections and assets from the {avatar} and {offer}, then assemble the sections in Figma; don't rely on them to build the final page, which came out ugly.
items.why: It built an ugly site, but the visuals were close to what he envisioned.
items.when: landing page and asset design with AI tools

items.title: Show the product in use and the result, not product after product
items.text: Don't fill a page with product shot after product shot; show a big bold headline, the product in use, a clear benefit or outcome, what's inside, how to use it, {creator}s talking about it and before-and-afters if possible, and lead with the {offer} and its total value.
items.why: A page of only product shots leaves you with no idea what it will do for you.

items.title: Split a page into layers a developer can change
items.text: For a page that needs fast swaps, separate every element (image, text container, sliders, selector buttons, badge) into stacked layers so headlines and images can change quickly; a flat image doesn't turn into a well-built page.
items.why: Throwing it into Claude does not come out looking like a well designed page.
items.when: handing page designs to developers or AI builders

items.title: Diagnose before you make more: reach problem vs product problem
items.text: Diagnose before making more: decide whether it's a reach problem or a product problem. In one case CPMs were 700+ and the content was fine but not captivating, so the fix was more captivating content ideas grounded in a better understanding of the customer, not changing the product.
items.why: Nothing is fundamentally wrong with the product or brand.
items.when: a brand whose ads aren't scaling

items.title: Make customer identification visible across every asset; social proof carries skincare
items.text: Put the customer (e.g. a generated picture of the sub-{avatar}) in every asset so the page feels alive, since most of it comes down to identifying with the customer. In categories like skincare, leading brands lean hard on social proof, so amplify it.
items.why: Most of it comes down to identifying with the customer.
items.when: pages and ads for identity-driven categories

items.title: Pull scroll-stopper and hook variations straight from the brief
items.text: Have the AI go back into the brief and produce the requested scroll-stopper and hook variations, e.g. three unique scroll stoppers and three unique hooks each tied to customer language; the blend shows which angle opens the conversation with the sub-{avatar}.
items.why: A blend of angles tells you which one opens the conversation with the sub avatar.
items.when: generating hook variations from a brief

items.title: Reject corny headlines that are not customer language
items.text: Throw out corny headlines that aren't customer language and keep the real ones the {avatar} would say; think about what the presenter would actually say to this customer.
items.why: It was corny and not customer language.

items.title: Make the scroll stopper literal: show exactly what the line says
items.text: Make the scroll stopper literal: show exactly what the hook line says, without overcomplicating it.
items.why: Literal visuals connect immediately.

items.title: The whole job is turning people's experiences into something they recognise
items.text: The whole job is resonance: analyze what people say, put it in a format they already consume, visualize the elements, arrange and caption them. Video editing is only arranging.
items.why: Nothing complicated; it is about resonance.

items.title: Layer a clip in steps: base clip, part two, product in hand, rubbing
items.text: Build AI-generated clips in layers: base clip, then a part two with the action, then the product added, then the product-use clip. Each step fixes a missing piece; expect several layers and roughly 30 minutes.
items.why: Each step fixes a missing piece.
items.when: AI video generation of product use

items.title: Research before the brief: Reddit and forum language updated into the customer language skill
items.text: Before a new brief, go deep on Reddit and forum research for the sub-{avatar}, update the customer language bank, then write the brief by breaking down the last winner and amplifying its elements.
items.why: Fresh insight goes into the brief so the ad speaks in the customer's words.
items.when: writing the next brief after a winner

items.title: Do not over-polish an expensive test; ship it to test the angle
items.text: When generation is expensive and you're testing angle, messaging and sub-{avatar}, don't over-polish small detail errors (a slightly off color); ship the assets and note fixes for a later QA pass.
items.why: Generation is expensive; this likely does not matter for the test.

items.title: Pick a format that is already viral in the space
items.text: Pick a format that is already viral in a neighbouring space whose vibe fits {brand} (e.g. natural/holistic wellness), even if {hero product} isn't strictly in that space. The format is proven; you test the angle on top.
items.why: The format is proven; we test the angle on top.

items.title: Look for high-intent organic posts: even likes and comments, clean headline
items.text: Look for high-intent organic posts: aligned with the {avatar}, a clean simple headline, and likes and comments roughly even (e.g. 175 likes, 168 comments). Even engagement says it resonates and shows what the market is already saying.
items.why: High intent means ultra aligned with the avatar; it is what the market is already saying and doing.

items.title: Creative strategy is transforming what people already say into a format they consume
items.text: Creative strategy isn't finding a novel idea; it's taking what the market already says and does and putting it in a medium they consume. Relatable comparisons people already make (e.g. 'finding the right one is like buying jeans') are already the hook; marketers over-engineer.
items.why: A relatable line makes people click and engage even before the video.

items.title: Ask the AI for an objective breakdown only: transcript and scenes, no interpretation
items.text: Ask the AI only for an objective breakdown of a swipe (transcript and scene by scene) and tell it not to analyze or assume; you do the interpretation of why it works.
items.why: That keeps the breakdown objective so you can interpret why it works.

items.title: Do the human learning first, then bring AI in
items.text: Do the human learning first: mark up the transcript yourself (hook, product intro, real experience, the reason people buy) before bringing AI in. Doing it all in one AI shot gives slop; use AI for the menial work, not the parts that make money.
items.why: AI cannot interpret what you are doing; it just puts things together.
items.when: swipe teardowns and brief writing with AI

items.title: Find the real meat of the video, not just the hook and product intro
items.text: Most marketers stop at the hook and product intro; study the part where the person describes actually using the product, because that's the real reason people buy and it reveals the desire.
items.why: It reveals the actual desire.

items.title: Adapt the swipe to what our customer actually says (feel, not look)
items.text: Adapt the swipe to what {brand}'s customers actually say: if the swipe talks about how the product looks but customer research says they care how it feels, swap in their real words so the ad says what they have said.
items.why: Customer research language shows the core desire.
items.when: rewriting a swipe for your brand

items.title: Compare the brand's speak vs the customer's speak to learn sophistication
items.text: Compare how brands talk on the packaging (technical claims and shade names) with how the customer actually talks in reality; the gap shows market sophistication and the customer journey and helps position {hero product} in their life.
items.why: It helps position the product in her life, not just another ad.

items.title: Give the AI two layers of context so it does not return generic
items.text: Give the AI two layers of context so it doesn't return generic output: what the swipe is, and what you want from {brand}'s side (the core desire to drive, the customer language available, the outcome you picture and the angle you saw).
items.why: Direction makes it directionally accurate.

items.title: Name the format by its structure, not just 'UGC yapping'
items.text: Name a format by its structure (e.g. comparison or relatable opener, then product, then real-time experience), not a loose label like 'UGC yapping' or 'AI animation'; structure tells a {creator} exactly what to make.
items.why: High-level labels like 'yapping UGC' or 'AI animation' do not matter; structure does.

items.title: Reframe the hook with customer-sourced comparison, e.g. spa vs my shower
items.text: Rebuild the swipe's comparison hook from what customers say, in natural tone (e.g. 'I used to spend $200 at the spa, now I do it in the shower for under $30'). The hook only opens the conversation, so it must match how the customer talks.
items.why: The hook only opens the conversation, so make it match how the customer talks.

items.title: Write the copy yourself; AI copy comes out robotic and wrong about usage
items.text: Let AI write the baseline script, then rewrite the copy yourself and finally check it against the customer language bank. AI copy comes out robotic and can be wrong about how people actually use {hero product}.
items.why: Writing, visualizing, then typing gives a crystal clear vision; AI versioning is extensive.

items.title: Save and bank everything you see
items.text: Save every interesting post to the swipe bank; a constant library of examples gives you the context to innovate better.
items.why: A mind full of previous context innovates better.

items.title: Winning brands run on volume of real creators, not a single polished ad
items.text: Winning brands run on volume from many real, normal-looking {creator}s acting out formats with insider-style hooks, all the time, not one to three polished ads. Creator communities reverse engineer what resonates and innovate headlines.
items.why: Real creator communities reverse engineer what resonates and innovate headlines.

items.title: The full loop: avatar, breakdown, reverse engineer, brief, test, data, learnings, repeat
items.text: Run one repeatable loop anyone on the team can follow: avatar framework, break down a swipe, reverse engineer, brief, test run, get data, categorize, run creative learnings, back through.
items.why: Anyone on the team can run it; they do not have to think too much.

items.title: Start from what is on the customer's mind, then match the product
items.text: People don't wake up thinking about buying a product; find what's at the back of the {avatar}'s mind (e.g. a tight back after a flight means they want a massage), then match {hero product} to it. Trust comes from understanding what motivates them.
items.why: The goal is trust, which only comes from understanding what motivates them.

items.title: Find cultural relevance by listening to how the group talks (e.g. 'pro-aging')
items.text: Find cultural relevance by listening to how the group talks: if they use a word of their own (e.g. 'pro-aging'), search it on YouTube and TikTok, listen to how they speak about it, and use shared interests to open the conversation.
items.why: If you speak totally different languages you cannot connect; shared interest builds common ground.

items.title: The brand resonance is the core differentiator and should run through everything
items.text: Know {brand}'s resonance, the core differentiator in its market (in one case, an identity shift into a new person), and run it through packaging, headlines, emails and overall vibe; tie copy back to it. It can come from the product's results and from comments after a video goes viral.
items.why: It came from the product (before/afters look like a different person) and from comments after a video went viral.

items.title: Understand brand, then avatar, then write - the avatar sheet informs all copy
items.text: Understand the brand, then the {avatar}, then write: read the core avatar sheet, draft from it with AI, then have the AI check the draft against the customer language bank so the system, not a person, confirms it sounds like the customer.
items.why: Fewer back and forth steps; the system should do the check, not a person.

items.title: Turn winning emails and videos into skills for checking future drafts
items.text: Organize winning {creator} videos and best-performing emails by format and turn each format into a reusable AI skill; then you name the type you're making and check the draft against that skill, without the {founder} in the loop.
items.when: building AI checks from past winners

items.title: Study what the creator already does well before briefing her
items.text: Before briefing a {creator}, download and transcribe their five best videos and watch them repeatedly; build the brief around what they do naturally (e.g. storytelling in their car in work clothes), not a generic product promo.
items.why: She is the one delivering the message, so focus on what she actually does.

items.title: Do not make the same basic product promo everyone else makes
items.text: Don't make the same basic product promo everyone makes (side-by-side or hands-only product posts got no views); use natural formats like an authority figure telling a story, build it around the {creator}'s life, then pitch.
items.why: We saw what happens when we do it like everybody else: no views.

items.title: Read the full picture of the creator's life to build a believable story
items.text: Learn the {creator}'s full picture (region, accent, family, activities, job) and build a story they plausibly live before pitching, instead of starting with the problem. The story only works if it fits who they are.
items.why: The story only works if it fits who she is.

items.title: Weave the story first, then the pitch and the offer
items.text: In creator story briefs, order it: realistic story, discovering the ingredient, refining the formula, then the product pitch and {offer}. You have to build up to 'this is what we sell'.
items.why: You have to build up to saying this is what we sell.

items.title: Look at what competitor brands brief their creators: key points, then run
items.text: Brands with weekly {creator} programs give creators baseline briefs with key points and hooks and let them run in natural formats (e.g. an authority figure in a car telling a story); structure yours the same way.
items.why: They are just taking natural formats.

items.title: Do not promise results the product cannot deliver in before and afters
items.text: Don't promise results {hero product} can't deliver in before-and-afters; tone down extreme ones, show realistic results and use real customer images later. Realistic expectations still help conversion.
items.why: Nobody is trying to scam anybody; realistic expectations still help conversion.

items.title: Before/after results look different on different skin tones
items.text: Before-and-after results look different across skin tones: on pale skin they are rarely dramatic, on skin with more melanin they look more pronounced. Keep that in mind so images show {hero product} realistically.
items.why: Show the product as realistically as possible.

items.title: Chop a raw UGC review at every scene change, then rearrange
items.text: Put a raw UGC review on the timeline, cut at every scene change so each section is separate, delete anything unrelated to the body, then rearrange the pieces into a direct-response order, which likely hits more often than the raw order.
items.why: A rearranged version follows direct response principles and likely hits more often than the raw order.

items.title: Run the creator's original version too
items.text: Also run the {creator}'s original raw version as the first version, as the baseline to compare recuts against.
items.why: It is the baseline to compare the recuts against.

items.title: Pick out small details the creator mentions as future angles
items.text: Note small details a {creator} mentions (their heritage, a first time trying an ingredient); they point to new {avatar}s or hook angles and build a web of concepts for future briefs.
items.why: Little nuggets become bigger concepts.

items.title: 'First time ever' is a strong hook: lines where she has never used the ingredient
items.text: When a {creator} says it's their first time ever using a key ingredient, that's a strong hook ('this might be the first time you've ever used X'); their surprise shows the market hasn't been educated on it.
items.why: A first positive experience with an unfamiliar ingredient is a unique hook.

items.title: Get a clean transcript, lay the sections out in Figma, then decide each piece's job
items.text: Get a clean transcript (some AI tools transcribe better), lay each section out as a block on a board, and mark each one's job: hook, offer-focused, drop, keep as is. Don't rush it; understand the market language.
items.why: Seeing every section lets you reorder deliberately.

items.title: Cut lines that do not serve; move offer or bonus lines to the end
items.text: Cut lines that don't serve (side products, packaging chatter) and move offer-style lines (bonuses, arrival condition) toward the end, where they belong near the close.
items.why: They are offer focused and belong near the close.

items.title: Product-aware UGC: go straight into the product, no problem-solution
items.text: An unboxing review is product-aware content: introduce the product, how it arrived, how it works, the experience, then point to learn more. Don't force a problem-solution structure on it.
items.why: It is more product awareness marketing, which is fine for this asset.

items.title: Cut little gaps so it flows, but keep the natural ending
items.text: Cut small gaps and awkward pauses so UGC moves quickly, but keep the {creator}'s natural closing line so it doesn't feel chopped.
items.why: Little pauses slow it down; a natural ending feels real.

items.title: Get a lot of juice out of one creative by re-watching it
items.text: After the baseline edit, rewatch the creative to find more hooks and interesting language and cut variation after variation; one creative can yield many.
items.why: One creative can yield many.

items.title: Make comment-reply versions to answer objections
items.text: Make comment-reply versions to handle objections: have the AI read the customer research, list objections the video already answers, phrase each as a viewer comment, and add it as a TikTok-style comment reply at the start.
items.why: Seeded creators handle objections naturally; the comment reply calls out the question.

items.title: Hand the mechanical recuts to an editor with a clean editing brief
items.text: When the remaining work is time-consuming mechanical recuts, have the AI write a clean editing brief and hand it to the {editor} instead of doing it yourself.
items.why: It would take too much of his time.

items.title: Curate slideshows that get millions of views repeatedly, then reverse engineer them
items.text: Curate slideshow formats on TikTok that get millions of views consistently, not once, then reverse engineer them with {hero product}. Consistency shows the format truly works.
items.why: Consistency shows the format is truly working.

items.title: Drop in a slideshow link and let the clipper do the work, then check it
items.text: Feed a slideshow link to an automated clipper that downloads it, analyzes the images, writes in {brand}'s product, {offer} and names, and returns a gallery with caption; then a person reviews it for quality.
items.why: It prints many slideshows without thinking about it.

items.title: Do not copy real people's faces; make a new unique look first
items.text: Never replicate real people's faces from a swipe you don't own; first generate a new, unique look from a few of the swipe's people (changed eyes, jaw, hair, etc.) before cloning the format.
items.why: We cannot replicate real people's faces.

items.title: Check the output gallery: story arc, the method, offer, and outdated product mentions
items.text: Check the output gallery for the story arc (problem bad, got worse, got solved, here is the method), then the timeline and {offer}, and remove outdated product mentions no longer being promoted.
items.why: The method is now the main focus rather than the older device.

items.title: The edit tool should answer: what do I put in this edit?
items.text: An edit tool should answer 'what do I put in this edit?': tear down the swipe, rewrite it for {brand}, suggest variations, and show exactly what to make and how to generate it, so the {editor} doesn't hunt for clips or guess caption styles.
items.why: Before, it gave clips you had to search for, and AI/stock choices sometimes made no sense.

items.title: Avoid reusing the same clips over and over
items.text: Don't reuse the same clips over and over, even in a strong edit; use suggestions for new clips or things to generate, or ask a {creator} to make it.
items.why: We reused a lot of clips and do not want to.

items.title: Tell the machine what worked so it learns
items.text: Record which video or scroll-stopper version worked so the system learns what type of content works and suggests what to make next.
items.why: So it can suggest in real time what to make next.
items.when: feeding results back into a creative system

items.title: Any piece of content can be made by AI or a human - break it down and brief either way
items.text: Any piece of content can be made by AI or by a person; break the video down until you fully understand it, then write the brief either way. Understanding matters, not the production method.
items.why: The point is understanding, not the production method.
items.when: deciding how to produce a swipe

items.title: Test several models on the same swipe to find the best clone
items.text: Run the same swipe through several video models side by side and compare each to the original to find the best frame-by-frame clone, while writing it for {brand}.
items.why: To see which model is the best at cloning frame by frame.

items.title: Tools pull from the brand, then the avatar and sub-avatar
items.text: Copy, video and static tools should all read from the same {brand} files, then the chosen {avatar} and sub-avatar (profiles, a language index, verbatims), so keep that data current and filed properly.
items.why: All tools work around the same avatar concept, so data hygiene matters.

items.title: Rebuild a proven video concept for our brand with AI end to end
items.text: Rebuild a proven video concept end to end with AI: keep the swipe's script structure, change the {avatar} and spokesperson, put in {hero product}, and have AI write, storyboard, generate actors, product, set, voiceover and edit. In one case it took about an hour.
items.why: Same exact script, new avatar and spokesperson, in about an hour.
items.when: AI video production from a proven swipe

items.title: Keep a slop bank: what had to be cut and what it cost
items.text: Keep a slop bank: every bad output you had to cut, what you said to fix it, and what it cost. It shows how to prevent slop at the start with a better storyboard and what it's costing.
items.why: Slop keeps coming, so the goal is to shrink it and know the price.

items.title: Know the cost: about 20 dollars vs 200 for a creator, aiming under 10
items.text: Know the cost per AI video: in one case a full draft cost about $20 (about $14 of it image variations) versus $200+ for a UGC {creator}; cut rerolls to push toward $10 or less, cheap enough to run jobs daily in parallel.
items.why: Cheap enough to run jobs concurrently every day.

items.title: Swap one variable at a time: avatar, product, spokesperson, hook
items.text: Keep the AI video chain modular so you can swap one variable at a time (only the {avatar}, only the product, only the spokesperson) or add scroll-stopper and headline-hook variations, each fully edited.
items.why: Scale by customizing the flow.

items.title: Send in accounts and posts that are crushing so the feed updates
items.text: Whenever you see an account or content that's crushing, send it into the research feed so it updates; share the same feeds with clippers for inspiration. Deep research is the input to videos at scale.
items.why: Deep research is the input to making videos at scale.

items.title: Clone organic concepts with AI at scale because it is cheap
items.text: Because AI production is cheap, clone organic concepts at volume: download viral videos, tear them down, reverse engineer into brief and script, recreate with AI. In one week this produced 100 new ads, some already getting sales.
items.why: The cost is very low, so volume is possible.

items.title: Clipping campaign: pay many creators for organic posts instead of buying reach
items.text: Run clipping campaigns: pay a budget to many clippers who post carousels and videos about {brand} daily instead of buying reach. One run produced 629 pieces for about $2,400, impressions at CPMs you can't get elsewhere and volume one person can't match.
items.why: You will not get CPMs like this anywhere else, and one person cannot go viral at that volume.

items.title: Put our product into a hot niche's existing format and funnel traffic to a quiz
items.text: Insert {hero product} into a hot niche's existing format (e.g. a self-improvement carousel), tag {brand}, and send viewers to a quiz funnel with a pixel so you can retarget; you're learning to convert very cold traffic from a format where people actively look for products.
items.why: A consumptive format where people actively look for products to become that guy.
items.when: organic carousels feeding a quiz funnel

items.title: Fix awkward pauses and leftover product pixels in a finished AI video
items.text: In a finished AI video, cut awkward pauses and patch leftover product artifacts (e.g. clone-stamp them out), and fix the cause: keep products out of the casting sheet so they don't get layered into later scenes.
items.why: Automated runs leave small errors; fix the cause for next time.

items.title: Do not put elements like flowers and bottles into the images themselves
items.text: Don't let the picture step put props (flowers, bottles, etc.) into the images themselves; keep those elements for later steps.
items.why: Not wanted in the image at all.
items.when: AI image generation inside a video chain

items.title: Get a real voice reference so the voice is not made up
items.text: Give the voice model a real voice reference or voice print for each character; the more references, the more realistic it sounds, otherwise the model makes something up.
items.why: Without them the model just makes something up.

items.title: Men's brands: attraction and humor beat clinical; skincare brands: add an expert
items.text: Every brand operates differently: for men's brands, attraction is a core angle and funny ads or ones with attractive women outperform clinical ones; for more traditional skincare brands, involve some kind of expert.
items.why: Test of time; every brand operates differently.
items.when: choosing angles by audience and category

items.title: Novel organic content plus a direct-response script that is proven
items.text: Open with novel organic-style content and put the proven direct-response pitch on the back; every {avatar} delivers the same backbone, only the delivery changes to feel like that person.
items.why: The proven pitch stays; the avatar makes it feel natural.
items.when: AI or creator video ads with a proven pitch

items.title: Plant proven scroll stoppers onto different bodies and avatars
items.text: Openings of videos that got millions of views are proven scroll stoppers; plant them onto different bodies delivered by different {avatar}s to get lower-risk variation paths.
items.why: Proven openers reduce risk.

items.title: Make the voice and script sound like the person (a pastor sounds like a pastor)
items.text: Make the script and voice carry the character's nuances (a pastor sounds like a pastor), and generate the voice section by section, then stitch it, to avoid awkward pauses.
items.why: Awkward pauses happen in generation.

items.title: Check lighting and quality against the swipe, and make it a bit fuzzy
items.text: Compare each generated clip to the swipe for lighting, room, angle and picture quality; if it looks too clean, make it fuzzier like the original so it's believable.
items.why: Matching the swipe makes it believable.

items.title: Go deep on one video at a time instead of three at once
items.text: Go deep on one video concept per batch (one hook, many deliverers) instead of three different videos at once; add other hooks after.
items.why: Deep focus on an individual batch works better.

items.title: When a prompt gets a better result, ask for it and add it to the writing tool
items.text: When someone's prompt gets better results (e.g. spicier scripts), get the exact prompt and add it to the shared writing tool so good prompts become shared tools.
items.why: Good prompts become shared tools.

items.title: An automated run will have slop; fix it in the chain so it improves
items.text: Expect a fully automated run to need fixes for a while; fix each problem in the chain's prompts once so the chain handles it next time. It's still cheaper and faster than anything before.
items.why: It is cheaper and faster than anything before.

items.title: Reuse existing assets: finished casting sheets, 3D product, generated elements
items.text: Reuse finished assets across videos (completed casting sheets, a real 3D product image, generated elements) instead of regenerating them; it makes editing much faster.
items.why: This makes the editing process much faster.

items.title: Direct the AI editor by timeline: captions do X, B-roll starts at time Y
items.text: Direct an AI editor from the timeline view: name the exact move (regenerate this clip, change captions, start B-roll at this time) and compare against the swipe alongside. In one case this got the edit about 90% end to end, with final nuances by a person.
items.why: It is about 90% end to end now, with final nuances by him.

items.title: Read the copy out loud: choppy script gets a spoken-word pass
items.text: Read the script out loud; if it's choppy, run it through a spoken-word pass that makes it deliverable (and add personality), then re-read. Choppy copy sounds robotic.
items.why: Choppy copy sounds robotic.

items.title: Rewrite a proven winner script to fit the new vibe
items.text: Start from a proven winner's script, whose message already works, and rewrite it to fit the new {avatar}'s vibe; the pitch that has consistently worked stays.
items.why: The message works; only the voice changes.

items.title: Swipe the right face and voice for AI avatars: slightly odd or already known
items.text: AI avatars that work tend to look slightly odd or like a type everyone culturally recognizes; if the voice is lackluster, find ultra-viral real people of that type on TikTok and swipe from them, since engagement proves them.
items.why: Proven to work, no need to overcomplicate.

items.title: Say 'skin expert', not 'dermatologist', to avoid compliance issues
items.text: Use titles like 'skin expert' instead of 'dermatologist' on screen, for every expert character variant, to avoid compliance issues.
items.why: That way we don't have any compliance issues.

items.title: Do high-intent assets one by one; save bulk for teardowns and analysis
items.text: Make high-intent assets one by one so you can refine them; use bulk runs for mass teardowns, analysis and strategy, then move forward with what's proven.
items.why: Refine first, then scale.

items.title: The AI skips steps you built in - check that it listened to the voice
items.text: Check that the AI actually did every step you built into the process (in one case it approved a voice without listening to it); listen yourself for clipped line ends and echo.
items.why: A straight automated run would catch more; manual runs expose gaps.

items.title: Let the AI make the badge or insert instead of going to Illustrator
items.text: Have the AI make simple graphics like a badge and place the insert on the timeline directly, instead of a round trip through a design app.
items.why: It saves a round trip.

items.title: Do many videos in the same concept at once after the research is done
items.text: Once research, teardown and writing are done for a concept, only fine-tuning remains, so run several videos on the same concept at the same time.
items.why: The work is already done up front.
items.when: AI video production after research is complete
